A skill is a compact representation of procedural knowledge that specifies when a strategy applies and how it should be executed through planning and tool use. One line of work retrieves skills or experience-derived guidance at inference time to improve planning and tool use without updating model parameters [14, 47]. Skill-augmented reinforcement learning extends this paradigm by integrating skill discovery and refinement into policy optimization, allowing the skill library to evolve alongside the policy [13, 39]. Despite this tighter integration, policy updates remain driven primarily by sparse outcome rewards, which provide no direct supervision over intermediate decisions [6, 45].

To address this limitation, rubric-based rewards decompose task success into explicit criteria and use a judge to evaluate a trajectory or its intermediate components against these criteria [11, 15, 32, 41]. By assessing verifiable intermediate objectives, rubrics can distinguish partial progress from complete failure among trajectories with the same unsuccessful outcome, providing more informative supervision than outcome rewards alone. The reliability of this supervision, however, depends critically on rubric quality. Expert-authored rubrics are costly and difficult to scale, whereas automatically generated rubrics rely on the generator to identify appropriate intermediate objectives and evidence requirements, which is particularly difficult for multimodal tool-use trajectories. Consequently, obtaining rubrics that are both scalable and aligned with the agent’s execution procedure remains challenging.

In seeking a principled source for reliable rubrics, we identify an overlooked structural connection to the skills already used to guide agents. A well-structured skill not only tells an agent how to act, but its procedural structure also naturally defines what should be evaluated and how. Specifically, as illustrated in Figure 1, its stages identify intermediate objectives, its quality criteria and expected evidence characterize successful completion, and its common mistakes specify failure conditions. This observation motivates representing each skill through two aligned views of the same procedural strategy: actor-facing guidance that specifies how to act and an evaluator-facing rubric that specifies how successful execution should be assessed. Deriving both views from a shared procedural source aligns task execution and process evaluation by construction.

Based on this insight, we introduce SkillRubric, a framework that unifies skill-guided execution and rubric-based policy learning in multimodal agents. SkillRubric operationalizes this insight

through dual-view skills: actor-facing guidance directs trajectory generation, while an evaluatorfacing rubric derived from the same strategy defines weighted, verifiable intermediate goals. Using screenshots and tool outputs as evidence, a multimodal verifier assesses goal completion and progress and attributes them to the responsible turns, thereby converting skill-derived rubrics into evidence-grounded turn-level rewards. As policy training progresses, residual failures expose deficiencies in both the guidance followed by the agent and the rubric used to evaluate it. SkillRubric therefore introduces an alternating co-evolution scheme that selects guidance revisions through paired rollouts under a frozen policy and validates rubric revisions offline under fixed guidance, enabling both components to improve without conflating changes in agent behavior with changes in the reward specification. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal agent benchmarks demonstrate consistent performance improvements, with further analyses validating evidence-grounded turn attribution, cost-aware multimodal verification, and alternating co-evolution. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• We introduce SkillRubric, which represents each reusable skill through two aligned views: actor-facing guidance for generating trajectories and an evaluator-facing rubric for assessing them. By grounding skill-defined goals in screenshots and tool outputs, SkillRubric turns the same procedural knowledge that guides the agent into evidence-grounded turn-level rewards. • We propose a controlled alternating co-evolution scheme that selects guidance updates through paired rollouts under a frozen policy and rubric updates through offline validation under fixed guidance. This separation allows both components to improve without confounding changes in agent behavior and reward specification. • Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal agent benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in agent performance. Controlled paired rollouts under a frozen policy further demonstrate that evolved skills provide more effective reusable guidance for task planning and tool use than their preceding versions.

## 2. Related Work

Multimodal agents and reusable procedural knowledge. Recent work distills interaction trajectories into reusable skills for planning and tool use. Inference-time methods retrieve textual or multimodal procedures from prior experience, whereas reinforcement-learning methods integrate skill discovery and refinement into policy optimization [3, 13, 14, 18, 39, 42, 47]. These approaches primarily use skills for action generation, leaving their role in reward specification largely unexplored; SkillRubric derives evaluator-facing rubrics from the same procedural knowledge.

Fine-grained supervision for agentic reinforcement learning. Fine-grained agentic supervision has been studied through turn-level advantage estimation, progress-based rewards, and self-distillation. Existing methods estimate local advantages from intermediate rewards or repeated states, derive progress signals from rollout structures or learned potentials, and transfer token-level guidance through privileged-context teachers [6, 20, 30, 33, 34, 38, 45]. These approaches infer local utility without explicit semantic targets, whereas SkillRubric defines verifiable process goals from reusable skills.

Rubric-based rewards and adaptive evaluation. Rubric-based research has advanced along three dimensions: scalable construction, fine-grained attribution, and adaptive evaluation. Existing methods synthesize instance-specific criteria, attribute them to reasoning steps or stages, and adapt rubric generation during policy training [5, 11, 15, 17, 19, 32, 41]. These approaches generally construct rubrics independently of reusable actor skills; SkillRubric derives guidance and evaluation criteria from a shared skill representation and validates their updates separately.

## 3. Methodology

In this section, we present SkillRubric, which pairs actor-facing guidance with an evaluatorfacing rubric to use each skill for both policy guidance and process supervision without exposing evaluator information to the actor. As shown in Figure 2, Stage 1 initializes the policy from successful multi-teacher trajectories and distills all trajectories into a dual-view SkillBank (Section 3.1). Stage 2 uses retrieved guidance for grouped rollouts and rubric verification for outcome-anchored, responsibility-aware process credit (Section 3.2). Stage 3 alternately validates guidance through frozen-policy rollouts and rubrics through delayed offline relabeling after 𝐻policy updates (Section 3.3).

### 3.1. Dual-View SkillBank Construction from Multi-Teacher Trajectories

SkillRubric first distills high-quality skills from multi-teacher trajectories, including both successes and failures. All are used for distillation, while successes additionally warm-start the student via SFT. To handle noise and cross-teacher biases, we apply a two-level hierarchical distillation mechanism, denoted by Mskill: (1) intra-teacher aggregation, which extracts task-specific candidate skills by contrasting successful and failed rollouts per teacher; and (2) cross-teacher consolidation, which merges these candidates into a unified skill set by reconciling outcome-based conflicts, preserving complementarity, and pruning redundancy. This two-tier design reduces both rollout-level noise and teacher-specific bias, yielding more robust skills than single-stage distillation.

Prior work typically represents such procedural knowledge through an applicability description and actor-facing guidance, using it primarily to improve trajectory generation while overlooking its potential for process supervision [14, 39, 47]. We instead represent each distilled skill as

𝑆= (𝑑, 𝑔, C), 𝑑: description, 𝑔: guidance, C : set of rubrics.

More specifically, the description 𝑑identifies the applicability of the skill, the guidance 𝑔provides reusable approaches for policy execution, and the rubrics in C define evaluator-facing criteria for assessing intermediate progress. The paired guidance and rubric are jointly derived by the Mskill from the distilled procedural abstraction: 𝑔summarizes how to execute the procedure, while C translates its critical effects into observable progress criteria. Importantly, to preserve transferability and generalization, Mskill removes task-specific answers and fixed execution paths from 𝑔, and excludes action- or tool-specific requirements from C. For instance, in visual entity identification, rather than instructing the policy to search for a particular candidate or evaluating whether it performs a specific search or zoom action, 𝑔recommends comparing discriminative visual attributes against independent evidence, while C assesses whether the evidence consistently supports the identification.

Besides, tasks with different surface forms often rely on the same underlying procedure, so retaining each task-level skill independently would fragment reusable knowledge and limit its transfer across tasks. To obtain more general skills, Mskill directly merges similar task-level skills according to their applicability, procedural guidance, and evaluation criteria. During merging, it consolidates shared principles, deduplicates overlapping instructions, and removes residual task-specific details. The merged entries form the SkillBank B, where each skill identity links an applicability description 𝑑with its aligned guidance 𝑔and rubric C. All prompt details and examples are provided in Appendices C and D.1.

### 3.2. Skill-Conditioned Policy Optimization with Turn-Level Rubrics

Having constructed the SkillBank B, we now describe how to employ it for skill-guided reinforcement learning on a target task. A skill 𝑆= (𝑑, 𝑔, C) is retrieved by matching its applicability 𝑑to the task description; its guidance 𝑔then conditions policy rollouts, while its rubric C provides turn-level process supervision. The resulting process advantage, combined with a global outcome advantage, forms the final learning signal for policy optimization.

Task-specific Skill Selection. To enable a skill-guided RL method for a target task, the first step is to retrieve the most appropriate skill from the SkillBank B. We accomplish this by computing cosine similarities between the task description and each skill’s applicability description 𝑑in a shared embedding space, and then selecting the skill with the highest similarity. Formally, for a skill 𝑆= (𝑑, 𝑔, C) in the bank and a target task described by 𝑞, the selected skill is given by 𝑆∗= arg max𝑆∈B cos( 𝑓emb(𝑞), 𝑓emb(𝑑)), where 𝑓emb(·) denotes the embedding function that maps textual descriptions into vector representations.

Turn-level Rubric-based Evaluation. The next step is to leverage the rubrics C = {𝑐𝑗} 𝑗=1,...,𝐽 for assigning process credit to the student roll-out trajectories {𝜏𝑖}𝑖=1,...,𝐺, where 𝑖denotes the roll-out index. The student trajectory typically follows a multi-turn structure, where each turn constitutes one trial involving specific tool use. Instead of using standard token-level rewards [4, 40, 44], we propose turn-level rubric evaluation. Under this scheme, the credit assigned to each token within a turn is determined by the outcome of the entire turn. More specifically, since the effectiveness of an action can often only be evaluated from the returned screenshot or tool output, the turn-level score is evaluated based on both the generated response 𝑎𝑡and the resulting observation 𝑜𝑡, where 𝑡indexes the turn. This formulation raises two critical challenges: (1) how should we assign each rubric 𝑐𝑗∈C to its corresponding turn? and (2) since turns are not

### 3.3. Outcome-Grounded Alternating Skill Co-Evolution

The initial SkillBank B is distilled from teacher trajectories, but these demonstrations are static and cannot anticipate the novel strategies or failure modes that emerge as the policy learns. As the student policy improves, its own trajectories begin to reflect its current capabilities, revealing successful patterns absent from the teacher data and recurring pitfalls that the initial skills fail to address [35, 37, 39]. This creates a natural need for the SkillBank to evolve alongside the policy, ensuring that the guidance and rubrics remain aligned with the policy’s ongoing experience rather than fixed to a frozen set of demonstrations.

Yet updating guidance and rubrics together poses a subtle but critical challenge: guidance shapes the trajectories the policy generates, while rubrics determine how those trajectories receive process credit. Changing both at once would make it impossible to attribute an observed improvement or regression to either factor, muddying the causal picture. To preserve interpretability and clean attribution, we therefore alternate their updates. For a skill 𝑆(𝑘) = (𝑑, 𝑔𝑘, C𝑘), we follow the sequence

(𝑑, 𝑔𝑘, C𝑘) −→(𝑑, 𝑔𝑘+1, C𝑘) −→(𝑑, 𝑔𝑘+1, C𝑘+1),

while keeping the applicability 𝑑and the outcome evaluator fixed. This ordering first isolates the effect of guidance on the trajectory distribution, and then adapts the rubric to the new distribution induced by the updated policy.

Concretely, each cycle follows a two-step alternating update procedure for the skills. • Guidance update (𝑔𝑘→𝑔𝑘+1). We begin by comparing the fixed outcome verdict with the current rubric C𝑘on trajectories generated under 𝑔𝑘. Their agreement or disagreement reveals specific deficiencies: joint failure may indicate insufficient guidance; rubric success with outcome failure suggests an over-permissive rubric; outcome success with rubric failure implies an overly strict rubric. Guided by these signals, the synthesizer distills a candidate e𝑔 only when recurring residual patterns support a guidance defect. To evaluate e𝑔, we freeze the policy and compare its performance with 𝑔𝑘under identical rollout conditions. We accept e𝑔 as 𝑔𝑘+1 only if it improves overall outcomes without causing excessive regressions, where a regression means that 𝑔𝑘succeeds but e𝑔fails; otherwise we retain 𝑔𝑘+1 = 𝑔𝑘. • Rubric update (C𝑘→C𝑘+1). After updating the guidance, we train the policy with (𝑔𝑘+1, C𝑘) and collect a fresh set of outcome-labeled trajectories. We then apply both the current rubric C𝑘and the candidate eC offline to these identical trajectories, isolating the effect of the rubric change. We accept eC as C𝑘+1 if it aligns more closely with the fixed outcome verdict without achieving this agreement by uniformly relaxing its criteria; otherwise we retain C𝑘+1 = C𝑘.

Repeating this alternating cycle progressively refines both guidance and supervision, while ensuring that each update remains grounded in final task outcomes. This co-evolutionary design allows the SkillBank to grow with the policy, turning the student’s own experience into a source of continuous improvement rather than a one-time distillation.

## 4. Experiments

### 4.1. Experimental Setup

Datasets. We evaluate our method on eight multimodal agent benchmarks. AgentVista [29], BrowseComp-VL [7], VDR-Bench [46], and VisualToolBench [12] constitute the in-distribution setting. We randomly sample 100 tasks from each benchmark for training and reserve disjoint tasks for evaluation, uniformly sampling 300 tasks from the remaining VDR-Bench pool. VisBrowse-Bench [49], MMSearch-Plus [31], MM-SearchExam [48], and TIR-Bench [16] are used

7


<!-- Page 8 -->


exclusively for out-of-distribution evaluation, with none of their tasks or trajectories included at any stage of training. Detailed dataset statistics and splits are provided in Appendix A.

Implementation Details. We evaluate SkillRubric with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [2] and Qwen3.5- 9B [25]. For each backbone, all RL methods share the same SFT initialization, constructed from success-filtered trajectories generated by GPT-5.5 [23], Claude Opus 4.8 [1], and Gemini 3.1 Pro [10], with three rollouts per teacher for each seed training task. We augment the 400 IID training tasks to 1k training instances through semantics-preserving instruction reformulation while retaining the original multimodal inputs, targets, and evaluation criteria. The initial SkillBank is constructed from the 400 seed tasks, with cross-task skill clustering and merging performed independently within each benchmark before the resulting entries are pooled into a unified SkillBank. This restriction prevents tasks with different objectives and evaluation semantics from being merged into overly generic guidance and rubrics. We train for one epoch with 8 task instances per batch and sample 8 on-policy trajectories for each instance. All agents operate in a unified tool environment comprising zoom, code interpreter, web search, image search, and webpage visit [14]. SkillRubric retrieves the top-1 skill to maintain a unique correspondence between its actor-facing guidance, evaluator-facing rubric, and evolution target. GPT-5-mini [22] serves as the fixed training-time outcome evaluator and coarse-stage rubric matcher, while Gemini 3.5 Flash performs fine-grained multimodal verification. We optimize the policy using a clipped GRPO objective with turn-level advantages and alternate guidance and rubric evolution every 10 optimization steps. During evaluation, we generate one trajectory per test task using fixed decoding parameters under the same system prompt, tool environment, and tool-call limits, and append the top-1 guidance retrieved from the final SkillBank only for our skill-guided variant. DeepSeek-V4-Flash [43] assigns a binary correctness label to each final prediction against the reference answers, with pass@1 computed as the mean correctness across tasks, whereas VisualToolBench reports the mean of its criterion-level judgments. Full experimental settings and implementation details are provided in Appendices B.1–B.5. Baselines. We compare SkillRubric with four representative skill-based methods: XSkill [14], SkillRL [39], Skill-SD [33], and SKILL0 [21]. Since these methods were not originally evaluated on our benchmark suite, we rerun their released implementations using the default hyperparameters reported in the corresponding papers. Detailed adaptations and baseline configurations are provided in Appendix B.6.

### 4.2. Main Results

As shown in Table 1, SkillRubric achieves the best performance among trained methods across all eight benchmarks and both backbones, outperforming the strongest baseline, SkillRL, by 4.76 percentage points on Qwen3-VL-8B and 3.55 percentage points on Qwen3.5-9B on average. These consistent improvements across IID and OOD benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of jointly using actor-facing guidance and evaluator-facing rubrics during policy optimization. The gains cannot be attributed solely to additional guidance at inference, as our policies without skill guidance still outperform all competing training methods on both backbones and every benchmark. This result indicates that skill-conditioned optimization with turn-level rubric supervision enables the policy to internalize reusable planning and tool-use behaviors, while the further improvements obtained by restoring skill guidance demonstrate its complementary benefit. 5. Conclusion Our work introduces SkillRubric, which pairs actor-facing guidance with evaluator-facing rubrics to turn reusable skills into both execution knowledge and evidence-grounded turnlevel supervision. Its alternating co-evolution updates guidance and rubrics against fixed outcomes while isolating their effects. Across eight benchmarks and two backbones, SkillRubric consistently outperforms prior skill-based methods, transfers across model families, and reduces interaction turns, demonstrating that shared procedural knowledge can jointly improve agent behavior and process supervision.

## Appendix

## A. Dataset Details

We evaluate SkillRubric on eight multimodal agent benchmarks under in-distribution (IID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings. Table 5 summarizes the benchmark statistics and data partitions. AgentVista, BrowseComp-VL, VDR-Bench, and VisualToolBench constitute the IID setting. We sample 100 seed training tasks from each benchmark, yielding 400 seed tasks in total. Their teacher-generated trajectories are used for SFT initialization and dual-view SkillBank construction. For reinforcement learning, we augment these seed tasks into 1,000 task instances through semantics-preserving instruction reformulation while retaining the original multimodal inputs, targets, and evaluation criteria. The corresponding evaluation tasks are disjoint from the training split.

VisBrowse-Bench, MMSearch-Plus, MM-SearchExam, and TIR-Bench constitute the OOD setting. None of their tasks or trajectories is used for SFT, SkillBank construction, or reinforcement learning. We evaluate on the complete VisBrowse-Bench, MMSearch-Plus, and MM-SearchExam datasets and sample 200 tasks from TIR-Bench. Benchmark samples not selected for either training or evaluation are not used elsewhere in our experiments. Unless otherwise specified, all sampled partitions are constructed with random seed 42.

AgentVista [29] is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating generalist multimodal agents on realistic visual tasks. It contains 209 expert-curated tasks spanning 25 subdomains and seven broad categories, including commerce, geography, entertainment, technology, society, academics, and culture. Each task is grounded in one or more visual inputs and typically requires longhorizon interaction with tools such as web search, image search, webpage navigation, and code-based image processing. We randomly sample 100 tasks for training and use the remaining 109 tasks for IID evaluation.

BrowseComp-VL [7] extends BrowseComp-style information-seeking tasks to the multimodal setting. It contains 399 tasks across two difficulty levels: 199 Level-1 tasks requiring challenging multi-hop retrieval and reasoning, and 200 Level-2 tasks in which key entities or attributes are further obscured to prevent direct lookup. Solving these tasks requires agents to combine visual perception with persistent web search, evidence aggregation, and multi-step reasoning. We randomly sample 100 tasks for training and use the remaining 299 tasks for IID evaluation.

VDR-Bench [46] evaluates multimodal deep-research systems under realistic visual-retrieval conditions. It contains 2,000 expert-curated visual question-answering tasks designed to reduce shortcuts arising from textual cues, model-internal knowledge, or near-exact image matches. The tasks generally require iterative visual localization, image-region inspection, textual retrieval, and cross-modal evidence integration. We randomly sample 100 tasks for training and uniformly sample 300 disjoint tasks from the remaining pool for IID evaluation. The other 1,600 tasks are not used in our experiments.

VisualToolBench [12] evaluates whether multimodal models can actively manipulate and reason over visual content rather than treating images as static context. It comprises 1,204 open-ended tasks, including 603 single-turn and 601 multi-turn instances across five domains. These tasks involve operations such as cropping, enhancement, transformation, measurement, and programmatic image analysis, often combined with multi-step reasoning. We restrict our experiments to the single-turn subset, randomly sampling 100 tasks for training and a disjoint set of 200 tasks for IID evaluation. The remaining 904 tasks, including all multi-turn instances,

B.2. Training and Optimization

Training data and SFT initialization. We use Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [2] and Qwen3.5-9B [25] as the student backbones. For each of the 400 IID training tasks, GPT-5.5 [23], Claude Opus 4.8 [1], and Gemini 3.1 Pro [10] each generate three trajectories. All successful and failed trajectories are used to construct the initial SkillBank B(0), while approximately 2,000 success-filtered trajectories are retained for SFT.

Both backbones are trained for one epoch using AdamW with a learning rate of 5 × 10−6, weight decay 0.01, a cosine learning-rate schedule, and a warmup ratio of 0.1. We use an effective SFT batch size of 16 and a maximum sequence length of 32,768 tokens. All non-vision parameters are updated, while the visual encoder is frozen. Training is performed in bfloat16. All RL methods using the same backbone are initialized from the corresponding SFT checkpoint.

Skill construction and retrieval. The frozen skill synthesizer Mskill is instantiated with GPT- 5.5 for both initial SkillBank construction and subsequent co-evolution proposals. We use a frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B model as 𝑓emb. Skill applicability descriptions are embedded and cached in advance, and all embeddings are ℓ2-normalized before cosine-similarity retrieval. Given a task, we retrieve the top-1 skill from the current SkillBank B(𝑣), establishing a unique correspondence among its applicability description, actor-facing guidance, evaluator-facing rubric, and co-evolution target.

Policy prompting. All policies use the base system prompt in Prompt B.1 during both training and evaluation. For a skill-guided rollout, the retrieved actor-facing guidance 𝑔𝑗is serialized into structured text and appended directly to the system message under the # Skill Guidance header, following the template in Prompt B.2. A final instruction emphasizes that the guidance is non-prescriptive and may be replaced by any method that reaches the same evidence state. The

Prompt B.1: Shared policy system prompt for training and evaluation

You are a visual reasoning agent. Answer the user’s question using the provided images and the available tools.

Use tools when needed to inspect visual details, perform calculations, or gather relevant evidence. You may call at most one tool in each assistant turn. After a tool returns, inspect its result before deciding on the next action.

Base your answer on the available evidence. When you have sufficient evidence, provide the entire final answer inside exactly one complete <answer>...</answer> block.

Prompt B.2: Actor-Facing Skill Guidance Suffix

{formatted_actor_facing_guidance}

These are suggestions, not mandates. Use another method if it reaches the same evidence state.

Policy rollouts. We optimize each backbone for one epoch over the 1k training tasks. Each rollout batch contains eight tasks, and 𝐺= 8 trajectories are sampled for each task. The eight trajectories generated for one task constitute a GRPO group. Thus, each rollout batch contains eight groups and 64 trajectories in total. During training, trajectories are sampled with temperature 0.7 and top-𝑝= 0.9. Each trajectory contains at most 20 assistant turns, with maximum context and response lengths of 32,768 tokens.

Policy objective. We optimize the policy using clipped GRPO with a learning rate of 3 × 10−6, clipping parameter 𝜀= 0.2, and KL coefficient 𝛽KL = 0.1. Unless otherwise specified, rubric criteria use equal weights 𝑤𝑐= 1. We set the incremental-progress scaling factor to 𝜔= 1 and clip the process advantage to [−𝛿, 𝛿] with 𝛿= 2. All policy-generated tokens within assistant turn 𝑡share 𝐴𝑖,𝑡, whereas screenshots, tool outputs, and other environment-generated content are excluded from the policy loss.

B.3. Outcome and Rubric Evaluation

Outcome evaluation. GPT-5 mini serves as the fixed outcome evaluator during policy training and SkillBank co-evolution. For benchmarks with verifiable reference answers, it assigns a binary correctness score 𝑟out 𝑖 ∈{0, 1} by comparing the final prediction with the acceptable reference answers. For VisualToolBench, it judges each benchmark-provided criterion independently and defines 𝑟out 𝑖 as the mean of these binary judgments. Trajectories without a valid final answer receive zero outcome reward. The training-time outcome evaluator is independent of the retrieved SkillBank rubric C𝑗and remains fixed throughout training and co-evolution. Final benchmark evaluation uses a separate DeepSeek-V4-Flash judge, as detailed in Appendix B.5.

Multimodal rubric verification. We instantiate the coarse-stage selector with GPT-5-mini and the fine-grained multimodal verifier with Gemini 3.5 Flash [9]. At the coarse stage, GPT-5-mini

<!-- Page 20 -->


summarizes each assistant turn using only the evidence available at that point, determines criterion applicability, and identifies candidate turns where the evidence state may have changed. At the fine stage, Gemini 3.5 Flash examines the selected turns, their raw responses and observations, and the relevant preceding evidence. For each applicable criterion 𝑐, it produces a binary satisfaction score 𝑠𝑖,𝑐∈{0, 1} and non-negative responsibility scores 𝛼𝑖,𝑐,𝑡over the selected turns. Criteria judged not applicable or unverifiable are excluded from process-advantage computation.

To estimate incremental progress, the fine verifier classifies the evidence state after each selected turn as missing, hypothesis, supported, verified, or contradicted. We map missing and contradicted to 0, and the remaining states to 0.25, 0.6, and 1, respectively. We then compute Δ𝜑𝑖,𝑐,𝑡from the change in the mapped evidence state introduced by assistant turn 𝑡. Positive, negative, and zero values indicate progress, regression, and no verified change, respectively. The complete prompt templates for the two stages are provided in Prompts B.3 and B.4.

B.6. Baseline Adaptation Details

The baseline methods adopt different skill representations and were not originally evaluated on our benchmark suite. We therefore initialize them from the same actor-facing projection of our initial SkillBank, B(0) actor = {(𝑑𝑗, 𝑔(0) 𝑗 )} 𝑗, while retaining their central mechanisms for skill utilization and policy optimization. This adaptation controls the source of procedural knowledge while preserving the defining differences among the baselines. The paired evaluator-facing rubrics C(0) 𝑗 are withheld from all baselines.

For XSkill [14], B(0) actor initializes its task-level skill stream, while its complementary experience stream is constructed from the same training rollouts using the original visually grounded extraction and consolidation procedure. We retain its task decomposition, experience retrieval, and context-aware skill adaptation, and freeze the resulting external knowledge base during held-out evaluation. SkillRL [39] organizes the actor-facing entries into general and task-specific skills, conditions policy rollouts on the retrieved skills, and updates the policy using outcomebased GRPO. Its SkillBank is expanded or refined from validation failures following the original recursive evolution procedure. Skill-SD [33] uses the actor-facing guidance only to condition its synchronized teacher view, while the student generates rollouts from the plain task prompt. The policy is optimized using its original combination of GRPO and importance-weighted self-distillation, and new trajectories are asynchronously summarized to update the skill bank. SKILL0 [21] organizes the actor-facing guidance into skill files and retains its context-rendering and helpfulness-driven curriculum, which progressively reduces the available skill budget during reinforcement learning until the policy operates without skill context. Both Skill-SD and SKILL0 are evaluated without skill injection, following their original inference protocols.

We retain the method-specific hyperparameters governing these defining mechanisms whenever applicable. For controlled comparison, all policy-training baselines use the same backbonespecific SFT initialization, training tasks, rollout budget, tool environment, and fixed outcome evaluator as SkillRubric. None has access to evaluator-facing rubrics, multimodal verifier feedback, or turn-level process credit.

C.3. Dual-View Guidance–Rubric Construction

The consolidated task-level skill is then transformed into the dual-view representation using the construction prompt in Prompt C.3. The guidance view describes reusable ways to approach the task, whereas the criteria view specifies observable states that indicate task progress. Both views are derived from the same procedural abstraction but remain operationally separated. Guidance may refer to actions and tools, while criteria must be state-based and method-agnostic. This separation prevents the evaluator from rewarding imitation of a particular tool sequence rather than genuine task progress.

The task question and its training annotation are included to preserve the causal relationship between each criterion and the correct task outcome. Explicit no-leakage constraints prevent task-specific answers, entities, and numerical values from being copied into the reusable criteria.

Prompt C.3: Dual-View Guidance–Rubric Construction

You are a Skill Architect for the SkillRubric framework. Your task is to restructure an existing skill document into a strict dual-view representation with GUIDANCE and CRITERIA. The two views must be lexically separated and operationally decoupled while remaining aligned with the same underlying task progress.

## Core Design Principles

### GUIDANCE

The GUIDANCE view is provided to the policy through the agent prompt.

- Purpose: Suggest HOW to approach the task through operational advice. - Nature: Treat all instructions as suggestions rather than mandatory action sequences. The agent MAY use alternative valid methods. - Granularity: Provide three to five high-level stages with concrete action suggestions.

### CRITERIA

The CRITERIA view is visible only to the evaluator and is used to construct the rubric.

- Purpose: Define WHAT observable task-progress states must be achieved. - Nature: Keep every criterion method-agnostic. The same state must receive the same evaluation regardless of the tool or method used. - Granularity: Provide three to five checkpoints with sufficient discriminative power to distinguish successful from failed execution. - Form: Write each Evaluates field as a concise declarative description of an observable task-progress state, rather than as a question or a clause beginning with "whether."

## Critical Constraints

1. **Lexical Isolation:** Guidance-specific tool names and action terms, including zoom, search, crop, code, visit, and OCR, must NEVER appear in the criteria.

2. **Method Agnosticism:** A criterion must receive the same score whether the agent uses zoom and OCR, direct observation, code_interpreter, or any other valid method.

3. **No Answer Leakage:** Criteria must not contain task-specific values, numbers, entities, labels, or answers.

4. **Discriminative Power:** Each criterion must distinguish whether its specific task-progress state has been achieved, independently of whether the final answer is correct.

C.4. Cross-Task Skill Aggregation

The preceding operations produce one structured dual-view skill 𝑆𝑖= (𝑑𝑖, 𝑔𝑖, C𝑖) for each training task. Because tasks with different surface forms may rely on the same underlying procedure, retaining all task-level skills independently would fragment reusable knowledge. We therefore group procedurally similar skills before constructing the initial SkillBank. Clustering and merging are performed independently within each benchmark, and the resulting capabilitylevel skills are subsequently pooled to form the unified SkillBank.

For each task-level skill, the fixed embedding model 𝑓emb separately encodes its applicability description, actor-facing guidance, and evaluator-facing criteria: e𝑑 𝑖= 𝑓emb(𝑑𝑖), e𝑔 𝑖= 𝑓emb(𝑔𝑖), eC 𝑖=

𝑓emb(C𝑖). For two skills 𝑆𝑖and 𝑆𝑗, their multi-view similarity is 𝑠𝑖𝑗= 𝑠𝑑 𝑖𝑗+𝑠𝑔 𝑖𝑗+𝑠C 𝑖𝑗 3 , 𝐷𝑖𝑗= 1 −𝑠𝑖𝑗, where each similarity component is the cosine similarity between the corresponding normalized embeddings.

Using the resulting distance matrix, we perform agglomerative clustering with complete linkage. Initially, each task-level skill forms an independent cluster. At each step, the two clusters with the smallest complete-linkage distance are merged, where the distance between two clusters is the maximum pairwise distance between their members. Merging stops when the smallest remaining cluster distance exceeds the fixed threshold 1 −𝜏cluster. This conservative criterion ensures that all members of a merged cluster have sufficiently similar applicability, procedural guidance, and evaluation criteria, while skills without compatible neighbors remain singleton clusters. The clustering procedure is deterministic and does not invoke an additional language model.

For each resulting cluster, we organize its member skills using a fixed Markdown schema and provide them to Mskill through the cross-task aggregation prompt in Prompt C.4. The synthesizer verifies procedural compatibility, extracts shared principles, preserves supported alternative strategies, removes residual task-specific information, and consolidates overlapping criteria into a compact set of method-agnostic checkpoints. If the source skills do not share a coherent underlying procedure, Mskill rejects the proposed merge and retains them as separate entries. The accepted capability-level skills jointly form the initial SkillBank B(0).

# Understanding the Weight Averaging Mechanism in LLM Training for Post-Training Quantization

**Authors:** Hanzhang Wang Tianqi Shen Zonglin Liu Junze He Difan Zou Ziye Ma ††thanks: Corresponding author. Difan Zou and Ziye Ma supervised this work. Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong The University of Hong Kong Email: hanzwang6-c@my.cityu.edu.hkdzou@cs.hku.hkziyema@cityu.edu.hk

## Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are typically pretrained in high precision but increasingly deployed with low-precision post-training quantization (PTQ). Recent studies have shown that using weight averaging during pretraining can improve PTQ performance compared with learning-rate decay, suggesting that it might provide a simple way to improve the pretraining-to-quantization transition. But the mechanism behind weight averaging remains insufficiently explained. This leads to inconsistent and fragile performance gains, thereby preventing practitioners from applying such a technique confidently. As a response, we formulate weight averaging as a trade-off between retaining training progress and improving robustness under perturbation. We further derive a continuous family of averaging kernels that unifies conventional strategies and achieves the Pareto frontier between the two competing goals. Critically, a theoretical framework for performing weight averaging under PTQ is developed. It can be shown that coarser quantization is more susceptible to perturbations, whereas finer quantization could be less affected. Thus, our results could provide unified theoretical guidance for performing weight averaging under different PTQ conditions. Experiments validate both the predicted behavior and the proposed averaging strategy. Code is available at https://github.com/MOFA-LAB/weight-averaging-for-ptq.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are typically pretrained at relatively high numerical precision (Workshop et al., 2022; Team et al., 2025a; Team et al., 2025b). As model scale continues to grow, post-training quantization (PTQ) has become increasingly important for reducing deployment costs by converting pretrained models to lower precision (Xiao et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025). This mismatch between training and deployment raises a key challenge at the training-to-quantization transition: better performance before quantization does not necessarily translate into better performance afterward (Ouyang et al., 2025; Kumar et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026).

Prior work has shown that training dynamics affect both training performance and sensitivity to quantization (Ahmadian et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026). Late-stage learning-rate (LR) decay can further reduce training loss, but may move the model into sharper regions that are more sensitive (Watts et al., 2026; Microsoft AI Team, 2026; Yano et al., 2026). By contrast, under a stable LR, after completing $T$ training steps, one can retain the last $M$ weights, $\bm{\theta}_{T},\ldots,\bm{\theta}_{T-M+1}$ , where $M$ denotes the number of retained weights. We index them by their age $d\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ , with $d=0$ corresponding to the most recent weight, and average them as

$$ \bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\theta}_{T-d},\qquad w_{d}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}=1, $$

where $\bm{w}=(w_{0},\ldots,w_{M-1})$ is the averaging kernel, with different choices corresponding to different averaging strategies. Recent work shows that such weight averaging can achieve high-precision performance comparable to LR decay while improving PTQ performance (Sanyal et al., 2023; Sandler et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2026). However, existing evidence for the benefits of weight averaging at the pretraining-to-quantization transition remains largely empirical (Ajroldi et al., 2025; Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c), and a theoretical understanding of how the averaging strategy affects PTQ is still lacking. This gap leaves unclear why weight averaging benefits PTQ and when a particular averaging kernel is effective. As a consequence, blindly applying any weight averaging strategy now cannot guarantee improved downstream PTQ performance; and in some cases, it might be even worse. This is exemplified by our discovery that the same averaging strategy could outperform another at higher precision but instead fall behind at lower precision. Specifically, Fig. 1(a) compares linearly weighted WMA with uniformly weighted LAWA on OPT-125M, showing that their performance ranking reverses between 4-bit and 2-bit PTQ. In short, favorable empirical findings may not generalize across settings, and extensive trial-and-error is usually required. This strongly motivates a unified theoretical framework to understand how weight averaging in pretraining affects later quantization, thereby providing principled guidance for averaging strategy selection across settings.

*Figure 1: Overview of our work. (a) Different averaging strategies’ rankings reverse between 4-bit and 2-bit PTQ. (b) Less lag favors better current performance (FP), while less noise favors greater robustness to quantization (2-bit). (c) We formulate weight averaging as a lag–noise trade-off and derive its Pareto frontier, LNWA. (d) Reduced lag can offset additional noise within a finite tolerance interval; beyond it, further noise leads to degradation. (e) The preferred balance reverses with precision, with lower precision favoring less noise and higher precision favoring less lag.*

Building upon prior art, we believe it is useful to evaluate a training trajectory through its genuine progress towards improved model abilities and its robustness to different kinds of noise and perturbations (Morales-Brotons et al., 2024; Block and Zhang, 2025). Specifically, we can decompose each retained weight as $\bm{\theta}_{t}=\bm{\mu}_{t}+\bm{\epsilon}_{t}$ at training step $t$ , where the latent mean state $\bm{\mu}_{t}$ denotes the expectation of $\bm{\theta}_{t}$ across repeated training runs over training randomness, with $\bm{\mu}_{T}$ serving as an idealized noise-free final model, and $\bm{\epsilon}_{t}$ denotes the corresponding zero-mean fluctuation arising from mini-batch sampling, data ordering, and other sources of training randomness. Applying weight averaging in Eq. (1) to the decomposition yields

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T} \displaystyle=-\underbrace{\left(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\mu}_{T-d}\right)}_{\text{temporal lag}}+\underbrace{\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}}_{\text{spatial noise}}. $$

Thus, the deviation of the averaged model from the idealized final model $\bm{\mu}_{T}$ decomposes into temporal lag and spatial noise. Temporal lag captures the genuine progress sacrificed by weight averaging, which can impair the model’s performance at the transition to PTQ. At the same time, weight averaging suppresses spatial noise by reducing the variance of stochastic fluctuations, thereby improving robustness to PTQ, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). The averaging kernel thus determines the balance between these two effects. We then derive Lag–Noise Trade-off Weight Averaging (LNWA), a closed-form kernel family that parameterizes the Pareto frontier of the lag–noise trade-off and includes classical averaging kernels as special cases, as shown in Fig. 1(c).

Building on this formulation, we develop a theoretical framework for weight averaging strategy selection under PTQ. We first study how moving along the lag–noise frontier affects PTQ performance at a fixed precision, quantifying how strongly the temporal lag could be reduced before PTQ performance degrades (Fig. 1(d)). Within this tolerance region, we then vary the quantization precision and show that lower precision favors less spatial noise, whereas higher precision favors less temporal lag (Fig. 1(e)); we further characterize the quantization precision threshold at which this preference reverses. Together, we extend conventional method-specific weight averaging selection into a unified theoretical framework under different PTQ conditions. Finally, experiments on LLMs from 125M to 1.3B parameters validate our theory. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- 1. We establish a theoretical framework for understanding weight averaging through a two-way decomposition in Eq. (2). Specifically, we separate its effects into temporal lag, which captures inherent training progress, and spatial noise, which captures the solution’s robustness to perturbations. We show that these two objectives are in competitive tension, and a careful trade-off is necessary.

- 2. A new class of weight averaging strategies called LNWA is proposed based on the aforementioned framework. It operates on the Pareto frontier between temporal lag and spatial noise (Theorem 4.1) and smoothly interpolates between them. This class generalizes existing strategies (see Table 1) and can achieve any desired Pareto-optimal trade-off between the two objectives.

- 3. We further provide a theoretical analysis of how the lag–noise balance affects PTQ performance (Sections 4.2 and 4.3). We show that this balance depends critically on quantization precision (Theorems 4.2 and 4.3) and therefore should not be selected universally. These results provide principled guidance for performing weight averaging across PTQ settings.

## 2 Related Work

Learning-rate decay. Late-stage LR decay is widely used in LLM pretraining to further improve final performance (Hu et al., 2024; Hägele et al., 2024). Prior work has mainly focused on understanding why LR decay benefits pretraining (Wen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026). However, recent studies show that LR decay can also affect how well the resulting model transfers to subsequent stages (Chen et al., 2026). Similar effects have been observed across various downstream tasks (Wang et al., 2025; Yano et al., 2026; Microsoft AI Team, 2026; Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026), suggesting that lower final pretraining loss does not necessarily imply a better transition to downstream adaptation.

Post-training quantization. PTQ converts a model to lower precision, reducing storage and inference costs (Chee et al., 2023). Various PTQ methods have been proposed (Nagel et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2024; Ashkboos et al., 2024; Dettmers et al., 2022; Egiazarian et al., 2024), and error compensation is one of the most well-established approaches (Yao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), with GPTQ as a widely used representative (Frantar et al., 2022). GPTQ reduces layerwise reconstruction error through second-order updates to the remaining unquantized weights (Frantar et al., 2022). Recent work has further improved PTQ through a range of transformation, clipping, and reconstruction techniques (Liu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024; Tseng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).

Weight averaging. Classical Polyak–Ruppert averaging established the variance-reduction benefit of averaging iterates (Polyak and Juditsky, 1992). Motivated by it, stochastic weight averaging (SWA) showed that averaging weights along the training trajectory can lead to wider optima and better generalization (Izmailov et al., 2018). Moreover, LAWA (Sanyal et al., 2023) uniformly averages recent weights sparsely, while EMA (Morales-Brotons et al., 2024) and WMA (Li et al., 2026c) assign larger coefficients to more recent weights through exponential and linear weighting, respectively. Recent work has applied LAWA to the pretraining-to-quantization transition, showing that the averaged models can match or outperform LR decay after PTQ (Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026).

## 3 Preliminaries

#### Notation.

Scalars are denoted by italic letters (e.g., $f$ ), vectors by bold lowercase letters (e.g., $\bm{f}$ ), matrices by bold uppercase letters (e.g., $\bm{F}$ ), and sets by calligraphic uppercase letters (e.g., $\mathcal{F}$ ).

Consider a fixed window of retained model weights $\bm{\theta}_{T},\ldots,\bm{\theta}_{T-M+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{P}$ ( $M\geq 2$ ), where $T$ is the training steps, $P$ is the number of parameters and age $d$ counts backward from the newest retained weight at $d=0$ . Let $\bm{w}=(w_{0},\ldots,w_{M-1})$ denote the averaging kernel, where $w_{d}$ is the averaging coefficient assigned to the weight $\bm{\theta}_{T-d}$ . Its feasible set $\mathcal{W}_{M}$ and the resulting averaged model $\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}$ are defined as

$$ \mathcal{W}_{M}=\left\{\bm{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}:w_{d}\geq 0,\ \sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}=1\right\},\qquad\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\theta}_{T-d}. $$

Thus $\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}$ lies in the convex hull of the retained weights. We first define the latent mean $\bm{\mu}_{t}$ , which provides an idealized noise-free reference to separate training progress from spatial noise.

#### Definition 3.1 (Latent-mean Trajectory).

Let $\mathcal{F}_{0}$ be the sigma-field generated by the information shared across stochastic training runs, such as the model configuration, common initialization, and training setup. Let $\xi$ index the run-specific stochasticity, such as data ordering and dropout. For the aligned state $\bm{\theta}_{T-d}(\xi)$ , assume $\mathbb{E}[\|\bm{\theta}_{T-d}(\xi)\|_{2}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}]<\infty$ . The conditional mean state $\bm{\mu}_{t}$ and the zero-mean spatial noise $\bm{\epsilon}_{t}$ at the training step $t$ of an individual run are

$$ \bm{\mu}_{t}:=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\bm{\theta}_{t}(\xi)\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}],\qquad\bm{\epsilon}_{t}(\xi):=\bm{\theta}_{t}(\xi)-\bm{\mu}_{t}. $$

For an averaging kernel $\bm{w}$ , write $\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}:=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\mu}_{T-d}$ for the mean of $\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}$ , and write $\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}:=\sum_{d}w_{d}\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}$ for the averaged spatial noise.

Besides, we model how PTQ reduces the reconstruction error. Let $\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}$ denote the parameter of output channel $i$ in layer $\ell$ , extracted from $\bm{\theta}$ . Quantization changes $\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)}$ by $\Delta\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)}$ , so the output error is $\bigl(\Delta\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)}\bigr)^{\top}\bm{X}$ for input activations $\bm{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}\times n}$ . Its mean squared reconstruction error is

$$ \frac{1}{n}\|\bigl(\Delta\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)}\bigr)^{\top}\bm{X}\|_{2}^{2}=\bigl(\Delta\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)}\bigr)^{\top}\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)}\Delta\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)}=\|\Delta\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)}\|_{\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)}}^{2}, $$

where $\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)}:=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}/n$ . GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) reduces errors by adjusting parameters that remain unquantized. We represent this procedure with two parameter groups: quantize the first group, use the second group to reduce the resulting output error, and then quantize the second group. For a parameter vector $\bm{z}$ , $\operatorname{quant}_{b}(\bm{z})$ denotes scale-and-zero-point quantization at precision $b$ using $\operatorname{round}$ .

#### Definition 3.2 (Simplified GPTQ Model).

Partition $\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)}$ into $\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}^{(\ell,i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{f}}}$ and $\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{r}}^{(\ell,i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{r}}}$ , where $d_{\mathrm{f}}+d_{\mathrm{r}}=d_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $d_{\mathrm{f}},d_{\mathrm{r}}\geq 1$ . Let $\bm{X}_{\mathrm{f}},\bm{X}_{\mathrm{r}}$ be the corresponding row blocks of $\bm{X}$ , and partition $\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)}$ accordingly. First quantize $\bm{q}_{\mathrm{f}}^{(\ell,i)}=\operatorname{quant}_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}^{(\ell,i)})$ , with quantization error $\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{(\ell,i)}:=\bm{q}_{\mathrm{f}}^{(\ell,i)}-\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}^{(\ell,i)}$ . Then use the remaining group to minimize the reconstruction error caused by $\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{(\ell,i)}$ :

$$ \bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{(\ell,i),\star}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{r}}}}\frac{1}{n}\left\|\bigl(\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{(\ell,i)}\bigr)^{\top}\bm{X}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{X}_{\mathrm{r}}\right\|_{2}^{2}. $$

Then quantize the corrected remaining group:

$$ \bm{q}_{\mathrm{r}}^{(\ell,i)}=\operatorname{quant}_{b}\!\left(\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{r}}^{(\ell,i)}+\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{(\ell,i),\star}\right). $$

The quantized $\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)}$ is $\bm{q}^{(\ell,i)}=((\bm{q}_{\mathrm{f}}^{(\ell,i)})^{\top},(\bm{q}_{\mathrm{r}}^{(\ell,i)})^{\top})^{\top}$ . At precision $b$ , applying these steps to every output channel of every linear layer gives the full-model simplified GPTQ $Q_{b}(\bm{\theta})$ (see Appendix A.5).

*Figure 2: Illustrative visualizations with a two-layer MLP on MNIST. (a) SGD training trajectories with different data orders and their estimated latent mean. (b) Weight averaging reduces spatial noise but introduces temporal lag compared with the stable training endpoint. (c) LNWA characterizes the Pareto frontier between temporal lag and spatial noise. Colors indicate validation loss.*

## 4 Lag–Noise Trade-off

In this section, we formulate weight averaging as a trade-off between temporal lag and spatial noise and derive its Pareto frontier (Section 4.1). We then connect lag and noise to PTQ and further characterize the tolerance-to-degradation transition at a fixed precision (Section 4.2) and the precision-dependent shift in the preferred lag–noise balance (Section 4.3).

### 4.1 Lag–noise decomposition and the LNWA frontier

Using the latent-mean trajectory in Definition 3.1, a retained weight can be written as $\bm{\theta}_{T-d}=\bm{\mu}_{T-d}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}$ . As illustrated in Fig. 2(a), across different data orders, the individual training trajectories fluctuate around a shared latent-mean trajectory. The latent mean captures the progress that is shared across runs, while the difference between an individual trajectory and the latent mean captures the fluctuation caused by run-specific randomness. Weight averaging therefore acts on both components. Let $\bm{v}_{t}:=\bm{\mu}_{t}-\bm{\mu}_{t-1},\quad T-M+2\leq t\leq T,$ denote the latent progress between adjacent retained weights. To quantify the effects of temporal lag and spatial noise in Eq. (2), define

$$ m(\bm{w}):=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}dw_{d},\qquad R(\bm{w}):=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}^{2}. $$

Here, $m(\bm{w})$ is the mean age of the averaged weights, which measures temporal lag; $R(\bm{w})$ is the squared $\ell_{2}$ norm of the averaging kernel, which determines the amount of spatial-noise variance retained after averaging. Lemma A.2 then gives

$$ \bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}=-m(\bm{w})\bm{v}_{T}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}+\bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}}, $$

where $\bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}}$ is a bounded trajectory remainder, and $\mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0})=R(\bm{w})\bm{\Sigma}.$ Fig. 2(b) visualizes how averaging acts on spatial noise and temporal lag. Weight averaging reduces the fluctuation across training runs (spatial noise), while shifting the averaged latent mean $\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}$ away from the latest latent mean $\bm{\mu}_{T}$ along the direction of genuine progress (temporal lag). These two effects therefore form a fundamental trade-off in weight averaging. We formalize this trade-off by minimizing retained spatial noise under a fixed temporal-lag budget (Lemma A.3). As the budget varies, the resulting solutions trace the lag–noise Pareto frontier. Thus, we can parameterize it with a one-parameter family of averaging kernels termed Lag–Noise Trade-off Weight Averaging (LNWA).

#### Theorem 4.1 (LNWA Kernel).

For $0\leq\lambda<\infty$ , let

$$ \bm{w}_{\lambda}:=\arg\min_{\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}}\left\{R(\bm{w})+\lambda m(\bm{w})^{2}\right\}. $$

For each finite $\lambda$ , the unique minimizer has an active prefix $S_{q}=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$ with $2\leq q\leq M$ , and its coefficients are

$$ (\bm{w}_{\lambda})_{d}=\begin{cases}q^{-1}+\lambda m_{q}(\lambda)(\bar{d}_{q}-d),&0\leq d<q,\\
0,&q\leq d<M,\end{cases} $$

where $m_{q}(\lambda)=\bar{d}_{q}/(1+\lambda D_{q})$ , $\bar{d}_{q}=(q-1)/2$ , and $D_{q}=q(q^{2}-1)/12$ . Define $\bm{w}_{\infty}:=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\bm{w}_{\lambda}=\bm{e}_{0}=(1,0,\ldots,0)^{\top}$ , the Stable endpoint. The extended family $\{\bm{w}_{\lambda}\}_{0\leq\lambda\leq\infty}$ parameterizes the complete Pareto frontier between temporal lag and spatial noise.

*Table 1: Relation between classical averaging kernels and LNWA. LAWA and Stable are the two endpoints, and WMA is an exact interior point. EMA is exact when $M=2$ . For $M>2$ , $\lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}$ gives a local approximation with error $\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2}M)$ , where $\eta=-\log\beta$ .*

| Stable | $\displaystyle\bm{e}_{0}=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ | $0$ | $1$ | $\checkmark$ |

In particular, for $0\leq\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}\leq\infty$ ,

$$ m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})>m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}}),\qquad R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})<R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}}). $$

Thus, increasing $\lambda$ moves the averaging kernel along the frontier toward larger spatial noise, while decreasing $\lambda$ moves it toward larger temporal lag. Lemma A.4 characterizes how the number of retained weights assigned nonzero averaging coefficients changes with $\lambda$ , while Lemma A.5 gives explicit formulas for the corresponding temporal lag and spatial noise. Fig. 2(c) visualizes the feasible lag–noise region induced by different averaging kernels, where LNWA traces its Pareto boundary. The distribution of validation loss across this region shows that the optimal averaging strategy depends on how these two factors are balanced. Several classical averaging kernels can also be viewed as special cases of the LNWA family: LAWA and Stable form its two endpoints (Proposition A.1); WMA is an exact interior kernel (Proposition A.2); and EMA admits an exact representation for $M=2$ and a local approximation for $M>2$ (Proposition A.4). Table 1 summarizes the lag–noise coordinates of these classical kernels.

### 4.2 Noise tolerance and quantitative degradation

As discussed above, increasing $\lambda$ along the LNWA frontier reduces temporal lag while increasing spatial noise. In this section, we quantify how much lag reduction can compensate for the accompanying increase in noise and thereby improve PTQ performance at a fixed precision.

We measure the effect of an averaging kernel by the expected output reconstruction error (defined in Eq. (5)) of the quantized model (defined in Definition 3.2) relative to the latest noise-free state $\bm{\mu}_{T}$ :

$$ \mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}):=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bigl\|Q_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}})-\bm{\mu}_{T}\bigr\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}\right]=\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w})+\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}(\bm{w}). $$

Here $\mathcal{P}_{0}$ is the error before quantization, $\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}$ is the reconstruction error introduced by quantization, and $\gamma_{b}$ is a precision-dependent coefficient. Lemma A.9 proves this decomposition. Next, we need to show that both $\mathcal{P}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ depend on temporal lag and spatial noise. Before quantization, these two effects are readily separated:

$$ \mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w}):=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}\right]=\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}+N_{G}R(\bm{w}),\qquad N_{G}:=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{G}). $$

The first term measures the error associated with temporal lag, while the second is proportional to the spatial-noise variance retained by the averaging kernel. However, the contributions of temporal lag and spatial noise are less direct after quantization. To make these contributions explicit, we decompose the quantization error change into separate terms and evaluate their expected contributions using Lemma A.8. This yields the quantization term in Lemma A.9, which depends on spatial noise and indirectly on temporal lag through the averaged latent mean:

$$ \mathcal{Q}(\bm{w})=\|\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\|_{2}^{2}+P\sigma^{2}R(\bm{w}),\qquad\gamma_{b}=\frac{c_{G}}{(2^{b}-1)^{2}}, $$

where $c_{G}>0$ collects the constants associated with the simplified GPTQ model. Thus, we can analyze how the total reconstruction error $\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w})$ changes along the LNWA frontier as temporal lag is reduced and more spatial noise is retained. Let $m_{0}:=(M-1)/2$ be the mean age of LAWA, and set $x:=1-m(\bm{w}_{\lambda})/m_{0}\in[0,1]$ to measure the fraction of this age removed. Thus $x=0$ gives LAWA, while $x=1$ selects only the most recent saved weight, corresponding to $\lambda=\infty$ . Thus, increasing $x$ reduces temporal lag and retains more spatial noise. Each $x$ specifies a frontier kernel $\bm{w}_{\lambda}$ ; we write its averaged latent mean and retained noise factor as $\bm{\mu}(x):=\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}_{\lambda}}$ and $R(x):=R(\bm{w}_{\lambda})$ . To identify the tolerance region, we compare $\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)$ with its value at LAWA, $\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)$ . We first examine the error on a fixed-support segment, where the frontier formulas in Lemma A.5 show that the averaged latent mean is affine in $x$ and $R(x)$ is quadratic. For $q\geq 2$ active weights, differentiating the reconstruction error gives

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}x^{2}}\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)=m_{0}^{2}\left[\bm{a}_{q}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{a}_{q}+2\gamma_{b}\|\bm{a}_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{2N_{G}+2\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2}}{D_{q}}\right]>0, $$

where $\bm{a}_{q}:=m_{0}^{-1}\mathrm{d}\bm{\mu}(x)/\mathrm{d}x$ is constant on the segment and $D_{q}:=q(q^{2}-1)/12$ . The positive curvature increases the error slope within each fixed-support segment. Although the slope may jump at support boundaries, Lemma A.10 controls these jumps. The comparison with the starting error $\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)$ therefore depends on their cumulative effect along $[0,x]$ . To track the sign of this comparison, we normalize the error difference by $x$ :

$$ F_{b}(x):=\frac{\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)}{x},\qquad x>0,\qquad F_{b}(0):=\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0^{+}). $$

For $x>0$ , $F_{b}(x)$ has the same sign as $\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)$ . Its derivative accounts for the curvature accumulated over $[0,x]$ and the slope jumps at boundaries crossed along the way. Lemma A.11 shows that, for sufficiently large $T$ , the positive curvature dominates any adverse cumulative contribution from these jumps. Eq. (69) therefore gives constants $0<k_{b}\leq K_{b}$ such that

$$ \frac{k_{b}}{2}\leq F_{b}^{\prime}(x)\leq\frac{K_{b}}{2}. $$

Since $F_{b}$ is continuous, the positive lower bound makes it strictly increasing over the entire frontier. Lemma A.11 also gives $F_{b}(1)=\mathcal{E}_{b}(1)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)>0$ . Integrating the derivative bounds gives the quantitative comparison in the following theorem.

#### Theorem 4.2 (Finite Noise Tolerance and Degradation).

Under Assumptions A.3–A.7, for all sufficiently large $T$ and every evaluated precision $b\geq 2$ , there exist constants $0<k_{b}\leq K_{b}$ and a unique threshold $\tau_{b}\in[0,1)$ . With $\ell=(M-1)/T$ , $g=\|\bm{G}\|_{2}$ , and $A_{*}=\|\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}+V\ell$ , where $V$ is the increment bound in Assumption A.6, the threshold satisfies

$$ 0\leq\tau_{b}\leq\frac{D_{M}V}{m_{0}T}\left(\frac{gV\ell}{N_{G}}+\frac{2A_{*}}{P\sigma^{2}}\right). $$

(i) Tolerance: for $0<x\leq\tau_{b}$ ,

$$ -\frac{K_{b}}{2}x(\tau_{b}-x)\leq\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)\leq-\frac{k_{b}}{2}x(\tau_{b}-x), $$

(ii) Degradation: for $\tau_{b}<x\leq 1$ ,

$$ \mathcal{E}_{b}(x)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)\geq\frac{k_{b}}{2}x(x-\tau_{b})>0. $$

Theorem 4.2 characterizes noise tolerance and degradation at a fixed precision. When $\tau_{b}>0$ , the recovery of recent progress compensates for the additional spatial noise and quantization error over $0<x<\tau_{b}$ ; beyond $\tau_{b}$ , the reconstruction error exceeds its value at $x=0$ and increases strictly. If $\tau_{b}=0$ , any positive movement causes degradation. This is because the model may be unable to tolerate any additional spatial noise at sufficiently low precision. The remaining question is: at what precision does the $\tau_{b}=0$ regime arise and favor less spatial noise?

### 4.3 Precision determines the preferred balance

By Eqs. (11) and (13), lower precision increases the weight on the quantization term $\mathcal{Q}$ . Lemma A.12 shows that the retained latent-mean norm cannot decrease as $x$ increases. The retained noise factor also increases, so on every open support segment,

$$ \mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(x)=2\bm{\mu}(x)^{\top}\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(x)+P\sigma^{2}R^{\prime}(x)>0,\qquad x>0. $$

Thus, $\mathcal{Q}$ increases as the kernel shifts toward more recent weights. Lemma A.13 gives $\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0^{+})<0$ , so $\mathcal{P}_{0}$ initially decreases. As precision varies, whether this decrease offsets the increase in $\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}$ determines which tolerance regime in Theorem 4.2 applies: $\tau_{b}>0$ when $\mathcal{E}_{b}$ initially decreases, and $\tau_{b}=0$ otherwise. To characterize where this change occurs, Lemma A.14 places the unquantized and evaluated-precision optima in the first support segment. Write $\bar{\bm{\mu}}=\bm{\mu}(0)$ and $\bm{u}=\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(0^{+})=m_{0}\bm{a}_{M}$ . On this segment, both error components are quadratic:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{0}(x)-\mathcal{P}_{0}(0)=\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0^{+})x+\frac{\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})}{2}x^{2},\quad\mathcal{Q}(x)-\mathcal{Q}(0)=\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(0^{+})x+\frac{\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})}{2}x^{2}. $$

Appendix A.6 gives $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(0^{+})\geq 0$ , $a:=\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})>0$ , and $c:=\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})>0$ . The unquantized optimum and the optimum at precision $b$ are

$$ x_{0}=\frac{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})}{a}, $$

and

$$ x_{b}=\max\left\{0,\frac{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})-2\gamma_{b}\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}}{a+c\gamma_{b}}\right\}\in[0,x_{0}). $$

Eq. (22) shows that quantization can make $x_{b}=0$ , corresponding to $\tau_{b}=0$ in Theorem 4.2. Lemma A.14 establishes that this $x_{b}$ is the global optimum across all support segments, so we can quantify the precision threshold in the next theorem.

#### Theorem 4.3 (Precision Threshold for Lag–Noise Preference).

Under Assumptions A.3–A.10, for sufficiently large $T$ , define the precision threshold

$$ b_{\mathrm{crit}}:=\log_{2}\!\left(1+\sqrt{\frac{2c_{G}\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}}{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})}}\right). $$

For every evaluated precision $b\geq b_{\min}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle b\leq b_{\mathrm{crit}} \displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad x_{b}=0,\quad\tau_{b}=0\qquad\text{{(less spatial noise)}}, \displaystyle b>b_{\mathrm{crit}} \displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad x_{b}>0,\quad\tau_{b}>0\qquad\text{{(less temporal lag)}}. $$

Moreover, $x_{b}$ is nondecreasing in $b$ and strictly increasing whenever $b>b_{\mathrm{crit}}$ . If $b_{\mathrm{crit}}<b_{\min}$ , all evaluated precisions lie in the second regime.

Theorem 4.3 answers the question left at the end of Section 4.2: $b_{\mathrm{crit}}$ marks where zero tolerance gives way to a positive tolerance interval. This threshold characterizes the reversal in the preferred lag–noise balance, from denoising at lower precision to reducing temporal lag at higher precision.

## 5 Experiments

Experimental setup. We pretrain OPT-series models (125M, 350M, and 1.3B) (Zhang et al., 2022) from scratch on FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024) with AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017). Following prior work (Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026), we save 10 weights at 500-step intervals near the end of training and average them. We then apply GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) at 4, 3, and 2 bits (denoted by W4, W3, W2) using the same C4 calibration set (Raffel et al., 2020), then evaluate the PTQ performance by perplexity (PPL; lower is better) on a held-out RefinedWeb set (Penedo et al., 2023). Complete settings and results are in Appendix C.

From noise tolerance to degradation. We evaluate LNWA across coefficients ranging from $\lambda=0$ (LAWA) to $\lambda=1$ . We report the performance change $\Delta\mathrm{NLL}(\lambda)$ relative to LAWA, where $\Delta\mathrm{NLL}(\lambda)=\mathrm{NLL}(\lambda)-\mathrm{NLL}(0)=\log\frac{\mathrm{PPL}(\lambda)}{\mathrm{PPL}(0)}$ , and negative values indicate an improvement.

*Figure 3: Comparison of $\Delta$ NLL across LNWA coefficients for OPT-125M under GPTQ and AWQ at 4-bit (W4) and 2-bit (W2).*

Figure 3 shows that NLL can fall below the LAWA baseline at small $\lambda$ , then rises above it at larger $\lambda$ . This indicates that the benefit of reducing temporal lag can offset or outweigh the cost of retaining additional spatial noise. Moving further along the frontier retains more noise and leads to performance degradation, consistent with the tolerance-to-degradation pattern characterized in Theorem 4.2.

Precision changes the preferred lag-noise balance. We compare LAWA, WMA, and LNWA in the small- $\lambda$ range by fitting PPL against the LNWA-equivalent averaging coefficient. Kernel choices and regression details are given in Appendix C.1.

*Figure 4: Comparison of PPL across LNWA-equivalent averaging coefficients for OPT-125M under GPTQ and AWQ at 4-bit (W4) and 2-bit (W2).*

Figure 4 shows a positive correlation between PPL and the averaging coefficient at W2 and a negative correlation at W4. Smaller coefficients retain less spatial noise, whereas larger coefficients reduce temporal lag. These correlations therefore indicate that lower precision favors less noise and higher precision favors less lag, supporting a precision-dependent reversal in preference in Theorem 4.3.

Comparison with learning-rate decay. We finally compare LNWA with two LR decay schedules on OPT-1.3B. As shown in Figure 5, LNWA achieves lower average PPL (Avg.) than both decay schedules under GPTQ and AWQ, with the largest improvement at W2. These results support weight averaging as an effective strategy for the pretraining-to-quantization handoff.

*Figure 5: Comparison of PPL between LR decay, Stable LR, and LNWA for OPT-1.3B under GPTQ and AWQ at 4-bit (W4), 3-bit (W3), 2-bit (W2), and their average.*

## 6 Conclusion

We developed a theoretical framework for weight averaging at the pretraining-to-quantization transition. Averaging suppresses spatial noise but introduces temporal lag by sacrificing recent optimization progress. We quantify this trade-off and derive LNWA, a closed-form family of averaging kernels that parameterizes its Pareto frontier. Through a simplified GPTQ model, we connect this trade-off to output reconstruction error and establish two main results. At a fixed precision, reduced lag can compensate for additional noise within a finite tolerance interval; beyond it, the error increases. Within this interval, we further show that lower precision favors less spatial noise, whereas higher precision favors less temporal lag. Experiments on LLMs support both results.

## Appendix A Theoretical Proofs

This section presents the detailed proofs of all theoretical results in Section 4.

### A.1 Setup

#### Definition A.1 (Finite Convex Weight Averaging).

Let $\bm{\theta}_{T},\bm{\theta}_{T-1},\ldots,\bm{\theta}_{T-M+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{P}$ be a window of $M\geq 2$ retained model weights. Age $d=0$ denotes the newest weights; $T$ denotes the training steps. Define

$$ \mathcal{W}_{M}=\left\{\bm{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}:w_{d}\geq 0,\ \sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}=1\right\},\qquad\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\theta}_{T-d}. $$

Here, $\mathcal{W}_{M}$ is the set of feasible averaging kernels, $\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}$ is an averaging kernel, and $\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}$ lies in the finite convex hull of the retained weights.

#### Definition A.2 (Latent-mean Trajectory).

Let $\mathcal{F}_{0}$ be the sigma-field generated by the information shared across stochastic training runs, such as the model configuration, common initialization, and training setup. Let $\xi$ index the run-specific stochasticity, such as data ordering and dropout. For the aligned state $\bm{\theta}_{T-d}(\xi)$ , assume $\mathbb{E}[\|\bm{\theta}_{T-d}(\xi)\|_{2}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}]<\infty$ . The conditional mean state $\bm{\mu}_{t}$ and the zero-mean spatial noise $\bm{\epsilon}_{t}$ at the training step $t$ of an individual run are

$$ \bm{\mu}_{T-d}:=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\bm{\theta}_{T-d}(\xi)\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}],\qquad\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}(\xi):=\bm{\theta}_{T-d}(\xi)-\bm{\mu}_{T-d}. $$

A stochastic training run therefore satisfies $\bm{\theta}_{T-d}=\bm{\mu}_{T-d}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}$ and $\mathbb{E}[\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}]=\bm{0}$ .

Throughout Appendix A, all expectations and covariances condition on $\mathcal{F}_{0}$ , and averaging kernels are fixed given $\mathcal{F}_{0}$ .

For ages $d,e\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ , define the conditional covariance blocks of the fluctuations around the latent-mean trajectory:

$$ \bm{\Gamma}_{de}:=\mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d},\bm{\epsilon}_{T-e}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}). $$

Within the retained stable-LR window, we use a common covariance for spatial noise and assume that fluctuations at different retained positions are uncorrelated.

#### Assumption A.1 (Common Covariance and Uncorrelated Spatial Noise).

Conditional on $\mathcal{F}_{0}$ , the spatial-noise vectors have finite second moments and satisfy, for $d,e\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}[\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}]=\bm{0},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}\bm{\epsilon}_{T-e}^{\top}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}]=\begin{cases}\bm{\Sigma},&d=e,\\
\bm{0},&d\neq e,\end{cases}\qquad\bm{\Sigma}\succeq 0. $$

Thus $\bm{\Gamma}_{dd}=\bm{\Sigma}$ and $\bm{\Gamma}_{de}=\bm{0}$ for $d\neq e$ .

Define the forward latent increment $\bm{v}_{T-j+1}=\bm{\mu}_{T-j+1}-\bm{\mu}_{T-j},1\leq j<M,$ and the cumulative old-weight mass $s_{j}(\bm{w})=\sum_{d=j}^{M-1}w_{d}$ , we have

$$ \bm{b}(\bm{w})=\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}s_{j}(\bm{w})\bm{v}_{T-j+1},\qquad\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d},\qquad R(\bm{w})=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}^{2}. $$

Generally, we have

$$ \mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0})=\sum_{d,e}w_{d}w_{e}\bm{\Gamma}_{de}. $$

Under Assumption A.1, this reduces to

$$ \mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0})=R(\bm{w})\bm{\Sigma}. $$

Accordingly, $R(\bm{w})^{-1}$ is a variance-equivalent effective sample size.

### A.2 Temporal lag and spatial noise

#### Lemma A.1 (Lag-noise Decomposition).

Every $\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}$ satisfies

$$ \bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bm{b}(\bm{w})+\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}. $$

Under Assumption A.1, its residual covariance is

$$ \mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0})=R(\bm{w})\bm{\Sigma}. $$

#### Proof.

The increments can be written as $\bm{\mu}_{T-d}=\bm{\mu}_{T}-\sum_{j=1}^{d}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}$ . Substituting this identity into $\sum_{d}w_{d}(\bm{\mu}_{T-d}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d})$ gives

$$ \sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}=\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}\left(\sum_{d=j}^{M-1}w_{d}\right)\bm{v}_{T-j+1}. $$

This proves Eq. (26). The conditional cross-covariances of distinct $\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}$ vanish by Assumption A.1, hence $\mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0})=\sum_{d}w_{d}^{2}\bm{\Sigma}=R(\bm{w})\bm{\Sigma}$ . ∎

#### Assumption A.2 (Bounded Adjacent Progress Variation).

Adjacent latent increments in the retained discrete window obey

$$ \|\bm{v}_{T-j+1}-\bm{v}_{T-j+2}\|_{2}\leq\kappa,\qquad 2\leq j<M, $$

for a finite $\kappa\geq 0$ .

Under Assumption A.2, the next lemma reduces the trajectory displacement to a scalar lag coordinate with a controlled remainder.

#### Lemma A.2 (Scalar Lag with Controlled Remainder).

Under Assumption A.2, define $m(\bm{w})=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}dw_{d}$ . Then

$$ \bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\bm{\mu}_{T}-m(\bm{w})\bm{v}_{T}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}+\bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}},\qquad\|\bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}}\|_{2}\leq\frac{\kappa}{2}\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}d(d-1). $$

When $\bm{v}_{T-j+1}=\bm{v}_{T}$ throughout the sampled window, $\bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}}=\bm{0}$ .

#### Proof.

The cumulative weights satisfy

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{M-1}s_{j}(\bm{w})=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}d\,w_{d}=m(\bm{w}). $$

Define the trajectory deviation $\bm{\delta}_{j}^{\mathrm{traj}}:=\bm{v}_{T-j+1}-\bm{v}_{T}$ for $1\leq j<M$ . Then

$$ \bm{b}(\bm{w})=m(\bm{w})\bm{v}_{T}+\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}s_{j}(\bm{w})\bm{\delta}_{j}^{\mathrm{traj}}. $$

Adjacent variation implies $\|\bm{\delta}_{j}^{\mathrm{traj}}\|_{2}\leq(j-1)\kappa$ . Non-negativity of the weights and

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{M-1}(j-1)s_{j}(\bm{w})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}d(d-1) $$

give Eq. (27) after setting

$$ \bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}}=-\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}s_{j}(\bm{w})\bm{\delta}_{j}^{\mathrm{traj}}. $$

∎

### A.3 Lag–noise Pareto frontier and closed-form LNWA kernel

The decomposition above motivates the kernel coordinates.

#### Definition A.3 (Lag–noise Coordinates).

For any $\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}$ , define

$$ \Phi(\bm{w})=\bigl(m(\bm{w}),R(\bm{w})\bigr),\qquad\mathcal{G}_{M}=\left\{\Phi(\bm{w}):\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}\right\}. $$

Here, $\Phi(\bm{w})$ denotes the lag–noise coordinates of the averaging kernel $\bm{w}$ , and $\mathcal{G}_{M}$ is the set of all feasible lag–noise coordinates.

Write $\operatorname{Eff}(\mathcal{G}_{M})$ for the set of Pareto-efficient points in $\mathcal{G}_{M}$ : a point belongs to this set if no feasible kernel has both a smaller or equal temporal lag and a smaller or equal spatial noise, with at least one strict inequality.

To identify the efficient set, first fix a lag budget $\ell$ :
