$$ \bm{w}^{\star}(\ell)=\arg\min_{\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}}R(\bm{w})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad m(\bm{w})\leq\ell,\qquad 0\leq\ell\leq\frac{M-1}{2}. $$

#### Lemma A.3 (Lag-noise Pareto Frontier).

For $0<\ell<(M-1)/2$ , Eq. (28) has a unique solution supported on the $q$ most recent saved weights, where

$$ q=q(\ell)=\min\{M,\lceil 3\ell+1\rceil\}\in\{2,\ldots,M\}. $$

Its coordinates are

$$ \bigl(\bm{w}^{\star}(\ell)\bigr)_{d}=\begin{cases}q^{-1}-\gamma_{q}(d-\bar{d}_{q}),&0\leq d<q,\\
0,&q\leq d<M,\end{cases} $$

where

$$ \bar{d}_{q}=\frac{q-1}{2},\quad D_{q}=\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(d-\bar{d}_{q})^{2}=\frac{q(q^{2}-1)}{12},\quad\gamma_{q}=\frac{\bar{d}_{q}-\ell}{D_{q}}, $$

and

$$ R^{\star}(\ell)=\frac{1}{q}+\frac{(\bar{d}_{q}-\ell)^{2}}{D_{q}}. $$

#### Proof.

The feasible set is compact, and the objective is strictly convex. Hence the minimizer is unique. With $\bm{d}=(0,1,\ldots,M-1)^{\top}$ , the Lagrangian is

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KKT}}(\bm{w},\tau,\nu,\bm{\alpha})=\|\bm{w}\|_{2}^{2}+\tau(\bm{d}^{\top}\bm{w}-\ell)+\nu(\bm{1}^{\top}\bm{w}-1)-\bm{\alpha}^{\top}\bm{w}. $$

Slater’s condition holds for $\ell>0$ , so the KKT conditions are

$$ 2\bm{w}+\tau\bm{d}+\nu\bm{1}-\bm{\alpha}=0,\qquad\tau(\bm{d}^{\top}\bm{w}-\ell)=0,\qquad\alpha_{d}w_{d}=0, $$

with $\tau\geq 0$ and $\bm{\alpha}\geq 0$ . If $\tau=0$ , they give the uniform simplex minimizer, which is infeasible because $(M-1)/2>\ell$ . Thus $\tau>0$ and the lag constraint is active. Stationarity and complementary slackness in Eq. (32) give

$$ \displaystyle w_{d}>0 \displaystyle\ \Longrightarrow\ \alpha_{d}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ w_{d}=-\frac{\nu+\tau d}{2}>0, \displaystyle w_{d}=0 \displaystyle\ \Longrightarrow\ -\frac{\nu+\tau d}{2}=-\frac{\alpha_{d}}{2}\leq 0. $$

Combining the two cases yields

$$ w_{d}=\left[-\frac{\nu+\tau d}{2}\right]_{+}. $$

Because $\tau>0$ , the expression inside the positive part decreases with $d$ . Hence the support is a prefix $S_{q}=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$ . For $d\in S_{q}$ , the positive-part operator is inactive and

$$ w_{d}=-\frac{\nu}{2}-\frac{\tau}{2}d. $$

Using $\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}w_{d}=1$ and $\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}d=q\bar{d}_{q}$ in Eq. (35) gives

$$ 1=-\frac{q\nu}{2}-\frac{\tau q\bar{d}_{q}}{2},\qquad-\frac{\nu}{2}=\frac{1}{q}+\frac{\tau}{2}\bar{d}_{q}. $$

Substitution back into Eq. (35) yields

$$ w_{d}=\frac{1}{q}-\frac{\tau}{2}(d-\bar{d}_{q}),\qquad d\in S_{q}. $$

Therefore, with $\bm{c}_{q}=(0,1,\ldots,q-1)^{\top}-\bar{d}_{q}\bm{1}_{q}$ ,

$$ \bm{w}^{\star}_{S_{q}}=q^{-1}\bm{1}_{q}-\frac{\tau}{2}\bm{c}_{q}. $$

Finally, the lag constraint is active, so

$$ \displaystyle\ell \displaystyle=\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}d\,w_{d} \displaystyle=\bar{d}_{q}-\frac{\tau}{2}\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}d(d-\bar{d}_{q}) \displaystyle=\bar{d}_{q}-\frac{\tau}{2}D_{q}. $$

Hence $\tau/2=(\bar{d}_{q}-\ell)/D_{q}=\gamma_{q}$ , which proves Eqs. (30)–(31). The last-active and first-inactive conditions reduce to

$$ \frac{q-2}{3}<\ell\leq\frac{q-1}{3}\quad(q<M),\qquad\ell>\frac{M-2}{3}\quad(q=M), $$

which gives Eq. (29). Finally, $\bm{1}_{q}^{\top}\bm{c}_{q}=0$ and $\|\bm{c}_{q}\|_{2}^{2}=D_{q}$ , so

$$ R(\bm{w}^{\star}(\ell))=\left\|q^{-1}\bm{1}_{q}-\frac{\tau}{2}\bm{c}_{q}\right\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{q}+\frac{(\bar{d}_{q}-\ell)^{2}}{D_{q}}. $$

∎

We next parameterize the budget-optimal kernels by a single coefficient.

#### Theorem A.1 (Lag-noise Trade-off Weight Averaging (LNWA) Kernel).

For $0\leq\lambda<\infty$ , define the Lag-noise Trade-off Weight Averaging (LNWA) kernel by

$$ \bm{w}_{\lambda}=\arg\min_{\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}}\{R(\bm{w})+\lambda m(\bm{w})^{2}\}. $$

The finite- $\lambda$ family satisfies

$$ \{\Phi(\bm{w}_{\lambda}):0\leq\lambda<\infty\}=\operatorname{Eff}(\mathcal{G}_{M})\setminus\{\Phi(\bm{e}_{0})\}. $$

Its unique solution has an active prefix of size $q\geq 2$ and

$$ (\bm{w}_{\lambda})_{d}=\begin{cases}q^{-1}+\lambda m_{q}(\lambda)(\bar{d}_{q}-d),&0\leq d<q,\\
0,&q\leq d<M,\end{cases} $$

where

$$ m_{q}(\lambda)=m(\bm{w}_{\lambda})=\frac{\bar{d}_{q}}{1+\lambda D_{q}},\qquad\bar{d}_{q}=\frac{q-1}{2},\qquad D_{q}=\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(d-\bar{d}_{q})^{2}=\frac{q(q^{2}-1)}{12}. $$

#### Proof.

Any kernel with $m(\bm{w})>(M-1)/2$ is dominated by the uniform kernel. For $0\leq\ell\leq(M-1)/2$ , uniqueness in Eq. (28) implies

$$ \operatorname{Eff}(\mathcal{G}_{M})=\{\Phi(\bm{w}^{\star}(\ell)):0\leq\ell\leq(M-1)/2\}. $$

Indeed, a dominator of $\bm{w}^{\star}(\ell)$ contradicts its optimality or uniqueness; conversely, $\bm{w}^{\star}(m(\bm{w}))$ dominates every feasible $\bm{w}$ that is not the budget minimizer.

For finite $\lambda$ , Eq. (36) is strictly convex. By the same stationarity and complementary-slackness argument as Eqs. (33)–(34), its KKT conditions give

$$ w_{d}=\left[-\frac{\nu}{2}-\lambda md\right]_{+},\qquad m=m(\bm{w}_{\lambda}), $$

so the active set is a prefix. Moreover, for sufficiently small $t>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle R\!\left((1-t)\bm{e}_{0}+t\bm{e}_{1}\right)+\lambda m\!\left((1-t)\bm{e}_{0}+t\bm{e}_{1}\right)^{2} \displaystyle=1-2t+(\lambda+2)t^{2}<1=R(\bm{e}_{0})+\lambda m(\bm{e}_{0})^{2}, $$

so $\bm{e}_{0}$ cannot solve Eq. (36); hence $q\geq 2$ . On the active prefix $S_{q}=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$ , Eq. (41) becomes

$$ w_{d}=-\frac{\nu}{2}-\lambda md,\qquad d\in S_{q}. $$

Using $\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}w_{d}=1$ and $\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}d=q\bar{d}_{q}$ gives

$$ 1=-\frac{q\nu}{2}-\lambda mq\bar{d}_{q},\qquad-\frac{\nu}{2}=\frac{1}{q}+\lambda m\bar{d}_{q}. $$

Substituting this identity into Eq. (43) yields

$$ w_{d}=\frac{1}{q}+\lambda m(\bar{d}_{q}-d),\qquad d\in S_{q}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle m \displaystyle=\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}d\,w_{d} \displaystyle=\bar{d}_{q}+\lambda m\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}d(\bar{d}_{q}-d) \displaystyle=\bar{d}_{q}-\lambda mD_{q}, $$

where

$$ \sum_{d=0}^{q-1}d(\bar{d}_{q}-d)=q\bar{d}_{q}^{2}-\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}d^{2}=-D_{q}. $$

Consequently,

$$ m=\frac{\bar{d}_{q}}{1+\lambda D_{q}}, $$

which proves Eqs. (38) and (39).

For $0<\ell<(M-1)/2$ , set

$$ \lambda=\frac{\gamma_{q}}{\ell}=\frac{\bar{d}_{q}-\ell}{D_{q}\ell}. $$

Then Eqs. (30) and (38) coincide, so every interior budget solution lies on the LNWA path. The budget endpoint $\ell=(M-1)/2$ is the uniform kernel $\bm{w}_{0}$ , whereas $\ell=0$ has the unique solution $\bm{e}_{0}$ . Eq. (42) excludes $\bm{e}_{0}$ for every finite $\lambda$ . Together with Eq. (40), these facts prove Eq. (37). ∎

#### Lemma A.4 (Global Structure of the LNWA).

The LNWA path has endpoints

$$ \bm{w}_{0}=\frac{1}{M}\bm{1},\qquad\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\bm{w}_{\lambda}=\bm{e}_{0}. $$

For $q\geq 3$ , define

$$ \lambda_{q}^{\mathrm{knot}}=\frac{6}{q(q-1)(q-2)}. $$

If $M>2$ , all $M$ coordinates are active on $[0,\lambda_{M}^{\mathrm{knot}})$ ; for each $q\in\{3,\ldots,M-1\}$ , exactly $q$ coordinates are active on $[\lambda_{q+1}^{\mathrm{knot}},\lambda_{q}^{\mathrm{knot}})$ ; and exactly two coordinates are active on $[\lambda_{3}^{\mathrm{knot}},\infty)$ . If $M=2$ , both coordinates remain active for every finite $\lambda$ . Defining $\bm{w}_{\infty}:=\bm{e}_{0}$ therefore completes the frontier:

$$ \{\Phi(\bm{w}_{\lambda}):0\leq\lambda\leq\infty\}=\operatorname{Eff}(\mathcal{G}_{M}). $$

Moreover, for $0\leq\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}\leq\infty$ ,

$$ m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})<m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}}),\qquad R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})>R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}}). $$

#### Proof.

At $\lambda=0$ , Eq. (36) reduces to minimizing $R(\bm{w})$ over $\mathcal{W}_{M}$ , whose unique solution is $\bm{w}_{0}=M^{-1}\bm{1}$ . This proves the first identity in Eq. (44).

Suppose the active prefix is $S_{q}=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$ . To verify that its size is exactly $q$ , we check its last active coefficient and the affine continuation to the next coordinate, denoted by $\widetilde{w}_{q}$ . Eqs. (38)–(39) give

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{w}_{q} \displaystyle:=q^{-1}+\lambda m_{q}(\lambda)(\bar{d}_{q}-q), \displaystyle(\bm{w}_{\lambda})_{q-1}>0 \displaystyle\iff\lambda<\lambda_{q}^{\mathrm{knot}} \displaystyle(q\geq 3), \displaystyle\widetilde{w}_{q}\leq 0 \displaystyle\iff\lambda\geq\lambda_{q+1}^{\mathrm{knot}} \displaystyle(q<M). $$

These two boundary conditions give $[\lambda_{q+1}^{\mathrm{knot}},\lambda_{q}^{\mathrm{knot}})$ ; at each knot, the oldest active coefficient reaches zero.

When $M>2$ , the two-coordinate segment is $\lambda\in[\lambda_{3}^{\mathrm{knot}},\infty)$ ; when $M=2$ , it is the entire finite path $\lambda\in[0,\infty)$ . On this segment, Theorem A.1 gives

$$ \bm{w}_{\lambda}=\left(\frac{\lambda+1}{\lambda+2},\frac{1}{\lambda+2},0,\ldots,0\right). $$

Taking $\lambda\to\infty$ in Eq. (46) gives

$$ \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\bm{w}_{\lambda}=\bm{e}_{0}. $$

This proves the second identity in Eq. (44).

To prove Eq. (45), first suppose $0\leq\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}<\infty$ . Optimality at the two coefficients gives

$$ \displaystyle R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})+\lambda_{1}m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})^{2} \displaystyle\leq R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})+\lambda_{1}m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})^{2}, \displaystyle R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})+\lambda_{2}m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})^{2} \displaystyle\leq R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})+\lambda_{2}m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})^{2}. $$

Adding Eqs. (47) and (48) yields

$$ (\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1})\left[m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})^{2}-m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})^{2}\right]\leq 0. $$

Thus,

$$ m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})\leq m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}}). $$

Equality would force $R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})=R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})$ by Eqs. (47)–(48), so strict convexity would give $\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}}=\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}}$ . But Eq. (43) gives $(\bm{w}_{\lambda})_{0}-(\bm{w}_{\lambda})_{1}=\lambda m(\bm{w}_{\lambda})$ , with $m(\bm{w}_{\lambda})>0$ for every finite $\lambda$ . Thus the same kernel cannot occur at distinct coefficients, and the inequality is strict. Eq. (47) then gives

$$ R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})-R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})\leq\lambda_{1}\left[m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})^{2}-m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})^{2}\right]\leq 0. $$

This is strict when $\lambda_{1}>0$ . For $\lambda_{1}=0$ , it is strict because $\bm{w}_{0}$ uniquely minimizes $R$ and $\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}}\neq\bm{w}_{0}$ . Thus,

$$ R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}})>R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}}). $$

Finally, Eq. (44) gives $m(\bm{w}_{\infty})=0$ and $R(\bm{w}_{\infty})=1$ . Every finite- $\lambda_{1}$ kernel has at least two positive coordinates, so

$$ \displaystyle m(\bm{w}_{\infty}) \displaystyle=0<m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}}), \displaystyle R(\bm{w}_{\infty}) \displaystyle=1>R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}}). $$

∎

For the PTQ analysis below, we record the closed-form coordinates of each fixed-support segment of the LNWA frontier.

#### Lemma A.5 (Closed-Form Coordinates of the LNWA Frontier).

On an active prefix of size $q\geq 2$ ,

$$ m(\bm{w}_{\lambda})^{2}=\frac{\bar{d}_{q}^{2}}{(1+D_{q}\lambda)^{2}},\qquad R(\bm{w}_{\lambda})=\frac{1}{q}+\frac{D_{q}\bar{d}_{q}^{2}\lambda^{2}}{(1+D_{q}\lambda)^{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

Eq. (39) gives the first identity. Using $\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)=0$ and $\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)^{2}=D_{q}$ in Eq. (38) gives

$$ \displaystyle R(\bm{w}_{\lambda}) \displaystyle=\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}\left[q^{-1}+\lambda m_{q}(\lambda)(\bar{d}_{q}-d)\right]^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{q}+\frac{2\lambda m_{q}(\lambda)}{q}\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)+\lambda^{2}m_{q}(\lambda)^{2}\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{q}+D_{q}\lambda^{2}m_{q}(\lambda)^{2}=\frac{1}{q}+\frac{D_{q}\bar{d}_{q}^{2}\lambda^{2}}{(1+D_{q}\lambda)^{2}}. $$

∎

Theorem A.1 derives the LNWA kernel and its finite- $\lambda$ Pareto path. Lemma A.4 then characterizes the global structure of this path, including its endpoints, support transitions, and monotonicity in $\lambda$ . Lemma A.5 gives its closed-form lag–noise coordinates on each fixed-support segment.

### A.4 Classical averaging kernels as LNWA special cases

This subsection shows that classical averaging kernels can be viewed as special cases of the LNWA framework. We first present its two endpoints, LAWA (uniform averaging) and Stable (the latest weight at the end of the stable-LR training trajectory), followed by WMA (linear weighting) and EMA (exponential weighting).

#### Proposition A.1 (The two endpoints).

The $\lambda=0$ endpoint of the extended LNWA path is LAWA, whereas its $\lambda=\infty$ endpoint is Stable. Their lag–noise coordinates are therefore

$$ \Phi(\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{LAWA}}})=\left(\frac{M-1}{2},\frac{1}{M}\right),\qquad\Phi(\bm{w}^{\mathrm{Stable}})=(0,1). $$

This proposition is established by Lemma A.4. We next locate the linearly weighted rule on the interior of the frontier.

#### Proposition A.2 (WMA on the LNWA Frontier).

The WMA kernel $\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{WMA}}}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}$ has coordinates $(\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{WMA}}})_{d}=2(M-d)/[M(M+1)]$ . Its lag–noise coordinates and corresponding LNWA coefficient are

$$ m_{\textnormal{{WMA}}}=\frac{M-1}{3},\qquad R_{\textnormal{{WMA}}}=\frac{2(2M+1)}{3M(M+1)},\qquad\lambda_{\textnormal{{WMA}}}=\frac{6}{M(M^{2}-1)}. $$

Consequently, $\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{WMA}}}=\bm{w}_{\lambda_{\textnormal{{WMA}}}}$ .

#### Proof.

Substituting the WMA coefficients into the definitions of $m$ and $R$ gives

$$ \displaystyle m_{\textnormal{{WMA}}} \displaystyle=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}d\,(\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{WMA}}})_{d}=\frac{2}{M(M+1)}\left(M\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}d-\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}d^{2}\right)=\frac{M-1}{3}, \displaystyle R_{\textnormal{{WMA}}} \displaystyle=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}\bigl((\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{WMA}}})_{d}\bigr)^{2}=\frac{4}{M^{2}(M+1)^{2}}\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}(M-d)^{2}=\frac{2(2M+1)}{3M(M+1)}. $$

On the full-support face, both kernels are affine in $d$ :

$$ \displaystyle(\bm{w}_{\lambda})_{d} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{M}+\lambda m(\bm{w}_{\lambda})(\bar{d}_{M}-d), \displaystyle(\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{WMA}}})_{d} \displaystyle=\frac{2}{M+1}-\frac{2}{M(M+1)}d. $$

Matching the coefficients of $d$ gives

$$ \lambda_{\textnormal{{WMA}}}m_{\textnormal{{WMA}}}=\frac{2}{M(M+1)}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\lambda_{\textnormal{{WMA}}}=\frac{6}{M(M^{2}-1)}. $$

For this coefficient, the intercept of the LNWA kernel is

$$ \frac{1}{M}+\lambda_{\textnormal{{WMA}}}m_{\textnormal{{WMA}}}\bar{d}_{M}=\frac{1}{M}+\frac{2}{M(M+1)}\frac{M-1}{2}=\frac{2}{M+1}, $$

which equals the WMA intercept in Eq. (50). Hence $\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{WMA}}}=\bm{w}_{\lambda_{\textnormal{{WMA}}}}$ . ∎

The next two propositions give the exact coordinates of EMA and its LNWA approximation.

#### Proposition A.3 (Exact Lag-Noise Coordinates of EMA).

For $M\geq 2$ and $0<\beta<1$ , the EMA kernel is

$$ (\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{EMA}}})_{d}=\frac{(1-\beta)\beta^{d}}{1-\beta^{M}}, $$

with exact coordinates

$$ \displaystyle m_{\textnormal{{EMA}}} \displaystyle=\frac{\beta-M\beta^{M}+(M-1)\beta^{M+1}}{(1-\beta)(1-\beta^{M})}, \displaystyle R_{\textnormal{{EMA}}} \displaystyle=\frac{(1-\beta)(1+\beta^{M})}{(1+\beta)(1-\beta^{M})}. $$

#### Proof.

The finite geometric series gives

$$ \sum_{d=0}^{M-1}(\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{EMA}}})_{d}=\frac{1-\beta}{1-\beta^{M}}\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}\beta^{d}=1. $$

Substitution into the definitions of $m$ and $R$ yields

$$ \displaystyle m_{\textnormal{{EMA}}} \displaystyle=\frac{1-\beta}{1-\beta^{M}}\beta\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\beta}\left(\frac{1-\beta^{M}}{1-\beta}\right)=\frac{\beta-M\beta^{M}+(M-1)\beta^{M+1}}{(1-\beta)(1-\beta^{M})}, \displaystyle R_{\textnormal{{EMA}}} \displaystyle=\left(\frac{1-\beta}{1-\beta^{M}}\right)^{2}\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}\beta^{2d}=\left(\frac{1-\beta}{1-\beta^{M}}\right)^{2}\frac{1-\beta^{2M}}{1-\beta^{2}}=\frac{(1-\beta)(1+\beta^{M})}{(1+\beta)(1-\beta^{M})}. $$

∎

#### Proposition A.4 (EMA on the LNWA Frontier).

For $M=2$ , EMA is exactly an LNWA kernel for every $0<\beta<1$ , with $\lambda=(1-\beta)/\beta$ . For $M>2$ , let $\eta=-\log\beta$ . For any $0<\rho\leq 1$ such that $\eta(M-1)\leq\rho$ , define

$$ \lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}:=\frac{\eta}{M\bar{d}_{M}-\eta D_{M}}. $$

Then the approximation residual satisfies

$$ \varepsilon_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}:=\left\|\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{EMA}}}-\bm{w}_{\lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}}\right\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{e^{\rho/2}\eta^{2}}{2M}\left[\frac{(M-1)^{2}}{4}+\left(1+\frac{\rho}{2}\right)\frac{M^{2}-1}{12}\right]=\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2}M). $$

Thus, EMA is an exact special case of LNWA when $M=2$ and an approximate special case with the above residual bound when $M>2$ .

#### Proof.

For $M=2$ , direct substitution gives

$$ \bm{w}^{\textnormal{{EMA}}}=\left(\frac{1}{1+\beta},\frac{\beta}{1+\beta}\right)=\left(\frac{\lambda+1}{\lambda+2},\frac{1}{\lambda+2}\right)=\bm{w}_{\lambda},\qquad\lambda=\frac{1-\beta}{\beta}. $$

For $M>2$ , $\eta(M-1)\leq\rho\leq 1$ gives

$$ M\bar{d}_{M}-\eta D_{M}=\frac{M(M-1)}{2}\left(1-\frac{\eta(M+1)}{6}\right)\geq\frac{M(M-1)}{2}\left(1-\frac{\rho(M+1)}{6(M-1)}\right)>0, $$

so $\lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}$ is well defined and positive. It remains to verify that the corresponding LNWA kernel has full support. By Lemma A.4, this is equivalent to $\lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}<\lambda_{M}^{\mathrm{knot}}$ . Substituting the definitions of $\lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}$ and $\lambda_{M}^{\mathrm{knot}}$ gives

$$ \lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}<\lambda_{M}^{\mathrm{knot}}\iff\eta(M-1)<2. $$

Because $\eta(M-1)\leq\rho\leq 1$ , this condition holds. Substituting $\lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}$ into Eq. (39) with $q=M$ gives

$$ \lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}m_{M}(\lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}})=\frac{\lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}\bar{d}_{M}}{1+\lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}D_{M}}=\frac{\eta}{M}. $$

Substituting Eq. (52) into Eq. (38) with $q=M$ gives

$$ (\bm{w}_{\lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}})_{d}=\frac{1}{M}-\frac{\eta}{M}(d-\bar{d}_{M}). $$

Define

$$ r_{d}:=e^{-\eta(d-\bar{d}_{M})}-\left[1-\eta(d-\bar{d}_{M})\right],\qquad\bar{r}:=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}r_{j}. $$

Since $|\eta(d-\bar{d}_{M})|\leq\rho/2$ , we can bound each $r_{d}$ ; averaging these bounds then gives the bound for $\bar{r}$ :

$$ 0\leq r_{d}\leq\frac{e^{\rho/2}\eta^{2}(d-\bar{d}_{M})^{2}}{2},\qquad 0\leq\bar{r}\leq\frac{e^{\rho/2}\eta^{2}D_{M}}{2M}. $$

Using $\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}(j-\bar{d}_{M})=0$ , the normalized EMA coefficient is exactly

$$ (\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{EMA}}})_{d}=\frac{e^{-\eta(d-\bar{d}_{M})}}{\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}e^{-\eta(j-\bar{d}_{M})}}=\frac{1-\eta(d-\bar{d}_{M})+r_{d}}{M(1+\bar{r})}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\left|(\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{EMA}}})_{d}-(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{\textnormal{{EMA}}}})_{d}\right| \displaystyle=\frac{\left|r_{d}-\bigl[1-\eta(d-\bar{d}_{M})\bigr]\bar{r}\right|}{M(1+\bar{r})} \displaystyle\leq\frac{e^{\rho/2}\eta^{2}}{2M}\left[(d-\bar{d}_{M})^{2}+\left(1+\frac{\rho}{2}\right)\frac{D_{M}}{M}\right]. $$

Taking the maximum over $d$ and using $|d-\bar{d}_{M}|\leq(M-1)/2$ and $D_{M}/M=(M^{2}-1)/12$ proves Eq. (51). ∎

Together, the preceding results establish the lag-noise decomposition, characterize the LNWA frontier, and relate classical averaging methods to LNWA. We next analyze how weight averaging affects PTQ, leading to our two main theorems.

### A.5 PTQ tolerance and degradation

We now ask how far an averaging kernel can move toward the newest weight before quantization performance begins to degrade. We measure performance by the expected output reconstruction error relative to the latest latent mean. We first compute the error introduced by the two quantization stages of simplified GPTQ model. This gives an exact expression for the expected reconstruction error. We then study this expression along the LNWA frontier and locate the transition from noise tolerance to degradation.

We use the latent-mean decomposition and write the mean of an averaged state as

$$ \bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}:=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\mu}_{T-d}=\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bm{b}(\bm{w}),\qquad\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}. $$

The term $-\bm{b}(\bm{w})$ is the displacement due to temporal lag, and $\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}$ is the retained spatial noise. Both will enter the output reconstruction error through the channel matrices defined below.

#### Assumption A.3 (Bounded Isotropic Spatial Noise).

In addition to Assumption A.1, assume

$$ \bm{\Sigma}=\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{P},\qquad\sigma>0,\qquad|[\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}]_{j}|\leq\sigma K_{\epsilon}\quad(0\leq d<M,\ 1\leq j\leq P) $$

almost surely, for a fixed finite $K_{\epsilon}$ .

Thus the averaged spatial noise has

$$ \mathbb{E}\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\bm{0},\qquad\mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}})=\sigma^{2}R(\bm{w})\bm{I}_{P}. $$

We measure the effect of a parameter perturbation by the reconstruction error it induces on the fixed calibration inputs. For each linear layer $\ell$ , let $i$ index its output channels and $n^{(\ell)}$ denote the number of calibration samples. Let $\bm{X}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}^{(\ell)}\times n^{(\ell)}}$ contain its fixed calibration inputs. The channel vector $\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)}$ is the transpose of row $i$ of that layer’s parameter matrix. A change $\bm{z}^{(\ell,i)}$ causes mean squared reconstruction error

$$ \frac{1}{n^{(\ell)}}\|(\bm{z}^{(\ell,i)})^{\top}\bm{X}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}^{2}=(\bm{z}^{(\ell,i)})^{\top}\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)}\bm{z}^{(\ell,i)},\qquad\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)}:=\frac{\bm{X}^{(\ell)}(\bm{X}^{(\ell)})^{\top}}{n^{(\ell)}}. $$

Let $\mathcal{I}$ be the set of layer–channel pairs included in the model, and stack their parameter vectors in a fixed order. The sum of their reconstruction errors is $\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{z}$ , where

$$ \bm{G}=\operatorname{diag}_{(\ell,i)\in\mathcal{I}}\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{G}^{(\ell_{1},i_{1})}&\bm{0}&\cdots\\
\bm{0}&\bm{G}^{(\ell_{2},i_{2})}&\cdots\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots\end{pmatrix},\qquad\|\bm{z}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}:=\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{z}. $$

The global matrix is block diagonal across channels. The stacked parameter dimension is $P=\sum_{(\ell,i)\in\mathcal{I}}d_{\mathrm{in}}^{(\ell)}$ .

Write $Q_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)$ for the model produced by the simplified GPTQ model at precision $b$ and scale $s$ , whose channel operations are specified below. We evaluate each averaging kernel using the expected reconstruction error

$$ \mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}):=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\|Q_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}};s(\bm{w}))-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}\right]. $$

This sums the squared channel-output differences between the quantized averaged model and the latest latent mean. It includes the temporal lag and spatial noise already present before quantization, together with the change caused by quantization. We assume that every channel matrix $\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)}$ is positive definite.

The simplified GPTQ model quantizes one group of coordinates and uses the other to compensate for its output error. Partition each channel into two nonempty groups $\mathrm{f}$ and $\mathrm{r}$ . Reorder the stacked coordinates so that all $\mathrm{f}$ entries precede all $\mathrm{r}$ entries, and apply the same permutation to every global vector and matrix. We retain the symbols $\bm{\theta}$ and $\bm{G}$ in this order. Then

$$ \bm{\theta}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}\\
\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{r}}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\bm{G}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{f}}&\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{r}}\\
\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{f}}&\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\end{pmatrix}. $$

To simplify the theoretical analysis, we do not model group-wise quantization scales. Instead, we assign the averaged state a single scale, computed before rounding from its RMS magnitude.

#### Assumption A.4 (Fixed RMS Scale).

For each averaging kernel $\bm{w}$ , the scale is

$$ s(\bm{w})^{2}:=\frac{1}{P}\mathbb{E}\|\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{\|\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\|_{2}^{2}}{P}+\sigma^{2}R(\bm{w}). $$

For each group $\mathrm{g}\in{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{r}}$ , we use a fixed range multiplier $H_{\mathrm{g}}>0$ , shared across kernels and precisions. Given the RMS scale $s(\bm{w})$ , the corresponding parameter-space and normalized quantization steps are

$$ \Delta_{b,\mathrm{g}}(\bm{w}):=\frac{2H_{\mathrm{g}}s(\bm{w})}{2^{b}-1},\qquad\bar{\Delta}_{b,\mathrm{g}}:=\frac{\Delta_{b,\mathrm{g}}(\bm{w})}{s(\bm{w})}=\frac{2H_{\mathrm{g}}}{2^{b}-1}. $$

Accordingly, the $2^{b}$ reconstruction levels for group $\mathrm{g}$ cover the range

$$ [-H_{\mathrm{g}}s(\bm{w}),\,H_{\mathrm{g}}s(\bm{w})]. $$

Deterministic rounding generally leads to less tractable rounding-error statistics (Alvarez et al., 2025; Zhang and Saab, 2026). To simplify the analysis, following Wannamaker et al. (2000), we instead use nonsubtractive triangular dither and define

$$ \operatorname{round}(t):=\left\lfloor t+U+V+\frac{1}{2}\right\rfloor,\qquad U,V\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\operatorname{Unif}[-1/2,1/2]. $$

Here $\operatorname{Unif}[a,b]$ denotes the uniform distribution on $[a,b]$ , and $\lfloor\cdot\rfloor$ denotes the floor operator, so $\operatorname{round}(t)$ returns an integer code.

For an input $\bm{z}$ , a scale $s>0$ , and group range $H_{\mathrm{g}}$ , write $\Delta=s\bar{\Delta}_{b,\mathrm{g}}$ . Quantization assigns the integer code and maps it back to parameter space as

$$ k_{j}=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,2^{b}-1]}\left(\operatorname{round}\left(\frac{z_{j}}{\Delta}+\frac{2^{b}-1}{2}\right)\right),\qquad[\operatorname{quant}_{b}(\bm{z};s,H_{\mathrm{g}})]_{j}=\Delta\left(k_{j}-\frac{2^{b}-1}{2}\right). $$

Here $\operatorname{clip}$ restricts the integer code to the displayed range. We next derive the compensation and write the full-model simplified GPTQ. At the common scale $s$ , the first group has rounding error

$$ \bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}:=\operatorname{quant}_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}};s,H_{\mathrm{f}})-\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}. $$

The remaining group is adjusted to minimize the output reconstruction error caused by this first rounding:

$$ \bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\star}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}}\begin{pmatrix}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\\
\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top}\bm{G}\begin{pmatrix}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\\
\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Differentiating this quadratic objective gives

$$ \bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\star}+\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}=\bm{0}. $$

Since $\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\succ 0$ , the compensation is

$$ \bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\star}=-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}},\qquad\bm{K}:=\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}^{-1}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{f}}. $$

The matrix $\bm{K}$ specifies how first-group rounding changes the remaining group. Write $B_{K}:=\|\bm{K}\|_{\infty}$ , where the matrix infinity norm is the maximum absolute row sum. The second rounding, applied after compensation, has error

$$ \bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}:=\operatorname{quant}_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}};s,H_{\mathrm{r}})-(\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}). $$

Thus the complete model-level map is

$$ Q_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\\
\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}=\operatorname{quant}_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}};s,H_{\mathrm{f}})-\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}. $$

We assume that the quantizer codebook has a sufficiently wide range to represent the parameter values in both quantization stages.

#### Assumption A.5 (Rounding Inputs within the Quantizer Range).

Let $b_{\min}=2$ . For every $\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}$ and integer $b\geq b_{\min}$ , the two rounding inputs satisfy

$$ \frac{\|(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}})_{\mathrm{f}}\|_{\infty}}{s(\bm{w})}<H_{\mathrm{f}}\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{b}-1}\right),\qquad\frac{\|(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}})_{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\|_{\infty}}{s(\bm{w})}<H_{\mathrm{r}}\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{b}-1}\right) $$

almost surely over the training distribution and the first-stage rounding randomness.

#### Lemma A.6 (A Sufficient Quantization Range).

Under Assumptions A.3 and A.4, define

$$ Z_{\max}:=\sqrt{P}+K_{\epsilon}\sqrt{M}. $$

If

$$ H_{\mathrm{f}}>\frac{3}{2}Z_{\max},\qquad H_{\mathrm{r}}>\frac{3}{2}\left(Z_{\max}+B_{K}H_{\mathrm{f}}\right), $$

then Assumption A.5 holds.

#### Proof.

For any $\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}$ , $R(\bm{w})\geq 1/M$ . Hence $s(\bm{w})\geq\sigma/\sqrt{M}$ and $\|\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\|_{2}/s(\bm{w})\leq\sqrt{P}$ . For each coordinate,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{|[\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}]_{j}|}{s(\bm{w})} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\|\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\|_{2}}{s(\bm{w})}+\frac{\sum_{d}w_{d}|[\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}]_{j}|}{s(\bm{w})} \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{P}+\frac{\sigma K_{\epsilon}}{s(\bm{w})} \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{P}+K_{\epsilon}\sqrt{M} \displaystyle=Z_{\max}. $$

Because $b\geq b_{\min}=2$ , $1-1/(2^{b}-1)\geq 2/3$ . The first-stage input therefore satisfies

$$ \frac{\|(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}})_{\mathrm{f}}\|_{\infty}}{s(\bm{w})}\leq Z_{\max}<\frac{2}{3}H_{\mathrm{f}}\leq H_{\mathrm{f}}\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{b}-1}\right). $$

For any scalar input $z$ satisfying the corresponding margin

$$ \frac{|z|}{s(\bm{w})}<H_{\mathrm{g}}\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{b}-1}\right), $$

we have

$$ \frac{1}{2}<\frac{z}{\Delta_{b,\mathrm{g}}}+\frac{2^{b}-1}{2}<2^{b}-\frac{3}{2}. $$

Since $-1\leq U+V\leq 1$ , it follows that

$$ 0<\frac{z}{\Delta_{b,\mathrm{g}}}+\frac{2^{b}-1}{2}+U+V+\frac{1}{2}<2^{b}. $$

Its floor therefore belongs to $\{0,\ldots,2^{b}-1\}$ , so clipping is inactive. The first-stage margin established above thus ensures that the perturbation has magnitude at most $\Delta_{b,\mathrm{f}}$ , and nearest-integer rounding adds at most $\Delta_{b,\mathrm{f}}/2$ . Thus

$$ \|\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{3}{2}\Delta_{b,\mathrm{f}}(\bm{w}),\qquad\frac{\|\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\|_{\infty}}{s(\bm{w})}\leq\frac{3B_{K}H_{\mathrm{f}}}{2^{b}-1}. $$

The second input consequently satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\|(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}})_{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\|_{\infty}}{s(\bm{w})} \displaystyle\leq Z_{\max}+\frac{3B_{K}H_{\mathrm{f}}}{2^{b}-1} \displaystyle\leq Z_{\max}+B_{K}H_{\mathrm{f}} \displaystyle<\frac{2}{3}H_{\mathrm{r}} \displaystyle\leq H_{\mathrm{r}}\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{b}-1}\right). $$

This is the second inequality in Assumption A.5; the first was established above. Hence that assumption holds for both quantization stages. ∎

We next derive the parameter error induced by the simplified GPTQ procedure and its corresponding output reconstruction error.

$$ \bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}:=\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{f}}-\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{r}}\bm{K}. $$

#### Lemma A.7 (Parameter and Reconstruction Errors of the Simplified GPTQ Model).

The Schur complement $\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}$ is positive definite. The quantization-induced global parameter error is

$$ \bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s):=Q_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)-\bm{\theta}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\\
-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Its output reconstruction error satisfies

$$ \bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)=\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}. $$

#### Proof.

Because $\bm{G}\succ 0$ , its principal block $\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}$ is positive definite. Let $J$ be the global reconstruction objective in Eq. (54). For a fixed first-group error, expanding and differentiating it gives

$$ \displaystyle J(\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}) \displaystyle=\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+2\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}, \displaystyle\nabla_{\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}}J \displaystyle=2\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+2\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}. $$

Setting this derivative to zero recovers $\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\star}=-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}$ .

Completing the square decomposes the reconstruction error into the residual error after optimal compensation and the additional error from a non-optimal compensation:

$$ J(\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}})=\underbrace{\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}}_{\text{residual error}}+\underbrace{(\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}+\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}})^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}(\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}+\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}})}_{\text{compensation error}}. $$

This identity holds for every first-group rounding error $\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}$ . At the optimum, $\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\star}=-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}$ , so the second term in Eq. (57) vanishes and

$$ \bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\\
-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top}\bm{G}\begin{pmatrix}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\\
-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\end{pmatrix}>0\qquad(\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\neq\bm{0}). $$

Hence $\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\succ 0$ . The second rounding introduces the additional error $\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}$ , so that

$$ \bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}=\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\star}+\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}, $$

therefore

$$ \bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}+\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}=\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}, $$

Substituting this expression into Eq. (57) gives

$$ J=\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}, $$

which proves Eq. (56). ∎

Lemma A.7 gives the parameter and reconstruction errors of the simplified GPTQ model. We use this result to analyze the quantization-induced contribution to $\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w})$ . Let

$$ \bm{a}:=\bm{\theta}-\bm{\mu}_{T}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{a}_{\mathrm{f}}\\
\bm{a}_{\mathrm{r}}\end{pmatrix}. $$

we have

$$ Q_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)-\bm{\mu}_{T}=\bm{a}+\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s), $$

and the change in reconstruction error introduced by quantization is

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\bm{a}+\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)\right\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{a}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2} \displaystyle=\bm{a}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{a}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}+\bm{a}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}+\frac{1}{2}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\frac{1}{2}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}. $$

Eq. (58) separates the quantization-induced change into linear and quadratic rounding terms. We first fix the input and take the expectation over the rounding randomness, then take the expectation over the spatial noise. The resulting moments give the exact expected contribution of each term. Partition $\bm{\mu}_{T}=(\bm{\mu}_{T,\mathrm{f}}^{\top},\bm{\mu}_{T,\mathrm{r}}^{\top})^{\top}$ in the same way as $\bm{\theta}$ . Substituting $\bm{a}=\bm{\theta}-\bm{\mu}_{T}$ into Eq. (58) and expanding the quadratic forms gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{a}+\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{a}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}\right]=\mathcal{T}_{1}+\mathcal{T}_{2}+\mathcal{T}_{3}+\mathcal{T}_{4}, $$

Here the four terms are

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{1} \displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}[\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}]+\mathbb{E}[\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}]+\mathbb{E}[\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}], \displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{2} \displaystyle:=-\bm{\mu}_{T,\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\mathbb{E}[\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}]-\bm{\mu}_{T,\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{r}}\mathbb{E}[\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}]-\bm{\mu}_{T,\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\mathbb{E}[\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}], \displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{3} \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}(\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}})_{jj}\mathbb{E}[(\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}})_{j}^{2}]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}(\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}})_{jj}\mathbb{E}[(\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}})_{j}^{2}], \displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{4} \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j\neq k}(\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}})_{jk}\mathbb{E}[(\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}})_{j}(\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}})_{k}]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j\neq k}(\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}})_{jk}\mathbb{E}[(\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}})_{j}(\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}})_{k}]. $$

$\mathcal{T}_{1}$ captures the coupling between the input parameters and rounding errors, while $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ contains rounding errors multiplied by the fixed reference $\bm{\mu}_{T}$ . The remaining terms are quadratic in the rounding errors: $\mathcal{T}_{3}$ collects coordinatewise squares, and $\mathcal{T}_{4}$ collects cross-coordinate products. The following lemma gives the conditional moments needed to evaluate these terms.

#### Lemma A.8 (Moments of Triangular-Dither Rounding).

Under Assumption A.5, let $\bm{z}$ be either the first-stage input $\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}$ or the compensated second-stage input $\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}$ , with its corresponding fixed step $\Delta>0$ . Let $e_{j}$ denote the parameter-space error introduced by $\operatorname{quant}_{b}(\cdot)$ in coordinate $j$ . For any integrable coefficient $\phi(\bm{z})$ , the conditional moments corresponding to $\mathcal{T}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{T}_{4}$ are

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\phi(\bm{z})e_{j}\mid\bm{z}] \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[e_{j}\mid\bm{z}] \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[e_{j}^{2}\mid\bm{z}] \displaystyle=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}, \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[e_{j}e_{k}\mid\bm{z}] \displaystyle=0\qquad(j\neq k). $$

Here the conditional expectation averages over the fresh rounding draws, which are independent across coordinates.

#### Proof.

Condition on the vector input $\bm{z}$ and fix a coordinate $j$ . Write $z=z_{j}$ . In parameter space, let $u,v$ be independent uniform variables on $[-\Delta/2,\Delta/2]$ . Fix $v$ and put $t=z+v$ . Let $a$ and $a+\Delta$ be the neighboring grid points with $a\leq t<a+\Delta$ , and set $r=t-a$ . Nearest rounding of $t+u$ returns $a$ with probability $1-r/\Delta$ and $a+\Delta$ with probability $r/\Delta$ . If $q$ denotes the output, direct calculation gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[q-t\mid z,v] \displaystyle=(-r)\left(1-\frac{r}{\Delta}\right)+(\Delta-r)\frac{r}{\Delta}=0, \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(q-t)^{2}\mid z,v] \displaystyle=r^{2}\left(1-\frac{r}{\Delta}\right)+(\Delta-r)^{2}\frac{r}{\Delta}=r(\Delta-r). $$

The full error is $e=q-z=(q-t)+v$ . Taking the expectation over $v$ therefore yields

$$ \mathbb{E}[e\mid z]=\mathbb{E}[v]=0. $$

As $v$ ranges uniformly over one grid cell, $r$ also ranges uniformly over $[0,\Delta)$ , irrespective of $z$ and the grid translation. By Eq. (60), the mixed term satisfies

$$ \mathbb{E}[v(q-t)\mid z]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[v\,\mathbb{E}[q-t\mid z,v]\mid z\right]=0. $$

Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[e^{2}\mid z] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(q-t)^{2}\mid z]+\mathbb{E}[v^{2}]+2\mathbb{E}[v(q-t)\mid z] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[r(\Delta-r)]+\mathbb{E}[v^{2}]+0 \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{0}^{\Delta}r(\Delta-r)\,\mathrm{d}r+\frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2}v^{2}\,\mathrm{d}v \displaystyle=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{6}+\frac{\Delta^{2}}{12}=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}. $$

This calculation holds for every coordinate of $\bm{z}$ . Since $\phi(\bm{z})$ is fixed conditional on $\bm{z}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}[\phi(\bm{z})e_{j}\mid\bm{z}]=\phi(\bm{z})\mathbb{E}[e_{j}\mid\bm{z}]=0. $$

Independent rounding draws across coordinates give

$$ \mathbb{E}[e_{j}e_{k}\mid\bm{z}]=\mathbb{E}[e_{j}\mid\bm{z}]\mathbb{E}[e_{k}\mid\bm{z}]=0\qquad(j\neq k). $$

This proves all four identities in the lemma. ∎

For the first group, condition on the full input $\bm{\theta}$ . For the remaining group, condition on both $\bm{\theta}$ and the first-stage error $\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}$ ; its compensated input is then fixed and its rounding draws are fresh. With $d_{\mathrm{f}}:=\dim\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}$ and $d_{\mathrm{r}}:=\dim\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{r}}$ , Lemma A.8 gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\mid\bm{\theta}] \displaystyle=\bm{0}, \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\mid\bm{\theta}] \displaystyle=\frac{\Delta_{b,\mathrm{f}}(\bm{w})^{2}}{4}\bm{I}_{d_{\mathrm{f}}}, \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}\mid\bm{\theta},\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}] \displaystyle=\bm{0}, \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\mid\bm{\theta},\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}] \displaystyle=\frac{\Delta_{b,\mathrm{r}}(\bm{w})^{2}}{4}\bm{I}_{d_{\mathrm{r}}}. $$

Eq. (61) gives

$$ \mathbb{E}[\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s(\bm{w}))\mid\bm{\theta}]=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{E}[\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\mid\bm{\theta}]\\
-\bm{K}\mathbb{E}[\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\mid\bm{\theta}]+\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}\mid\bm{\theta},\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}]\mid\bm{\theta}]\end{pmatrix}=\bm{0}. $$

Thus the mixed contribution in Eq. (58) has zero expectation. In the four-term expansion, $\mathcal{T}_{1}=\mathcal{T}_{2}=\mathcal{T}_{4}=0,$ and

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{3} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}(\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}})_{jj}\frac{\Delta_{b,\mathrm{f}}(\bm{w})^{2}}{4}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}(\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}})_{jj}\frac{\Delta_{b,\mathrm{r}}(\bm{w})^{2}}{4} \displaystyle=\frac{\Delta_{b,\mathrm{f}}(\bm{w})^{2}}{8}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}})+\frac{\Delta_{b,\mathrm{r}}(\bm{w})^{2}}{8}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}). $$

This evaluates the quantization contribution. The next lemma combines it with the temporal lag and spatial noise present before quantization.

#### Lemma A.9 (Exact Expected Reconstruction Error).

Under Assumptions A.3, A.4, and A.5, the simplified GPTQ model satisfies, for every $\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}$ and integer $b\geq b_{\min}$ ,

$$ \mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w})=\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w})+\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}(\bm{w}), $$

where the reconstruction error before quantization is

$$ \mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w}):=\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}+N_{G}R(\bm{w}),\qquad N_{G}:=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{G}). $$

The quantization contribution separates into the parameter energy

$$ \mathcal{Q}(\bm{w}):=\mathbb{E}\|\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\|_{2}^{2}=Ps(\bm{w})^{2}=\|\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\|_{2}^{2}+P\sigma^{2}R(\bm{w}) $$

and the precision-dependent coefficient

$$ \gamma_{b}:=\frac{c_{G}}{(2^{b}-1)^{2}},\qquad c_{G}:=\frac{H_{\mathrm{f}}^{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}})+H_{\mathrm{r}}^{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}})}{2P}>0. $$

#### Proof.

The latent-mean decomposition and zero-mean spatial noise give

$$ \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\|\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{G})R(\bm{w})=\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w}). $$

Set $\bm{a}=\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}$ and use the conditional zero mean of $\bm{\delta}_{b}$ . Expanding the definition of $\mathcal{E}_{b}$ and then applying Eq. (56) gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\|Q_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}};s(\bm{w}))-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\|\bm{a}+\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}};s(\bm{w}))\|_{\bm{G}}^{2} \displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w})+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{G}\mathbb{E}[\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}};s(\bm{w}))\mid\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}]\right]+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\|\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}};s(\bm{w}))\|_{\bm{G}}^{2} \displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w})+\frac{1}{8}\left[\Delta_{b,\mathrm{f}}(\bm{w})^{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}})+\Delta_{b,\mathrm{r}}(\bm{w})^{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}})\right] \displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w})+\frac{H_{\mathrm{f}}^{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}})+H_{\mathrm{r}}^{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}})}{2P(2^{b}-1)^{2}}\,Ps(\bm{w})^{2} \displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w})+\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}(\bm{w}). $$

This proves the identity for every averaging kernel in the stated model. ∎

Eq. (62) connects the expected reconstruction error to the lag-induced displacement of the averaged mean and the retained spatial noise. To make this dependence explicit along the LNWA frontier, we use mean age to parameterize temporal lag, derive the corresponding retained noise factor, and track the averaged latent mean. These relations determine the transition from tolerance to degradation.

Recall that the LNWA frontier is the family $\bm{w}_{\lambda}$ . The LAWA kernel $\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{LAWA}}}$ has mean age $m_{0}:=m(\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{LAWA}}})=(M-1)/2$ . We measure the reduction from LAWA by

$$ y:=m_{0}-m(\bm{w}_{\lambda}),\qquad 0\leq y\leq m_{0}. $$

Thus $y=0$ corresponds to LAWA, while $y=m_{0}$ corresponds to the most recent saved weight. The frontier coordinates in Lemma A.5 show that mean age decreases strictly as $\lambda$ increases. Hence each $y<m_{0}$ determines a unique $\lambda(y)$ . To simplify notation, we write $\bm{w}(y):=\bm{w}_{\lambda(y)}$ for that kernel. We also write $m(y):=m(\bm{w}(y))=m_{0}-y$ and $R(y):=R(\bm{w}(y))$ for its mean age and retained noise factor. For notational consistency, primes below denote derivatives along this parameterized frontier. In particular,

$$ \mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y):=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(y)),\qquad\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime\prime}(y):=\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}y^{2}}\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(y)), $$

and analogously for $\mathcal{P}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ . After the later change of variable to $x$ , primes correspondingly denote derivatives with respect to $x$ . Thus mean weight age decreases linearly with $y$ ; the accompanying change in spatial noise is determined next from the frontier kernel.

On a segment with $q\geq 2$ active saved weights, the positive coefficients have ages $0,\ldots,q-1$ . Uniform averaging over these weights has mean age $\bar{d}_{q}=(q-1)/2$ . The reduction relative to this local baseline is

$$ z_{q}:=\bar{d}_{q}-m(y)=y-\frac{M-q}{2}. $$

Lemma A.5 then gives the kernel coefficients

$$ w_{d}(y)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{q}+\frac{z_{q}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)}{D_{q}},&0\leq d<q,\\[4.0pt]
0,&d\geq q,\end{cases} $$

where $D_{q}:=q(q^{2}-1)/12$ . Squaring and summing the coefficients therefore gives the spatial noise factor

$$ R(y)=\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}w_{d}(y)^{2}=\frac{1}{q}+\frac{z_{q}^{2}}{D_{q}}, $$

whose derivatives are

$$ R^{\prime}(y)=\frac{2z_{q}}{D_{q}},\qquad R^{\prime\prime}(y)=\frac{2}{D_{q}}. $$

Finally, the original frontier parameter is recovered from $z_{q}=D_{q}\lambda m(y)$ as

$$ \lambda(y)=\frac{z_{q}}{D_{q}(m_{0}-y)}. $$

The endpoint is $y=m_{0}$ , with $\lambda(m_{0})=\infty$ . Write $\bm{\mu}(y):=\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}(y)}$ for the latent mean of this averaged state. It is affine within each support segment because the averaging coefficients are affine there. Using the latent-mean increments defined in Appendix A.1, its derivative is

$$ \displaystyle\bm{a}_{q}:=\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{D_{q}}\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)\bm{\mu}_{T-d} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{D_{q}}\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)\left(\bm{\mu}_{T-q+1}+\sum_{j=d+1}^{q-1}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{D_{q}}\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\left(\sum_{d=0}^{j-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)\right)\bm{v}_{T-j+1} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{D_{q}}\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\left(j\bar{d}_{q}-\frac{j(j-1)}{2}\right)\bm{v}_{T-j+1} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\frac{j(q-j)}{2D_{q}}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}. $$

The coefficients are nonnegative and satisfy

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\frac{j(q-j)}{2D_{q}}=1. $$

Thus $\bm{a}_{q}$ is a convex combination of the retained mean increments; its norm is at most $\bar{v}:=\max_{1\leq j<M}\|\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\|_{2}$ . We use this increment bound below to control changes in the averaged mean at support boundaries.

On a fixed-support segment, $\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y)=\bm{a}_{q}$ is constant and $R^{\prime\prime}(y)=2/D_{q}$ . The two components have second derivatives

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime\prime}(y) \displaystyle=\bm{a}_{q}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{a}_{q}+\frac{2N_{G}}{D_{q}}>0, \displaystyle\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime}(y) \displaystyle=2\|\bm{a}_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{2P\sigma^{2}}{D_{q}}>0. $$

Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime\prime}(y) \displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime\prime}(y)+\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime}(y) \displaystyle=\bm{a}_{q}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{a}_{q}+2\gamma_{b}\|\bm{a}_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{2N_{G}+2\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2}}{D_{q}}>0. $$

These results describe movement within one support segment. When the oldest positive averaging coefficient reaches zero, the active set changes and $\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y)$ can jump. We next relate these changes to the evolution of the latent mean over the retained window.

Across nearby saved weights in a stable training phase, latent-mean increments are small and change gradually with normalized training time. The following regularity condition bounds their magnitudes and adjacent variation.

#### Assumption A.6 (Local Regularity of the Latent Mean).

Measure training time as $t/T$ . The $M$ consecutive retained weights span the normalized length $\ell:=(M-1)/T$ , with spacing $h:=1/T=\ell/(M-1)$ . The forward latent increments satisfy

$$ \|\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\|_{2}\leq Vh\quad(1\leq j<M),\qquad\|\bm{v}_{T-j+1}-\bm{v}_{T-j+2}\|_{2}\leq Ah^{2}\quad(2\leq j<M), $$

where $V,A\geq 0$ are uniform over the considered late-training windows and independent of the spacing $h$ .

Summing the $d$ increments between $\bm{\mu}_{T-d}$ and $\bm{\mu}_{T}$ gives

$$ \|\bm{\mu}_{T-d}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}\leq Vdh. $$

Denote the mean under LAWA by $\bar{\bm{\mu}}:=M^{-1}\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}\bm{\mu}_{T-d}$ , and let $D_{\mu}:=\max_{d}\|\bm{\mu}_{T-d}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}$ . Averaging the preceding bound yields

$$ \|\bar{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}\leq\frac{1}{M}\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}Vdh=\frac{V\ell}{2}. $$

The second bound in Assumption A.6 verifies Assumption A.2 with $\kappa=Ah^{2}$ . The first bound controls $D_{\mu}$ and the LAWA mean displacement. Collecting these consequences gives

$$ \kappa=\frac{A\ell^{2}}{(M-1)^{2}},\qquad D_{\mu}\leq V\ell,\qquad\|\bar{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}\leq\frac{V\ell}{2}. $$

At a support transition, both the averaging kernel and the averaged latent mean remain continuous, although the mean slope may change. The following lemma bounds that change and the cumulative effect of the transitions.

#### Lemma A.10 (Slope Changes at Support Boundaries).

Under Assumption A.2, let $y_{j}$ , $1\leq j\leq M-2$ , be the internal support boundaries in increasing order, and write $\Delta\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y_{j}):=\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y_{j}+)-\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y_{j}-)$ . At every such boundary,

$$ \|\Delta\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y_{j})\|_{2}\leq\frac{\kappa}{2},\qquad R^{\prime}(y_{j}-)=R^{\prime}(y_{j}+). $$

For $0<y\leq m_{0}$ , their positions satisfy

$$ \frac{\sum_{y_{j}\leq y}y_{j}}{y^{2}}\leq H_{M}, $$

where

$$ H_{2}=0,\qquad H_{M}=\frac{12(M-2)(M-1)}{(3M-5)^{2}}\quad(M\geq 3). $$

#### Proof.

At a transition from $q+1$ to $q$ active weights, subtracting the two coefficient derivatives in Eq. (63) gives

$$ \Delta w_{d}^{\prime}=\frac{12(q-1-3d)}{q(q-1)(q+1)(q+2)}\quad(0\leq d<q),\qquad\Delta w_{q}^{\prime}=\frac{6}{(q+1)(q+2)}. $$

Set

$$ K_{qj}:=\frac{6j(j+1)(q-j)}{q(q-1)(q+1)(q+2)}\quad(1\leq j<q),\qquad K_{q0}=K_{qq}=0. $$

The corresponding change in the mean slope is

$$ \Delta\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y_{j})=\sum_{r=1}^{q-1}K_{qr}(\bm{\mu}_{T-r-1}-2\bm{\mu}_{T-r}+\bm{\mu}_{T-r+1}). $$

Expanding the second differences reproduces the coefficient changes: the endpoint coefficients are $K_{q1}$ and $K_{q,q-1}$ , and an interior coefficient is $K_{q,j-1}-2K_{qj}+K_{q,j+1}$ . Summing the coefficients gives

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{q-1}K_{qj}=\frac{6}{q(q-1)(q+1)(q+2)}\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}j(j+1)(q-j)=\frac{1}{2}. $$

Assumption A.2 therefore gives

$$ \|\Delta\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y_{j})\|_{2}\leq\kappa\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}K_{qj}=\frac{\kappa}{2}. $$

The oldest coefficient becomes zero at $z_{q+1}=(q+2)/6$ . Substituting this in the definition of $z_{q+1}$ gives $y_{j}=(M+2j-1)/6$ for $1\leq j\leq M-2$ . At the same transition, $z_{q}=(q-1)/6$ , and hence

$$ R^{\prime}(y_{j}-)=\frac{2z_{q+1}}{D_{q+1}}=\frac{4}{q(q+1)}=\frac{2z_{q}}{D_{q}}=R^{\prime}(y_{j}+). $$

Between consecutive boundaries the numerator in Eq. (67) is constant, and its ratio to $y^{2}$ decreases. At the $j$ th boundary the ratio is

$$ \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{j}y_{i}}{y_{j}^{2}}=\frac{6j(M+j)}{(M+2j-1)^{2}}. $$

This expression increases for $1\leq j\leq M-2$ , treating $j$ as a real variable, the sign of its derivative is the sign of $M(M-1)-2j>0$ . Its last value is $H_{M}$ . There are no internal boundaries when $M=2$ .

∎

For each precision $b$ , write the curvature on a segment with $q$ active weights as

$$ a_{q,b}:=\bm{a}_{q}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{a}_{q}+2\gamma_{b}\|\bm{a}_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{2N_{G}+2\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2}}{D_{q}},\qquad 2\leq q\leq M, $$

as given by Eq. (65), and define

$$ a_{\min,b}:=\min_{2\leq q\leq M}a_{q,b},\qquad a_{\max,b}:=\max_{2\leq q\leq M}a_{q,b}. $$

In particular,

$$ a_{\min,b}\geq\frac{2N_{G}+2\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2}}{D_{M}}>0. $$

Write $A_{\mu}:=\max_{0\leq d<M}\|\bm{\mu}_{T-d}\|_{2}$ and $g:=\|\bm{G}\|_{2}$ . The gradient with respect to the averaged mean satisfies

$$ \|\nabla_{\bm{\mu}}\mathcal{E}_{b}\|_{2}=\|\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}-\bm{\mu}_{T})+2\gamma_{b}\bm{\mu}\|_{2}\leq gD_{\mu}+2\gamma_{b}A_{\mu}=:G_{\mathcal{E},b}. $$

On each fixed-support segment, differentiation with respect to $y$ gives

$$ \mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y)=\bigl[\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}(y)-\bm{\mu}_{T})+2\gamma_{b}\bm{\mu}(y)\bigr]^{\top}\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y)+(N_{G}+\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2})R^{\prime}(y). $$

At a transition point $y_{j}$ , $\bm{\mu}(y)$ is continuous and Lemma A.10 gives $R^{\prime}(y_{j}-)=R^{\prime}(y_{j}+)$ . Thus the $R^{\prime}$ term has no jump, and

$$ \displaystyle|\Delta\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y_{j})| \displaystyle=\left|\bigl[\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}(y_{j})-\bm{\mu}_{T})+2\gamma_{b}\bm{\mu}(y_{j})\bigr]^{\top}\Delta\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y_{j})\right| \displaystyle\leq\frac{G_{\mathcal{E},b}\kappa}{2}. $$

Thus the adjacent-increment bound controls the effect of changing the active set on the slope of the expected reconstruction error.

We now locate where the expected reconstruction error along the frontier changes from tolerance to degradation. Define its average change from the starting kernel by

$$ F_{b}(y):=\frac{\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(y))-\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(0))}{y}\quad(y>0),\qquad F_{b}(0):=\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0+). $$

Thus $F_{b}(y)<0$ marks a kernel with lower error than the starting kernel, while $F_{b}(y)>0$ marks degradation. To determine whether this sign can change more than once, we bound the slope of $F_{b}$ across both support segments and their boundaries.

For a point $t$ away from the support boundaries, its slope equals the initial right slope plus the curvature accumulated within the support segments and the slope jumps at all preceding boundaries:

$$ \mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(t)=\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0+)+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime\prime}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s+\sum_{y_{j}<t}\Delta\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y_{j}). $$

Integrating this slope over $t\in[0,y]$ and exchanging the order of integration gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(y))-\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(0)) \displaystyle=y\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0+)+\int_{0}^{y}\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime\prime}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{y}\sum_{y_{j}<t}\Delta\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y_{j})\,\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle=y\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0+)+\int_{0}^{y}(y-t)\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sum_{y_{j}<y}(y-y_{j})\Delta\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y_{j}). $$

Each curvature value at $t$ contributes over the remaining interval of length $y-t$ , while a slope jump at $y_{j}$ contributes over the remaining interval of length $y-y_{j}$ .

For $y>0$ away from a support boundary, the quotient rule gives

$$ y^{2}F_{b}^{\prime}(y)=y\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y)-\bigl[\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(y))-\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(0))\bigr]. $$

Substituting the two preceding identities cancels the initial-slope terms. The remaining terms simplify as

$$ \displaystyle y^{2}F_{b}^{\prime}(y) \displaystyle=y\int_{0}^{y}\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t-\int_{0}^{y}(y-t)\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle+y\sum_{y_{j}<y}\Delta\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y_{j})-\sum_{y_{j}<y}(y-y_{j})\Delta\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y_{j}) \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{y}t\,\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sum_{y_{j}<y}y_{j}\Delta\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y_{j}). $$

The segment curvatures and Eqs. (67) and (68) bound its two terms by

$$ \frac{a_{\min,b}y^{2}}{2}\leq\int_{0}^{y}t\,\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\frac{a_{\max,b}y^{2}}{2},\qquad\left|\sum_{y_{j}<y}y_{j}\Delta\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y_{j})\right|\leq\frac{H_{M}G_{\mathcal{E},b}\kappa y^{2}}{2}. $$

Hence, with

$$ c_{b}:=a_{\min,b}-H_{M}G_{\mathcal{E},b}\kappa,\qquad C_{b}:=a_{\max,b}+H_{M}G_{\mathcal{E},b}\kappa, $$

we obtain

$$ \frac{c_{b}}{2}\leq F_{b}^{\prime}(y)\leq\frac{C_{b}}{2}. $$

The bounds extend to one-sided derivatives at support boundaries. It remains to establish $c_{b}>0$ and show that the error eventually exceeds its starting value. Eq. (66) gives $D_{\mu}\leq V\ell$ ; the triangle inequality then yields

$$ A_{\mu}=\max_{0\leq d<M}\|\bm{\mu}_{T-d}\|_{2}\leq\|\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}+D_{\mu}\leq A_{*}:=\|\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}+V\ell. $$

Substituting these bounds gives

$$ \displaystyle c_{b} \displaystyle\geq\frac{2N_{G}+2\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2}}{D_{M}}-H_{M}(gD_{\mu}+2\gamma_{b}A_{\mu})\kappa \displaystyle\geq\left[\frac{2N_{G}}{D_{M}}-\frac{H_{M}gVA}{(M-1)^{2}}\ell^{3}\right]+2\gamma_{b}\left[\frac{P\sigma^{2}}{D_{M}}-\frac{H_{M}A_{*}A}{(M-1)^{2}}\ell^{2}\right]. $$

The possible loss from boundary jumps decreases with the window length, whereas both positive curvature terms remain bounded below.

The same trajectory bounds also determine the comparison between the two endpoints. The corresponding means and noise factors are

$$ (\bm{\mu}(0),R(0))=(\bar{\bm{\mu}},1/M),\qquad(\bm{\mu}(m_{0}),R(m_{0}))=(\bm{\mu}_{T},1). $$

Here $y=0$ gives LAWA, while $y=m_{0}$ selects the most recent saved weight. Write $c_{M}:=1-1/M$ . The mean-norm difference satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\left|\|\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}^{2}-\|\bar{\bm{\mu}}\|_{2}^{2}\right| \displaystyle=\left|(\bm{\mu}_{T}+\bar{\bm{\mu}})^{\top}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})\right| \displaystyle\leq 2A_{*}\|\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}}\|_{2}\leq A_{*}V\ell. $$

Substituting these endpoint means and noise factors into $\mathcal{E}_{b}$ therefore yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(m_{0}))-\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(0)) \displaystyle=N_{G}c_{M}-\frac{1}{2}\|\bar{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}+\gamma_{b}\left(\|\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}^{2}-\|\bar{\bm{\mu}}\|_{2}^{2}+P\sigma^{2}c_{M}\right) \displaystyle\geq\left[N_{G}c_{M}-\frac{gV^{2}\ell^{2}}{8}\right]+\gamma_{b}\left[P\sigma^{2}c_{M}-A_{*}V\ell\right]. $$

We retain a fixed number of consecutive saved weights as $T$ increases. Their normalized time span therefore tends to zero.

#### Assumption A.7 (Fixed Retained Count under Time Refinement).

Consider a family of training trajectories indexed by $T\to\infty$ on the normalized time interval $[0,1]$ . The number $M\geq 2$ of consecutive retained weights is fixed across the family. The model dimension $P$ , calibration matrix $\bm{G}$ , and spatial-noise level $\sigma>0$ are fixed across the family. The constants $V,A$ in Assumption A.6 are uniform in $T$ , and $\sup_{T}\|\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}<\infty$ . Thus $\ell=(M-1)/T\to 0$ .

#### Lemma A.11 (Finite-Window Criterion and Its Consequences).

Under Assumptions A.3–A.6, let $A_{*}:=\|\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}+V\ell$ and $c_{M}:=1-1/M$ . If the normalized window length satisfies

$$ \displaystyle 0<\ell\leq\min\biggl\{\left(\frac{N_{G}(M-1)^{2}}{H_{M}gVAD_{M}}\right)^{1/3},\left(\frac{P\sigma^{2}(M-1)^{2}}{2H_{M}A_{*}AD_{M}}\right)^{1/2},\frac{2\sqrt{N_{G}c_{M}}}{\sqrt{g}\,V},\frac{P\sigma^{2}c_{M}}{2A_{*}V}\biggr\}, $$

where a term with zero denominator is $+\infty$ , then the expected reconstruction error obeys

$$ \displaystyle c_{b} \displaystyle\geq\frac{N_{G}+\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2}}{D_{M}}>0, \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(m_{0}))-\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(0)) \displaystyle\geq\frac{(N_{G}+\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2})c_{M}}{2}>0. $$

Under Assumption A.7, there is a $T_{0}$ , independent of $b$ , such that the displayed short-window criterion and hence Eq. (72) hold for every $T\geq T_{0}$ .

#### Proof.

The displayed condition is equivalent to the four inequalities

$$ \begin{gathered}\frac{H_{M}gVA\ell^{3}}{(M-1)^{2}}\leq\frac{N_{G}}{D_{M}},\qquad\frac{H_{M}A_{*}A\ell^{2}}{(M-1)^{2}}\leq\frac{P\sigma^{2}}{2D_{M}},\\
\frac{gV^{2}\ell^{2}}{8}\leq\frac{N_{G}c_{M}}{2},\qquad A_{*}V\ell\leq\frac{P\sigma^{2}c_{M}}{2}.\end{gathered} $$

The first row inserted into Eq. (70) gives

$$ c_{b}\geq\frac{N_{G}}{D_{M}}+\gamma_{b}\frac{P\sigma^{2}}{D_{M}}=\frac{N_{G}+\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2}}{D_{M}}>0. $$

The second row inserted into Eq. (71) gives

$$ \mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(m_{0}))-\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(0))\geq\frac{N_{G}c_{M}}{2}+\gamma_{b}\frac{P\sigma^{2}c_{M}}{2}>0. $$

These are the two bounds in Eq. (72).

To show that the four inequalities eventually hold, set $B_{\mu}:=\sup_{T}\|\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}<\infty$ . Since $M$ is fixed and $\ell=(M-1)/T\to 0$ , we have $A_{*}\leq B_{\mu}+V$ for all sufficiently large $T$ . The left sides of the four inequalities therefore tend to zero, while their right sides are fixed and positive because $N_{G}=\sigma^{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{G})/2>0$ , $P\sigma^{2}>0$ , and $c_{M}>0$ . Hence all four hold for the same $T_{0}$ . They contain no $b$ , so this $T_{0}$ is independent of precision. ∎

Eq. (69) bounds the change in $F_{b}$ along the frontier. Lemma A.11 makes its lower slope bound positive and places the final frontier point above the starting error. These facts locate the transition from tolerance to degradation. Normalize the age reduction as $x:=y/m_{0}=1-m(y)/m_{0}$ , with $x=0$ at the starting kernel and $x=1$ at the most recent saved weight.

#### Theorem A.2 (Finite Noise Tolerance and Degradation).

Under Assumptions A.3–A.7, for sufficiently large $T$ , consider the expected reconstruction error $\mathcal{E}_{b}=\mathcal{P}_{0}+\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}$ at a fixed precision $b\geq b_{\min}$ . Write $\mathcal{E}_{b}(x):=\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(m_{0}x))$ and set $k_{b}=m_{0}^{2}c_{b}>0$ , $K_{b}=m_{0}^{2}C_{b}$ . There is a unique threshold $\tau_{b}\in[0,1)$ . It is zero if $\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0+)\geq 0$ ; otherwise, it is the unique positive solution of $\mathcal{E}_{b}(\tau_{b})=\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)$ . It satisfies the explicit upper bound

$$ 0\leq\tau_{b}\leq\frac{D_{M}V}{m_{0}T}\left(\frac{gV\ell}{N_{G}}+\frac{2A_{*}}{P\sigma^{2}}\right). $$

(i) Tolerance: for $0<x\leq\tau_{b}$ ,

$$ -\frac{K_{b}}{2}x(\tau_{b}-x)\leq\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)\leq-\frac{k_{b}}{2}x(\tau_{b}-x). $$

(ii) Degradation: for $\tau_{b}<x\leq 1$ ,

$$ \mathcal{E}_{b}(x)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)\geq\frac{k_{b}}{2}x(x-\tau_{b})>0. $$

Moreover, $\mathcal{E}_{b}$ is strictly increasing beyond $\tau_{b}$ .

#### Proof.

Recall that $F_{b}(y)$ is the error change from $\bm{w}(0)$ divided by $y$ , with $F_{b}(0)$ equal to the initial right slope in $y$ . Since $y=m_{0}x$ , $\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0+)=m_{0}F_{b}(0)$ , so the two initial slopes have the same sign.

The frontier kernels make $\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(y))$ continuous and piecewise quadratic, so $F_{b}$ is continuous. Eq. (69) and Lemma A.11 give $F_{b}^{\prime}(y)\geq c_{b}/2>0$ on each support segment, including the one-sided bounds at its boundaries. Thus $F_{b}$ is strictly increasing. The endpoint bound in that lemma gives $F_{b}(m_{0})>0$ .

If $F_{b}(0)<0$ , there is a unique zero $y_{b}\in(0,m_{0})$ ; set $\tau_{b}=y_{b}/m_{0}$ . If $F_{b}(0)\geq 0$ , set $y_{b}=\tau_{b}=0$ . This establishes the threshold claimed in the theorem.

We next bound its location. At $y=0$ , $R^{\prime}(0)=0$ and $\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(0+)=\bm{a}_{M}$ , so

$$ F_{b}(0)=\bigl[\bm{G}(\bar{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu}_{T})+2\gamma_{b}\bar{\bm{\mu}}\bigr]^{\top}\bm{a}_{M},\qquad|F_{b}(0)|\leq(gD_{\mu}+2\gamma_{b}A_{\mu})\|\bm{a}_{M}\|_{2}. $$

The convex-combination representation of $\bm{a}_{M}$ gives $\|\bm{a}_{M}\|_{2}\leq V/T$ ; also $D_{\mu}\leq V\ell$ and $A_{\mu}\leq A_{*}$ . For $y_{b}>0$ ,

$$ -F_{b}(0)=F_{b}(y_{b})-F_{b}(0)=\int_{0}^{y_{b}}F_{b}^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\geq\int_{0}^{y_{b}}\frac{c_{b}}{2}\,\mathrm{d}t=\frac{c_{b}y_{b}}{2}. $$

Using $c_{b}\geq(N_{G}+\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2})/D_{M}$ from Lemma A.11 then gives

$$ \displaystyle\tau_{b} \displaystyle\leq\frac{2|F_{b}(0)|}{m_{0}c_{b}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{2D_{M}\|\bm{a}_{M}\|_{2}}{m_{0}}\frac{gD_{\mu}+2\gamma_{b}A_{\mu}}{N_{G}+\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{2D_{M}V}{m_{0}T}\left(\frac{gV\ell}{N_{G}}+\frac{2A_{*}}{P\sigma^{2}}\right). $$

Assumption A.7 fixes $M$ and bounds $A_{*}$ , so for sufficiently large $T$ this preliminary bound is smaller than $(M+1)/[3(M-1)]$ , the end of the first support segment in $x$ . On that segment, $\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(y))-\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(0))=F_{b}(0)y+a_{M,b}y^{2}/2$ , hence

$$ 0=F_{b}(y_{b})=F_{b}(0)+\frac{a_{M,b}}{2}y_{b}. $$

Using $a_{M,b}\geq 2(N_{G}+\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2})/D_{M}$ now gives the upper bound:

$$ \displaystyle\tau_{b} \displaystyle=\frac{-2F_{b}(0)}{m_{0}a_{M,b}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{D_{M}\|\bm{a}_{M}\|_{2}}{m_{0}}\frac{gD_{\mu}+2\gamma_{b}A_{\mu}}{N_{G}+\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{D_{M}V}{m_{0}T}\left(\frac{gV\ell}{N_{G}}+\frac{2A_{*}}{P\sigma^{2}}\right). $$

When $y_{b}=0$ , the upper bound is immediate.

For $y_{b}>0$ and $0\leq y\leq y_{b}$ , Eq. (69) and $F_{b}(y_{b})=0$ give

$$ -\frac{C_{b}}{2}(y_{b}-y)\leq-\int_{y}^{y_{b}}F_{b}^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=F_{b}(y)-F_{b}(y_{b})=F_{b}(y)\leq-\frac{c_{b}}{2}(y_{b}-y). $$

Multiplying by $y$ and setting $y=m_{0}x$ , $y_{b}=m_{0}\tau_{b}$ proves Eq. (73). If $y_{b}=0$ , that bound concerns only $x=0$ . For $y>y_{b}$ ,

$$ F_{b}(y)=F_{b}(y_{b})+\int_{y_{b}}^{y}F_{b}^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\geq F_{b}(y_{b})+\frac{c_{b}}{2}(y-y_{b})\geq\frac{c_{b}}{2}(y-y_{b}); $$

the last inequality also holds when $y_{b}=0$ , since then $F_{b}(0)\geq 0$ . Therefore

$$ \mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(y))-\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(0))=yF_{b}(y)\geq\frac{c_{b}}{2}y(y-y_{b}), $$

which proves Eq. (74).

Finally, for $y>y_{b}$ away from support boundaries,

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(y))=F_{b}(y)+yF_{b}^{\prime}(y)\geq\frac{c_{b}}{2}(2y-y_{b})>0. $$

The same inequality holds for both one-sided derivatives at a boundary. Multiplying by $m_{0}$ yields $\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)/\mathrm{d}x\geq k_{b}(2x-\tau_{b})/2>0$ . Continuity across the finitely many boundaries then gives strict increase throughout $(\tau_{b},1]$ . ∎

The corresponding threshold in the original frontier parameter is $\lambda_{{\rm tol},b}=\lambda(m_{0}\tau_{b})$ , obtained from Eq. (64). The next subsection characterizes precision-dependent averaging preferences.

### A.6 Precision-dependent averaging preference

The first main theorem compares the expected reconstruction error $\mathcal{E}_{b}$ with its value at LAWA for a fixed precision. We now determine how quantization precision shifts the preferred kernel and identify the precision at which its lag–noise preference changes.

Recall that $x=1-m/m_{0}$ increases from uniform averaging toward the most recent saved weight. Increasing $x$ reduces mean weight age and retains more spatial noise. Write $\bm{\mu}(x)=\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}(m_{0}x)}$ and $R(x)=R(\bm{w}(m_{0}x))$ . For any frontier function in this subsection, an argument $x$ means evaluation at $\bm{w}(m_{0}x)$ ; in particular, $\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)=\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(m_{0}x))$ . The exact identity in Lemma A.9 separates the unquantized error and the quantization contribution:

$$ \mathcal{E}_{b}(x)=\mathcal{P}_{0}(x)+\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}(x), $$

where $\gamma_{b}:=c_{G}/(2^{b}-1)^{2}$ . Its two precision-independent components are

$$ \mathcal{P}_{0}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}(x)-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}+N_{G}R(x),\qquad\mathcal{Q}(x)=\|\bm{\mu}(x)\|_{2}^{2}+P\sigma^{2}R(x). $$

Here $\mathcal{P}_{0}$ is the unquantized reconstruction error, and $\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}$ is the quantization contribution under the simplified GPTQ model. The coefficients $N_{G}$ and $c_{G}>0$ were defined in the preceding subsection. Precision enters $\mathcal{E}_{b}$ through $\gamma_{b}$ , which increases as precision decreases. The effect of this increase depends on how $\mathcal{Q}$ varies with $x$ .

We assume that, during a stable training phase, latent-mean increments are aligned with one another and with the latent mean at the start of the retained window.

#### Assumption A.8 (Pairwise Alignment of Latent-Mean Increments).

The latent increments in the retained window satisfy

$$ \bm{v}_{T-i+1}^{\top}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\geq 0\qquad(1\leq i,j<M). $$

#### Assumption A.9 (Alignment with the Oldest Retained Latent Mean).

The latent increments also satisfy

$$ \bm{\mu}_{T-M+1}^{\top}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\geq 0\qquad(1\leq j<M). $$

Assumption A.8 says that the progress increments do not oppose one another; Assumption A.9 says that they do not oppose the oldest retained latent mean. Their magnitudes and directions may differ. The next lemma uses both sets of inner products to show that favoring more recent saved weights cannot decrease the latent-mean norm.

#### Lemma A.12 (Latent-Mean Norm along LNWA).

Under Assumptions A.8 and A.9, every open LNWA support segment satisfies

$$ \bm{\mu}(x)^{\top}\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(x)\geq 0. $$

#### Proof.

Express each retained latent mean using the oldest mean and the progress made since that position:

$$ \bm{\mu}_{T-d}=\bm{\mu}_{T-M+1}+\sum_{j=d+1}^{M-1}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}. $$

Averaging these expressions, with $s_{j}(\bm{w})=\sum_{d=j}^{M-1}w_{d}$ as in Appendix A.1, gives

$$ \bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\bm{\mu}_{T-M+1}+\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}\bigl[1-s_{j}(\bm{w})\bigr]\bm{v}_{T-j+1}. $$

The coefficient $1-s_{j}(\bm{w})$ is the averaging mass assigned to saved weights that include the $j$ th increment. These coefficients are nonnegative, so Assumptions A.8 and A.9 give

$$ (\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}})^{\top}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}=\bm{\mu}_{T-M+1}^{\top}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}+\sum_{i=1}^{M-1}\bigl[1-s_{i}(\bm{w})\bigr]\bm{v}_{T-i+1}^{\top}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\geq 0. $$

On a segment with an active prefix of size $q\geq 2$ , differentiating the kernel in Eqs. (38)–(39) with respect to $x=1-m/m_{0}$ yields

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{m_{0}}{D_{q}}\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)\bm{\mu}_{T-d} \displaystyle=\frac{m_{0}}{2D_{q}}\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}j(q-j)\bm{v}_{T-j+1}. $$

The second equality follows from Eq. (75) and $\sum_{d=0}^{j-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)=j(q-j)/2$ . Each coefficient in this last sum is positive. Taking its inner product with $\bm{\mu}(x)$ and applying the preceding inequality proves $\bm{\mu}(x)^{\top}\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(x)\geq 0$ . ∎

Alignment describes the direction of recent progress. We further assume that the latent mean continues to change near the end of training.

#### Assumption A.10 (Nonvanishing Local Progress).

Let $h=1/T$ be the spacing in Assumption A.6 and $v_{*}:=\|\bm{v}_{T}\|_{2}$ . For constant $\nu>0$ independent of $h$ , the newest increment satisfies, for all sufficiently small $h$ ,

$$ v_{*}\geq\nu h. $$

Together with Assumptions A.6 and A.7, Assumption A.10 yields the quantitative local-progress bound in Lemma A.13.

#### Lemma A.13 (Local Progress Bound).

Under Assumptions A.6, A.7, and A.10, for sufficiently large $T$ , let $\rho_{T}:=((M-2)A/\nu)h$ . Then

$$ \max_{1\leq j<M}\|\bm{v}_{T-j+1}-\bm{v}_{T}\|_{2}\leq\rho_{T}v_{*},\qquad\rho_{T}\longrightarrow 0. $$

#### Proof.

Eq. (66) gives $\kappa=Ah^{2}$ . By the adjacent-increment bound and Assumption A.10,

$$ \|\bm{v}_{T-j+1}-\bm{v}_{T}\|_{2}\leq(j-1)\kappa\leq(M-2)Ah^{2}\leq\frac{(M-2)A}{\nu}h\,v_{*}=\rho_{T}v_{*}. $$

Since $M$ , $A$ , and $\nu$ are fixed and $h\to 0$ , we have $\rho_{T}\to 0$ , proving Eq. (76). ∎

In the interior of the first support segment, all $M$ averaging coefficients are positive. Its right endpoint is

$$ x_{\rm F}:=\frac{M+1}{3(M-1)},\qquad Y:=m_{0}x_{\rm F}=\frac{M+1}{6}. $$

For $M=2$ , this segment extends to $x=1$ . Let $\bm{u}:=m_{0}\bm{a}_{M}$ denote the change in the averaged mean per unit increase of $x$ on this segment. The frontier formulas give

$$ \bm{\mu}(x)=\bar{\bm{\mu}}+x\bm{u},\qquad R(x)=\frac{1}{M}+\frac{m_{0}^{2}x^{2}}{D_{M}},\qquad 0\leq x\leq x_{\rm F}. $$

The first derivatives at $x=0$ are

$$ \mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0^{+})=\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bar{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}),\qquad\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(0^{+})=2\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}. $$

Here $R^{\prime}(0^{+})=0$ , so spatial noise has no first-order contribution. To determine the signs of these slopes, write the two vectors in the first expression as averages of the retained increments:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\bm{u}}{m_{0}} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}\frac{j(M-j)}{2D_{M}}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}, \displaystyle\frac{\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}}}{m_{0}} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}\frac{2(M-j)}{M(M-1)}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}. $$

Both sets of nonnegative coefficients sum to one. By Lemma A.13, each average is within $\rho_{T}v_{*}$ of $\bm{v}_{T}$ in Euclidean norm. Thus $\bm{G}\succ 0$ and $\rho_{T}\to 0$ give, for sufficiently large $T$ ,

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0^{+})}{m_{0}^{2}} \displaystyle=\left(\frac{\bm{u}}{m_{0}}\right)^{\top}\bm{G}\left(\frac{\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}}}{m_{0}}\right) \displaystyle\geq\bigl[\lambda_{\min}(\bm{G})-\|\bm{G}\|_{2}(2\rho_{T}+\rho_{T}^{2})\bigr]v_{*}^{2}>0. $$

For the other slope, Assumptions A.8 and A.9 give $\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\geq 0$ by Eq. (75). Since the first average above has nonnegative coefficients,

$$ \mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(0^{+})=\frac{m_{0}}{D_{M}}\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}j(M-j)\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\geq 0. $$

Hence increasing $x$ initially lowers the unquantized error and changes the quantization contribution at the nonnegative rate $\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(0^{+})$ . Their second derivatives are constant on this segment:

$$ a:=\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})=\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{u}+\frac{2N_{G}m_{0}^{2}}{D_{M}}>0,\qquad c:=\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})=2\|\bm{u}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{2P\sigma^{2}m_{0}^{2}}{D_{M}}>0. $$

Consequently, the following quadratic expansions are exact throughout the first support segment:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{0}(x)-\mathcal{P}_{0}(0) \displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0^{+})x+\frac{\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})}{2}x^{2}, \displaystyle\mathcal{Q}(x)-\mathcal{Q}(0) \displaystyle=\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(0^{+})x+\frac{\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})}{2}x^{2}. $$

Under the assumptions of Theorem A.2, the upper bound on $\tau_{b}$ lies below $x_{\rm F}$ for sufficiently large $T$ . Hence Eq. (77) applies throughout the tolerance interval. We next use these quadratics to locate the minimizers of $\mathcal{P}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{b}$ and show that they are global.

#### Lemma A.14 (Optima on the First Support Segment).

Under Assumptions A.3–A.10, for sufficiently large $T$ , the unique minimizer of $\mathcal{P}_{0}$ on $[0,1]$ is $x_{0}=\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})/a\in(0,x_{\rm F})$ . For every evaluated precision $b\geq b_{\min}$ , the unique minimizer of $\mathcal{E}_{b}$ on $[0,1]$ is

$$ x_{b}=\max\left\{0,\frac{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})-2\gamma_{b}\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}}{a+c\gamma_{b}}\right\}\in[0,x_{0}). $$

#### Proof.

The preceding estimates give $\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0^{+})<0$ and $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(0^{+})\geq 0$ . We next show that the unquantized error increases beyond the first segment. Set $\bar{v}:=\max_{1\leq j<M}\|\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\|_{2}$ . Assumptions A.6 and A.7 give $\bar{v}\leq Vh$ and, for sufficiently large $T$ ,

$$ \sqrt{g}\,(M-1)\bar{v}\leq\sqrt{g}\,V\ell\leq 2\sqrt{N_{G}/M}. $$

In the mean-age coordinate $y$ , the increment bound and the convex coefficients in $\bm{a}_{q}$ imply

$$ \|\bm{\mu}(y)-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}\leq\bar{v}\,m(y)\leq m_{0}\bar{v},\qquad\|\bm{a}_{q}\|_{2}\leq\bar{v}. $$

The derivative $R^{\prime}(y)$ is continuous and increasing across the support segments. For $y\geq Y$ , it is at least $R^{\prime}(Y)=2Y/D_{M}=4/[M(M-1)]$ . Consequently, on every such segment,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w}(y)) \displaystyle=\bm{a}_{q}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}(y)-\bm{\mu}_{T})+N_{G}R^{\prime}(y) \displaystyle\geq-gm_{0}\bar{v}^{2}+\frac{4N_{G}}{M(M-1)} \displaystyle\geq\frac{2N_{G}}{M(M-1)}>0. $$

The final inequality uses the displayed bound on $\bar{v}$ and $m_{0}=(M-1)/2$ . The same estimates apply to the one-sided derivatives at support boundaries. For $M=2$ , they apply to the left derivative at $Y=m_{0}$ .

On the first segment, $\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0^{+})<0$ and $\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime\prime}=a>0$ . Its derivative is positive at $x_{\rm F}$ by the preceding bound, so it vanishes once at $x_{0}=\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})/a\in(0,x_{\rm F})$ . Thereafter $\mathcal{P}_{0}$ increases on every segment. Continuity at their boundaries makes $x_{0}$ its unique global minimum.

For $\mathcal{E}_{b}$ , the initial slope is $\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bar{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu}_{T})+2\gamma_{b}\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}$ . If it is nonnegative, Theorem A.2 gives $\tau_{b}=0$ and strict increase for $x>0$ , so $x_{b}=0$ . If it is negative, Lemma A.12 gives $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(x)=2\bm{\mu}(x)^{\top}\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(x)+P\sigma^{2}R^{\prime}(x)>0$ for $x>0$ within each segment. In particular, $\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(x_{0})=\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(x_{0})>0$ . Solving the affine derivative of Eq. (77) therefore gives the unique zero in $(0,x_{0})$ stated in Eq. (78). Beyond the first segment, both $\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime}$ and $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ are positive. Hence this zero is the unique global minimizer of $\mathcal{E}_{b}$ . ∎

Lemma A.14 gives the global minimizer at each evaluated precision. In Eq. (78), precision enters only through $\gamma_{b}$ : lower precision increases this coefficient and gives more weight to the quantization cost, while higher precision reduces it. This changes the optimal trade-off between denoising and reducing temporal lag. The following theorem identifies the precision at which that preference changes and proves how the optimum responds.

#### Theorem A.3 (Precision-Dependent Averaging Preference).

Under Assumptions A.3–A.10, for sufficiently large $T$ , define

$$ b_{\mathrm{crit}}:=\log_{2}\!\left(1+\sqrt{\frac{2c_{G}\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}}{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})}}\right). $$

For every evaluated precision $b\geq b_{\min}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle b\leq b_{\mathrm{crit}} \displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad x_{b}=0,\quad\tau_{b}=0\qquad\text{{(less spatial noise)}}, \displaystyle b>b_{\mathrm{crit}} \displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad x_{b}>0,\quad\tau_{b}>0\qquad\text{{(less temporal lag)}}. $$

The optimal position $x_{b}$ is nondecreasing in $b$ and strictly increasing in the regime $b>b_{\mathrm{crit}}$ . If $b_{\mathrm{crit}}<b_{\min}$ , all evaluated precisions lie in the second regime.

#### Proof.

By Lemma A.14, $x_{b}$ is determined by the sign of $\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0^{+})$ . Since
