## Appendix B Detailed Proofs for Sections 3 and 4

### B.1 Stationarity notions

Let $g:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}$ be twice-continuously differentiable. We say that $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ is a first-order stationary point if $\nabla g(Y)=0.$ We say that $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ is a second-order stationary point (SOSP) if $\nabla g(Y)=0$ and $\nabla^{2}g(Y)[H,H]\geq 0$ for any direction $H\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}.$ We say that $Y$ is a local minimum if there exists an open ball $B$ containing $Y$ such that $g(Y)\leq g(Y^{\prime})$ for every $Y^{\prime}\in B$ . $Y$ is a global minimum if $g(Y)\leq g(Y^{\prime})$ for every $Y^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ . A spurious local minimum is a local minimum that is not global. A standard result shows that gradient descent with random initialization avoids strict saddles almost surely; when the iterates converge, this makes SOSPs the relevant local optimality objects [Lee et al., 2016]. In particular, every local minimum is an SOSP.

### B.2 Proof that $l_{2}$ regularization induces a nuclear-norm target

#### Proof.

Fix a matrix $M\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}$ with $\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r$ . For every factorization $UV^{\top}=M$ , the balancing term is nonnegative, and the standard variational characterization of the nuclear norm gives

$$ \|M\|_{*}\leq\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr). $$

Therefore

$$ \frac{\mu}{4}\,\|U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\,\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)\geq\lambda\|M\|_{*}. $$

Taking the infimum over all pairs $(U,V)$ with $UV^{\top}=M$ yields the lower bound

$$ \inf_{U,V:\,UV^{\top}=M}\left[\frac{\mu}{4}\,\|U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\,\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)\right]\geq\lambda\|M\|_{*}. $$

To prove the reverse inequality, let

$$ M=P\Sigma Q^{\top} $$

be a compact SVD, where $\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times s}$ and $s=\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r$ . Define the square-root lift

$$ U:=[P\Sigma^{1/2},\,0_{n_{1}\times(r-s)}],\qquad V:=[Q\Sigma^{1/2},\,0_{n_{2}\times(r-s)}]. $$

Then $UV^{\top}=M$ , and

$$ U^{\top}U=V^{\top}V=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma,0_{r-s}), $$

so the balancing penalty vanishes. Moreover,

$$ \frac{\lambda}{2}\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma+\operatorname{tr}\Sigma\bigr)=\lambda\,\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\lambda\|M\|_{*}. $$

Hence the infimum over factorizations with fixed product $M$ is $\lambda\|M\|_{*}$ .

Now minimize first over all factor pairs with fixed product $M$ , and then over all matrices with $\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r$ . This gives

$$ \inf_{U,V}h_{\mu,\lambda}(U,V)=\inf_{\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r}\bigl[\widehat{L}(M)+\lambda\|M\|_{*}\bigr]=\inf_{\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r}F_{\lambda}(M), $$

which is the matrix-space equivalence used in the main text. ∎

### B.3 Detailed Proof of Theorem 4.2

The proof is organized around one lifted error matrix. We compare the candidate factors with the balanced lift of the regularized matrix target, and then show that any nonzero lifted error creates a descent-or-negative-curvature certificate. This is why the proof is carried out in the stacked factor variable $X$ , rather than directly in the product $UV^{\top}$ : the SOSP condition is a factor-space condition, while the curvature assumption is a matrix-space condition. The stacked notation lets us pass between the two.

We retain a general balancing weight $0<\mu<\alpha_{k}$ throughout the certificate construction and specialize to $\mu=\alpha_{k}/2$ when concluding the main theorem. The corresponding general- $\mu$ guarantee is stated in Appendix B.3.2.

Throughout this subsection, fix a candidate pair $(U,V)$ , write

$$ M:=UV^{\top},\qquad\Delta:=M-M_{\star}^{\lambda},\qquad X:=\begin{bmatrix}U\\
V\end{bmatrix},\qquad Z:=\begin{bmatrix}U_{\star}\\
V_{\star}\end{bmatrix},\qquad E:=XX^{\top}-ZZ^{\top}, $$

and let

$$ J:=\operatorname{diag}(I_{n_{1}},-I_{n_{2}}). $$

Recall that $U_{\star}V_{\star}^{\top}=M_{\star}^{\lambda}$ and $U_{\star}^{\top}U_{\star}=V_{\star}^{\top}V_{\star}$ , so

$$ Z^{\top}JZ=0. $$

If $E=0$ , then the $(1,2)$ -block of $XX^{\top}=ZZ^{\top}$ already gives $UV^{\top}=M_{\star}^{\lambda}$ . The proof therefore assumes $E\neq 0$ and derives a contradiction with second-order stationarity.

#### KKT slack for the regularized target.

The theorem targets the nuclear-norm-regularized matrix-space minimizer $M_{\star}^{\lambda}$ , so the correct stationarity condition is a KKT condition rather than $\nabla\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})=0$ . The slack form below is the device that keeps the regularized target in the proof: it creates a positive-semidefinite term that vanishes on the target lift $Z$ , and hence can only help when we upper-bound the certificate.

#### Proposition B.1 (KKT slack form of the regularized target).

There exists a matrix

$$ S_{\star}=P_{\star}Q_{\star}^{\top}+W_{\star}\in\partial\|M_{\star}^{\lambda}\|_{*} $$

such that

$$ \nabla\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})+\lambda S_{\star}=0, $$

where

$$ P_{\star}^{\top}W_{\star}=0,\qquad W_{\star}Q_{\star}=0,\qquad\|W_{\star}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 1. $$

If

$$ \widetilde{S}_{\star}:=\begin{bmatrix}0&S_{\star}\\
S_{\star}^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix}, $$

then

$$ I-\widetilde{S}_{\star}\succeq 0,\qquad(I-\widetilde{S}_{\star})Z=0. $$

#### Proof.

Since $M_{\star}^{\lambda}$ minimizes $F_{\lambda}(M)=\widehat{L}(M)+\lambda\|M\|_{*}$ and $\widehat{L}$ is differentiable, Fermat’s rule gives

$$ 0\in\nabla\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})+\lambda\,\partial\|M_{\star}^{\lambda}\|_{*}. $$

Hence Eq. (11) holds for some $S_{\star}\in\partial\|M_{\star}^{\lambda}\|_{*}$ . Writing the compact SVD $M_{\star}^{\lambda}=P_{\star}\Sigma_{\star}Q_{\star}^{\top}$ , the standard subgradient formula for the nuclear norm yields

$$ S_{\star}=P_{\star}Q_{\star}^{\top}+W_{\star},\qquad P_{\star}^{\top}W_{\star}=0,\qquad W_{\star}Q_{\star}=0,\qquad\|W_{\star}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 1. $$

Because $\|\widetilde{S}_{\star}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|S_{\star}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 1$ , we have $I-\widetilde{S}_{\star}\succeq 0$ . Moreover,

$$ S_{\star}V_{\star}=(P_{\star}Q_{\star}^{\top}+W_{\star})Q_{\star}\Sigma_{\star}^{1/2}=P_{\star}\Sigma_{\star}^{1/2}=U_{\star}, $$

because $W_{\star}Q_{\star}=0$ . Similarly,

$$ S_{\star}^{\top}U_{\star}=V_{\star}. $$

Therefore

$$ \widetilde{S}_{\star}Z=\begin{bmatrix}S_{\star}V_{\star}\\
S_{\star}^{\top}U_{\star}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}U_{\star}\\
V_{\star}\end{bmatrix}=Z, $$

which proves Eq. (12). ∎

#### Lifted operators and differential identities.

We next rewrite the first- and second-order conditions of the factorized objective in lifted coordinates. The averaged operator below comes from expanding the matrix-space loss along the segment from $M_{\star}^{\lambda}$ to $M=UV^{\top}$ ; the pointwise operator is the Hessian that appears in the SOSP condition at the current factor pair. Both inherit the same lower and upper curvature constants after lifting, up to the balancing curvature.

Define the segment-average Hessian

$$ \overline{H}_{\Delta}[H]:=\int_{0}^{1}\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda}+t\Delta)[H]\,dt, $$

its block lift

$$ \widetilde{\overline{H}}_{\Delta}[E]:=\begin{bmatrix}0&\overline{H}_{\Delta}[E_{12}]\\
\overline{H}_{\Delta}[E_{12}]^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix}, $$

and the composite lifted operator

$$ \mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E]:=2\widetilde{\overline{H}}_{\Delta}[E]+2\mu JEJ. $$

Also define

$$ g_{\mu,\lambda}(X):=4\,h_{\mu,\lambda}(U,V),\qquad G_{M}:=\nabla\widehat{L}(M),\qquad\widetilde{G}_{M}:=\begin{bmatrix}0&G_{M}\\
G_{M}^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix}. $$

For a lifted direction $D=\begin{bmatrix}\Delta U\\ \Delta V\end{bmatrix},$ set

$$ \widetilde{H}_{M}[E]:=\begin{bmatrix}0&\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}(M)[E_{12}]\\
\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}(M)[E_{12}]^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\mu,X}[E]:=2\widetilde{H}_{M}[E]+2\mu JEJ. $$

A direct differentiation gives

$$ \displaystyle\bigl\langle\nabla g_{\mu,\lambda}(X),D\bigr\rangle \displaystyle=\Bigl\langle 2\widetilde{G}_{M}+2\mu JXX^{\top}J+2\lambda I,\;DX^{\top}+XD^{\top}\Bigr\rangle, \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\bigl\langle\nabla^{2}g_{\mu,\lambda}(X)[D],D\bigr\rangle \displaystyle=\Bigl\langle 2\widetilde{G}_{M}+2\mu JXX^{\top}J+2\lambda I,\;DD^{\top}\Bigr\rangle \displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{2}\Bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\mu,X}[DX^{\top}+XD^{\top}],\;DX^{\top}+XD^{\top}\Bigr\rangle. $$

By the pathwise rank- $k$ RSC/RSS assumption for the candidate product $M$ , the curvature bounds apply along the segment $\{M_{\star}^{\lambda}+t\Delta:t\in[0,1]\}$ and at the current point $M$ corresponding to $t=1$ . In particular, let

$$ \displaystyle m_{\mu} \displaystyle:=2\min\{\mu,\alpha_{k}-\mu\},\quad L_{\mu}:=2\max\{\mu,\beta_{k}-\mu\}, \displaystyle\kappa_{\mu} \displaystyle:=\frac{L_{\mu}}{m_{\mu}},\quad s_{\mu}:=\frac{L_{\mu}+m_{\mu}}{2},\quad d_{\mu}:=\frac{L_{\mu}-m_{\mu}}{2}. $$

For a lifted symmetric matrix

$$ B=\begin{bmatrix}B_{11}&B_{12}\\
B_{12}^{\top}&B_{22}\end{bmatrix} $$

with $\operatorname{rank}(B_{12})\leq k$ , the RSC/RSS assumption and the identity $\langle JBJ,B\rangle=\|B_{11}\|_{F}^{2}+\|B_{22}\|_{F}^{2}-2\|B_{12}\|_{F}^{2}$ give

$$ \displaystyle\bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[B],B\bigr\rangle \displaystyle=4\int_{0}^{1}\langle\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda}+t\Delta)[B_{12}],B_{12}\rangle\,dt+2\mu\langle JBJ,B\rangle. $$

Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[B],B\bigr\rangle \displaystyle\geq 2\mu(\|B_{11}\|_{F}^{2}+\|B_{22}\|_{F}^{2})+(4\alpha_{k}-4\mu)\|B_{12}\|_{F}^{2}, \displaystyle\bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[B],B\bigr\rangle \displaystyle\leq 2\mu(\|B_{11}\|_{F}^{2}+\|B_{22}\|_{F}^{2})+(4\beta_{k}-4\mu)\|B_{12}\|_{F}^{2}. $$

Since $\|B\|_{F}^{2}=\|B_{11}\|_{F}^{2}+\|B_{22}\|_{F}^{2}+2\|B_{12}\|_{F}^{2}$ , this implies

$$ m_{\mu}\|E\|_{F}^{2}\leq\bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E],E\bigr\rangle\leq L_{\mu}\|E\|_{F}^{2} $$

for every lifted symmetric matrix $E$ whose off-diagonal block has rank at most $k$ . The same calculation at the point $M$ gives

$$ m_{\mu}\|H\|_{F}^{2}\leq\bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\mu,X}[H],H\bigr\rangle\leq L_{\mu}\|H\|_{F}^{2} $$

for every lifted direction $H$ whose off-diagonal block has rank at most $k$ .

The next decomposition is the algebraic hinge of the proof. It rewrites the first-order expression at $X$ as the sum of a curvature term applied to the lifted error $E$ and a PSD slack $N_{\mu,\lambda}$ . The slack is harmless in the later upper bounds because it is positive semidefinite and annihilates $Z$ .

#### Lemma B.2 (Exact decomposition with KKT slack).

Define

$$ N_{\mu,\lambda}:=2\mu JZZ^{\top}J+2\lambda(I-\widetilde{S}_{\star}). $$

Then

$$ 2\widetilde{G}_{M}+2\mu JXX^{\top}J+2\lambda I=\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E]+N_{\mu,\lambda}. $$

Moreover,

$$ N_{\mu,\lambda}\succeq 0,\qquad N_{\mu,\lambda}Z=0. $$

#### Proof.

By the fundamental theorem of calculus,

$$ G_{M}=\nabla\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})+\overline{H}_{\Delta}[\Delta]. $$

Using Eq. (11), this becomes

$$ G_{M}=-\lambda S_{\star}+\overline{H}_{\Delta}[\Delta]. $$

Since $E_{12}=\Delta$ , we have

$$ 2\widetilde{G}_{M}=-2\lambda\widetilde{S}_{\star}+2\widetilde{\overline{H}}_{\Delta}[E]. $$

Also,

$$ JXX^{\top}J=JEJ+JZZ^{\top}J. $$

Substituting these identities yields

$$ 2\widetilde{G}_{M}+2\mu JXX^{\top}J+2\lambda I=2\widetilde{\overline{H}}_{\Delta}[E]+2\mu JEJ+2\mu JZZ^{\top}J+2\lambda(I-\widetilde{S}_{\star}), $$

which is Eq. (18).

By Eq. (12), $I-\widetilde{S}_{\star}\succeq 0$ and $(I-\widetilde{S}_{\star})Z=0$ . Also, $(JZ)(JZ)^{\top}\succeq 0$ and

$$ (JZ)(JZ)^{\top}Z=JZ(Z^{\top}JZ)=0 $$

because $Z^{\top}JZ=0$ . Therefore Eq. (19) follows. ∎

#### B.3.1 Admissible Loss Class and Universal Envelope

The direct theorem proof can be carried out using only the actual empirical loss $\widehat{L}$ . For the Section 5 interface, however, it is helpful to separate the certificate calculation from the specific loss and retain only the matrix-space target condition and curvature bounds actually used by the argument.

For the fixed pair $(X,Z)$ , define the matrix-space path

$$ M_{t}:=M_{\star}^{\lambda}+t\Delta,\qquad t\in[0,1]. $$

Relative to the fixed curvature parameters $(\alpha_{k},\beta_{k})$ and a rank level $k\geq r+r_{\star}$ , define the admissible loss class

$$ \mathcal{F}_{\lambda,\alpha_{k},\beta_{k}}^{(k)}(X,Z):=\left\{\begin{aligned} h\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}};\mathbb{R})\ :\ &M_{\star}^{\lambda}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{M}\bigl[h(M)+\lambda\|M\|_{*}\bigr],\\
&\alpha_{k}\|H\|_{F}^{2}\leq\langle\nabla^{2}h(M_{t})[H],H\rangle\leq\beta_{k}\|H\|_{F}^{2},\\
&\text{for all }t\in[0,1]\text{ and all }H\text{ with }\operatorname{rank}(H)\leq k\end{aligned}\right\}. $$

For each $h\in\mathcal{F}_{\lambda,\alpha_{k},\beta_{k}}^{(k)}(X,Z)$ , let

$$ g_{\mu,\lambda}^{h}(X):=4\left(h(UV^{\top})+\frac{\mu}{4}\|U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)\right) $$

denote the lifted objective obtained by replacing $\widehat{L}$ with $h$ . The corresponding fixed-loss certificate is

$$ \psi_{\lambda,h}(t_{1},t_{2}):=t_{1}\,\bigl\langle\nabla g_{\mu,\lambda}^{h}(X),D_{0}\bigr\rangle+\frac{t_{2}}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{r_{\star}}\bigl\langle\nabla^{2}g_{\mu,\lambda}^{h}(X)[D_{i}],D_{i}\bigr\rangle, $$

and the universal envelope is

$$ \Psi_{\lambda}(t_{1},t_{2}):=\sup_{h\in\mathcal{F}_{\lambda,\alpha_{k},\beta_{k}}^{(k)}(X,Z)}\psi_{\lambda,h}(t_{1},t_{2}). $$

Here the curvature parameters $(\alpha_{k},\beta_{k})$ are fixed throughout the subsection, so we suppress them from the notation of $\Psi_{\lambda}$ . Under Assumptions 3.1 and 4.1, the actual loss $\widehat{L}$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda,\alpha_{k},\beta_{k}}^{(k)}(X,Z)$ . Hence

$$ \psi_{\lambda,\widehat{L}}(t_{1},t_{2})\leq\Psi_{\lambda}(t_{1},t_{2}). $$

The detailed proof below still bounds $\psi_{\lambda,\widehat{L}}$ directly. We keep the envelope formulation because it makes explicit which ingredients of the proof are loss-specific and which are purely geometric, and this is the separation reused later in Section 5.

#### Certificate family.

We now construct the directions used to test second-order stationarity. The lifted error has a part seen by the current column space of $X$ and a part orthogonal to it. The direction $D_{0}$ probes the former through the first-order condition, while the directions $D_{i}$ probe the latter through the second-order condition. The scalar weights $t_{1},t_{2}$ choose how much of each probe to use.

Let

$$ \Pi_{X}:=XX^{\dagger},\qquad Z_{\perp}:=(I-\Pi_{X})Z. $$

Split the lifted error into tangent and normal components:

$$ E_{T}:=\Pi_{X}E+E\Pi_{X}-\Pi_{X}E\Pi_{X},\qquad E_{N}:=(I-\Pi_{X})E(I-\Pi_{X})=-Z_{\perp}Z_{\perp}^{\top}, $$

so that $E=E_{T}+E_{N}$ and $\langle E_{T},E_{N}\rangle=0$ .

Choose a unit vector $u\in\mathbb{R}^{r}$ satisfying

$$ u^{\top}X^{\top}Xu=\lambda_{\min}(X^{\top}X), $$

and define

$$ D_{0}:=\left(I-\frac{1}{2}XX^{\dagger}\right)Z(X^{\dagger}Z)^{\top}-\frac{1}{2}X,\qquad D_{i}:=Z_{\perp}e_{i}u^{\top},\quad i=1,\dots,r_{\star}. $$

Direct expansion gives the basic identities

$$ D_{0}X^{\top}+XD_{0}^{\top}=-E_{T}, $$

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{r_{\star}}D_{i}D_{i}^{\top}=-E_{N}. $$

In the nontrivial case $X\neq 0$ and $Z_{\perp}\neq 0$ , define

$$ a:=\frac{\|Z_{\perp}Z_{\perp}^{\top}\|_{F}}{\|E\|_{F}},\qquad b_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\frac{\lambda_{\min}(X^{\top}X)\,\operatorname{tr}(Z_{\perp}Z_{\perp}^{\top})}{\|E\|_{F}\,\|Z_{\perp}Z_{\perp}^{\top}\|_{F}}. $$

For $\tau\in[0,a]$ , let

$$ t_{1}(\tau):=\sqrt{\frac{1-\tau^{2}}{1-a^{2}}},\qquad t_{2}(\tau):=\frac{\tau}{a},\qquad F_{\tau}:=t_{1}(\tau)E_{T}+t_{2}(\tau)E_{N}. $$

Then

$$ \|F_{\tau}\|_{F}=\|E\|_{F},\qquad\langle E,F_{\tau}\rangle=\bigl(\sqrt{1-a^{2}}\sqrt{1-\tau^{2}}+a\tau\bigr)\|E\|_{F}^{2}. $$

All averaged-curvature applications below are admissible under Assumption 4.1: the lifted matrices $E$ , $F_{\tau}$ , and their linear combinations have column space contained in $\operatorname{span}(X,Z)$ , hence rank at most $r+r_{\star}$ , and therefore their $(1,2)$ -blocks have rank at most $r+r_{\star}\leq k$ . For the pointwise Hessian terms, each $\dot{E}_{i}:=D_{i}X^{\top}+XD_{i}^{\top}$ has rank at most two, so its $(1,2)$ -block also has rank at most $2\leq k$ .

Specializing Eq. (21) to the actual empirical loss $\widehat{L}$ , define

$$ \psi_{\lambda}(t_{1},t_{2}):=\psi_{\lambda,\widehat{L}}(t_{1},t_{2}). $$

If $(U,V)$ is an SOSP of $h_{\mu,\lambda}$ , then

$$ \psi_{\lambda}(t_{1},t_{2})\geq 0\qquad\text{for all }t_{1},t_{2}\geq 0. $$

For $\eta\geq 0$ , define

$$ \phi_{\eta}(\tau;a,b_{\mathrm{geo}}):=\sqrt{1-a^{2}}\sqrt{1-\tau^{2}}+\bigl(a-(1+\eta)b_{\mathrm{geo}}\bigr)\tau-\eta. $$

The remaining lemmas justify that this certificate family is rich enough. The scalar clipping and blockwise Eckart–Young bounds are purely geometric; they quantify how the extra $r-r_{\star}$ factor directions contribute to the certificate. This is the only place where the rank threshold enters the proof.

$$ \phi_{\eta}(\tau;a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})=\bigl(1+b_{\mathrm{geo}}\tau\bigr)\left[\frac{\sqrt{1-a^{2}}\sqrt{1-\tau^{2}}+a\tau-b_{\mathrm{geo}}\tau}{1+b_{\mathrm{geo}}\tau}-\eta\right]. $$

#### Lemma B.3 (Scalar clipping bound).

Let $p$ be positive, let $u_{1},\dots,u_{p}\geq s\geq 0$ , and let $d\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{p}$ satisfy $S:=\mathbf{1}^{\top}d>0$ and $Q:=\|d\|_{2}^{2}>0$ . Then

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{p}u_{j}^{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{p}(u_{j}-d_{j})_{+}^{2}\geq\begin{cases}\displaystyle s^{2}S^{2}/Q,&sS\leq Q,\\[3.99994pt]
\displaystyle 2sS-Q,&sS>Q.\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

If $s=0$ , both claimed lower bounds reduce to zero and are immediate. Assume $s>0$ , and write $x_{j}:=d_{j}/s$ , $T:=\mathbf{1}^{\top}x$ , and $R:=\|x\|_{2}^{2}$ . For fixed $d\geq 0$ , the map $\varphi_{d}(t):=t^{2}-(t-d)_{+}^{2}$ is nondecreasing on $t\geq 0$ . Hence

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{p}u_{j}^{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{p}(u_{j}-d_{j})_{+}^{2}\geq s^{2}\left[p-\sum_{j=1}^{p}(1-x_{j})_{+}^{2}\right]. $$

First suppose $T\leq R$ . Let $\gamma:=T/R\leq 1$ and $w:=\gamma x$ . Then $\mathbf{1}^{\top}w=\|w\|_{2}^{2}=T^{2}/R$ . We claim

$$ p-\|w\|_{2}^{2}\geq\|(1-w)_{+}\|_{2}^{2}. $$

Indeed, using $\mathbf{1}^{\top}w=\|w\|_{2}^{2}$ ,

$$ \sum_{w_{j}\leq 1}w_{j}(1-w_{j})=\sum_{w_{j}>1}w_{j}(w_{j}-1)\geq\sum_{w_{j}>1}(w_{j}-1), $$

which is exactly the displayed inequality after expanding both sides. Since $\gamma\leq 1$ , we also have $(1-w_{j})_{+}\geq(1-x_{j})_{+}$ for every $j$ . Therefore

$$ p-\sum_{j=1}^{p}(1-x_{j})_{+}^{2}\geq T^{2}/R. $$

Multiplying by $s^{2}$ gives $s^{2}S^{2}/Q$ .

Now suppose $T>R$ . For each coordinate,

$$ 1-(1-x_{j})_{+}^{2}\geq 2x_{j}-x_{j}^{2}: $$

the two sides are equal when $x_{j}\leq 1$ , while for $x_{j}>1$ this reduces to $(x_{j}-1)^{2}\geq 0$ . Summing gives

$$ p-\sum_{j=1}^{p}(1-x_{j})_{+}^{2}\geq 2T-R. $$

Multiplying by $s^{2}$ yields $2sS-Q$ . ∎

#### Lemma B.4 (Blockwise regularized Eckart–Young bound).

Let $A\succeq 0$ be an $r\times r$ matrix with eigenvalues $s_{1}\geq\cdots\geq s_{r}=s$ , and let $D\succeq 0$ be an $r_{\star}\times r_{\star}$ matrix with eigenvalues $0\leq d_{1}\leq\cdots\leq d_{r_{\star}}$ , not all zero. For any $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r_{\star}}$ , define

$$ \mathcal{E}(A,Y,D):=\|A-YY^{\top}\|_{F}^{2}+2\langle D,Y^{\top}Y\rangle+\|D\|_{F}^{2}. $$

Set $S:=\operatorname{tr}D=\sum_{j}d_{j}$ and $Q:=\|D\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{j}d_{j}^{2}$ . Then

$$ \mathcal{E}(A,Y,D)\geq Q+\frac{r}{r_{\star}}\frac{(sS)^{2}}{Q}\quad\text{whenever }sS\leq Q, $$

and

$$ \mathcal{E}(A,Y,D)\geq 2sS-Q+\frac{r-r_{\star}}{r_{\star}}\frac{(sS)^{2}}{Q}\quad\text{whenever }sS>Q. $$

#### Proof.

Let $p:=r_{\star}$ . The objective is invariant under orthogonal changes of basis, so diagonalize $A$ and $D$ . Let $z_{1}\geq\cdots\geq z_{p}\geq 0$ be the eigenvalues of $Y^{\top}Y$ . The trace inequalities give

$$ \langle A,YY^{\top}\rangle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{p}s_{j}z_{j},\qquad\langle D,Y^{\top}Y\rangle\geq\sum_{j=1}^{p}d_{j}z_{j}, $$

where the second inequality pairs the largest $z_{j}$ ’s with the smallest eigenvalues of $D$ . Thus, for every $Y$ ,

$$ \mathcal{E}(A,Y,D)\geq Q+\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\left[z_{j}^{2}-2(s_{j}-d_{j})z_{j}\right]. $$

Minimizing the right-hand side over $z_{j}\geq 0$ gives

$$ \mathcal{E}(A,Y,D)\geq Q+\sum_{i=p+1}^{r}s_{i}^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\left[s_{j}^{2}-(s_{j}-d_{j})_{+}^{2}\right]. $$

Since $s_{i}\geq s$ , the inactive directions contribute $\sum_{i=p+1}^{r}s_{i}^{2}\geq(r-p)s^{2}$ , and Lemma B.3 applied to $u_{j}=s_{j}$ yields

$$ \mathcal{E}(A,Y,D)\geq\begin{cases}\displaystyle Q+(r-p)s^{2}+s^{2}S^{2}/Q,&sS\leq Q,\\[3.99994pt]
\displaystyle 2sS+(r-p)s^{2},&sS>Q.\end{cases} $$

Finally, Cauchy’s inequality gives $S^{2}\leq pQ$ . Hence $(r-p)s^{2}\geq\frac{r-p}{p}\frac{(sS)^{2}}{Q}$ , which proves the first regime. The same inequality also gives

$$ 2sS+(r-p)s^{2}\geq 2sS-Q+\frac{r-p}{p}\frac{(sS)^{2}}{Q}, $$

proving the second regime. ∎

#### Lemma B.5 (Admissible geometry for $(a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})$ ).

In the nontrivial case $X\neq 0$ and $Z_{\perp}\neq 0$ , the scalars $a$ and $b_{\mathrm{geo}}$ satisfy

$$ a^{2}+\frac{r}{r_{\star}}b_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}\leq 1+\bigl[(b_{\mathrm{geo}}-a)_{+}\bigr]^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

This lemma isolates the only step where the search rank $r$ enters the SOSP recovery argument. We reduce the geometry to a block decomposition, and then use the regularized Eckart–Young mechanism to extract the extra $r-r_{\star}$ degrees of freedom into an explicit coefficient $r/r_{\star}$ .

Because $a$ and $b_{\mathrm{geo}}$ are invariant under left orthogonal changes of coordinates, we may assume that the lifted factors are written in block form as

$$ X=\begin{bmatrix}X_{1}\\
0\end{bmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{bmatrix}Z_{1}\\
Z_{2}\end{bmatrix}, $$

where $X_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}$ , $Z_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r_{\star}}$ , and $Z_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-r)\times r_{\star}}$ with $n:=n_{1}+n_{2}$ . Let

$$ s_{i}:=\lambda_{i}(X_{1}X_{1}^{\top}),\qquad i=1,\dots,r, $$

and

$$ d_{i}:=\lambda_{i}(Z_{2}^{\top}Z_{2}),\qquad i=1,\dots,r_{\star}. $$

Then

$$ s_{r}=\lambda_{\min}(X^{\top}X),\qquad\|d\|_{2}=\|Z_{\perp}Z_{\perp}^{\top}\|_{F},\qquad 1^{\top}d=\operatorname{tr}(Z_{\perp}Z_{\perp}^{\top}), $$

so the two geometric scalars become

$$ a=\frac{\|d\|_{2}}{\|E\|_{F}},\qquad b_{\mathrm{geo}}=\frac{s_{r}\,1^{\top}d}{\|E\|_{F}\,\|d\|_{2}}. $$

Now expand the lifted error blockwise:

$$ \|E\|_{F}^{2}=\|X_{1}X_{1}^{\top}-Z_{1}Z_{1}^{\top}\|_{F}^{2}+2\langle Z_{2}^{\top}Z_{2},\;Z_{1}^{\top}Z_{1}\rangle+\|Z_{2}^{\top}Z_{2}\|_{F}^{2}. $$

The right-hand side is exactly $\mathcal{E}(A,Z_{1},D)$ from Lemma B.4, with

$$ A:=X_{1}X_{1}^{\top},\qquad D:=Z_{2}^{\top}Z_{2},\qquad s:=s_{r}. $$

Moreover, by Eq. (30), the regimes $b_{\mathrm{geo}}\leq a$ and $b_{\mathrm{geo}}>a$ are equivalent to $s_{r}\,\mathbf{1}^{\top}d\leq\|d\|_{2}^{2}$ and $s_{r}\,\mathbf{1}^{\top}d>\|d\|_{2}^{2}$ , respectively. Applying Lemma B.4 therefore yields

$$ \displaystyle\|E\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle\geq\frac{r}{r_{\star}}\,\frac{(s_{r}\,1^{\top}d)^{2}}{\|d\|_{2}^{2}}+\|d\|_{2}^{2}\qquad\text{when }b_{\mathrm{geo}}\leq a, \displaystyle\|E\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle\geq 2s_{r}\,1^{\top}d-\|d\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{r-r_{\star}}{r_{\star}}\,\frac{(s_{r}\,1^{\top}d)^{2}}{\|d\|_{2}^{2}}\qquad\text{when }b_{\mathrm{geo}}>a. $$

The factor $r/r_{\star}$ is thus a geometric consequence of the block decomposition: the $r-r_{\star}$ inactive singular directions of $X$ contribute extra $s_{r}^{2}$ -scale curvature, and $(1^{\top}d)^{2}\leq r_{\star}\|d\|_{2}^{2}$ converts this surplus into the same scale as the normal block.

When $b_{\mathrm{geo}}\leq a$ , dividing Eq. (31) by $\|E\|_{F}^{2}$ and using Eq. (30) gives

$$ 1\geq a^{2}+\frac{r}{r_{\star}}b_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}. $$

When $b_{\mathrm{geo}}>a$ , dividing Eq. (32) by $\|E\|_{F}^{2}$ gives

$$ 1\geq 2ab_{\mathrm{geo}}-a^{2}+\frac{r-r_{\star}}{r_{\star}}b_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}=a^{2}+\frac{r}{r_{\star}}b_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}-(b_{\mathrm{geo}}-a)^{2}. $$

Thus the first regime gives Eq. (29) with $(b_{\mathrm{geo}}-a)_{+}=0$ , and the second gives Eq. (29) with $(b_{\mathrm{geo}}-a)_{+}=b_{\mathrm{geo}}-a$ . This proves Eq. (29). ∎

#### Lemma B.6 (Positivity of the one-dimensional gain).

If

$$ \eta<\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{r_{\star}/r}}, $$

then there exists some $\tau\in[0,a]$ such that

$$ \phi_{\eta}(\tau;a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})>0. $$

#### Proof.

Introduce the ratio

$$ \delta(a,b_{\mathrm{geo}}):=\sup_{0\leq\tau\leq a}\frac{\sqrt{1-a^{2}}\sqrt{1-\tau^{2}}+a\tau-b_{\mathrm{geo}}\tau}{1+b_{\mathrm{geo}}\tau} $$

By Eq. (28), finding $\tau\in[0,a]$ with $\phi_{\eta}(\tau;a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})>0$ is equivalent to showing

$$ \delta(a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})>\eta. $$

Once Lemma B.5 is in place, the proof becomes a one-dimensional optimization over the admissible $(a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})$ -region. The required scalar maximization is the same elementary two-region reduction used in sharp overparameterization analyses [Zhang, 2025a, Lemma 5.4]; for completeness we spell out the two cases below.

If

$$ b_{\mathrm{geo}}\geq\frac{a}{1+\sqrt{1-a^{2}}}, $$

then the closed-form optimizer shows that the smallest admissible value of $\delta(a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})$ on this branch is attained on the boundary

$$ b_{\mathrm{geo}}=\frac{a}{1+\sqrt{1-a^{2}}}. $$

Thus it remains to analyze the boundary and the complementary low- $b_{\mathrm{geo}}$ branch.

If instead

$$ b_{\mathrm{geo}}\leq\frac{a}{1+\sqrt{1-a^{2}}}, $$

then in particular $b_{\mathrm{geo}}\leq a$ , so we may write

$$ a=\gamma b_{\mathrm{geo}},\qquad\gamma\geq 1. $$

Set

$$ \varrho:=\sqrt{r/r_{\star}}. $$

In this region the plus-term in Eq. (29) vanishes, and the admissible constraint becomes

$$ (\gamma^{2}+\varrho^{2})b_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}\leq 1. $$

On this branch, the scalar maximization reduces to

$$ \delta(a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})=\frac{1-2ab_{\mathrm{geo}}+b_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}}{1-b_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}}=\frac{1-(2\gamma-1)b_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}}{1-b_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}}. $$

For every fixed $\gamma\geq 1$ , this quantity is decreasing in $b_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}$ , so its minimum over the admissible region is attained when the constraint is tight:

$$ b_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}=\frac{1}{\gamma^{2}+\varrho^{2}}. $$

Substituting this value gives the one-variable function

$$ \delta(a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})\geq\frac{\gamma^{2}+\varrho^{2}-2\gamma+1}{\gamma^{2}+\varrho^{2}-1}. $$

A direct derivative computation shows that the right-hand side is minimized at

$$ \gamma=1+\varrho. $$

Evaluating there yields

$$ \delta(a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})\geq\frac{\varrho}{1+\varrho}=\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{r_{\star}/r}}. $$

Since the high- $b_{\mathrm{geo}}$ branch attains its worst value on the same boundary, this lower bound also controls the first region.

Therefore the worst admissible value of $\delta(a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})$ is

$$ \delta(a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})\geq\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{r_{\star}/r}}. $$

Hence, if $\eta<1/(1+\sqrt{r_{\star}/r})$ , there exists some $\widehat{\tau}\in[0,a]$ such that

$$ \frac{\sqrt{1-a^{2}}\sqrt{1-\widehat{\tau}^{2}}+a\widehat{\tau}-b_{\mathrm{geo}}\widehat{\tau}}{1+b_{\mathrm{geo}}\widehat{\tau}}>\eta. $$

Multiplying by $1+b_{\mathrm{geo}}\widehat{\tau}>0$ and using Eq. (28) yields

$$ \phi_{\eta}(\widehat{\tau};a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})>0. $$

∎

#### Lemma B.7 (Trivial certificate cases).

Assume $E\neq 0$ .

- 1. If $X\neq 0$ and $Z_{\perp}=0$ , then

$$ \psi_{\lambda}(1,0)\leq-m_{\mu}\|E\|_{F}^{2}<0. $$

- 2. If $X=0$ , then

$$ \psi_{\lambda}(0,1)\leq-m_{\mu}\|E\|_{F}^{2}<0. $$

#### Proof.

These two cases do not need the full rank-threshold geometry. If the error is entirely tangent to the current factor span, $D_{0}$ already detects it. If $X=0$ , the second-order probes $D_{i}$ detect the whole error. In both cases the PSD slack can be discarded in the favorable direction.

If $X\neq 0$ and $Z_{\perp}=0$ , then $E=E_{T}$ . Using Eq. (13), Eq. (18), and Eq. (23),

$$ \psi_{\lambda}(1,0)=\bigl\langle\nabla g_{\mu,\lambda}(X),D_{0}\bigr\rangle=-\bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E]+N_{\mu,\lambda},E\bigr\rangle. $$

Because $N_{\mu,\lambda}\succeq 0$ and $N_{\mu,\lambda}Z=0$ ,

$$ \langle N_{\mu,\lambda},E\rangle=\langle N_{\mu,\lambda},XX^{\top}-ZZ^{\top}\rangle=\langle N_{\mu,\lambda},XX^{\top}\rangle\geq 0. $$

Together with Eq. (16), this gives

$$ \psi_{\lambda}(1,0)\leq-\bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E],E\bigr\rangle\leq-m_{\mu}\|E\|_{F}^{2}. $$

If $X=0$ , then $E=E_{N}$ . Using Eq. (14), Eq. (18), and Eq. (24),

$$ \psi_{\lambda}(0,1)=\left\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E]+N_{\mu,\lambda},\sum_{i=1}^{r_{\star}}D_{i}D_{i}^{\top}\right\rangle=-\bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E]+N_{\mu,\lambda},E\bigr\rangle, $$

because the pointwise Hessian term vanishes when $X=0$ . The same argument yields

$$ \psi_{\lambda}(0,1)\leq-m_{\mu}\|E\|_{F}^{2}. $$

∎

#### Lemma B.8 (Nontrivial certificate upper bound).

Assume $E\neq 0$ , $X\neq 0$ , and $Z_{\perp}\neq 0$ . Then for every $\tau\in[0,a]$ ,

$$ \psi_{\lambda}\bigl(t_{1}(\tau),t_{2}(\tau)\bigr)\leq-s_{\mu}\,\phi_{\vartheta_{\mu}}(\tau;a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})\,\|E\|_{F}^{2}, $$

where $\vartheta_{\mu}=(\kappa_{\mu}-1)/(\kappa_{\mu}+1)=d_{\mu}/s_{\mu}$ .

#### Proof.

This is the nontrivial case where neither the first-order nor the second-order probe alone is guaranteed to be enough. We combine them through $F_{\tau}$ . The lower curvature bound controls the averaged term in the direction of $F_{\tau}$ , the upper curvature bound controls the pointwise Hessian terms generated by $D_{i}$ , and the PSD slack again has the right sign. The function $\phi_{\vartheta_{\mu}}$ records the net gain after these contributions are combined.

Let $\dot{E}_{i}:=D_{i}X^{\top}+XD_{i}^{\top}$ . Using Eq. (13), Eq. (14), Eq. (23), Eq. (24), and Eq. (18), we obtain

$$ \psi_{\lambda}\bigl(t_{1}(\tau),t_{2}(\tau)\bigr)=-\Bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E]+N_{\mu,\lambda},F_{\tau}\Bigr\rangle+\frac{t_{2}(\tau)}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{r_{\star}}\bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\mu,X}[\dot{E}_{i}],\dot{E}_{i}\bigr\rangle. $$

Because $N_{\mu,\lambda}\succeq 0$ and $N_{\mu,\lambda}Z=0$ , the same PSD-slack argument as above gives

$$ -\bigl\langle N_{\mu,\lambda},F_{\tau}\bigr\rangle\leq 0. $$

Also, as noted in the certificate construction, each $\dot{E}_{i}$ has admissible off-diagonal rank, so Eq. (17) yields

$$ \bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\mu,X}[\dot{E}_{i}],\dot{E}_{i}\bigr\rangle\leq L_{\mu}\|\dot{E}_{i}\|_{F}^{2}. $$

By polarization and Eq. (16),

$$ \bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E],F_{\tau}\bigr\rangle\geq s_{\mu}\langle E,F_{\tau}\rangle-d_{\mu}\|E\|_{F}^{2}. $$

Substituting this bound and Eq. (25), and using the geometric identity

$$ \frac{t_{2}(\tau)}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{r_{\star}}\|\dot{E}_{i}\|_{F}^{2}=\tau\,b_{\mathrm{geo}}\|E\|_{F}^{2}, $$

we get

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{\lambda}\bigl(t_{1}(\tau),t_{2}(\tau)\bigr) \displaystyle\leq-\Bigl[s_{\mu}\bigl(\sqrt{1-a^{2}}\sqrt{1-\tau^{2}}+a\tau\bigr)-d_{\mu}\Bigr]\|E\|_{F}^{2}+L_{\mu}\tau b_{\mathrm{geo}}\|E\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle=-s_{\mu}\,\phi_{\vartheta_{\mu}}(\tau;a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})\,\|E\|_{F}^{2}. $$

∎

#### Proof of Theorem 4.2.

Assume toward contradiction that $E=XX^{\top}-ZZ^{\top}\neq 0$ .

Second-order stationarity implies that every nonnegative combination of the certificates above must be nonnegative. The lemmas show that, under the rank condition, every possible nonzero shape of $E$ admits one certificate that is strictly negative. This contradiction is the recovery argument.

If $X=0$ , then Lemma B.7(2) gives

$$ \psi_{\lambda}(0,1)<0, $$

contradicting Eq. (27).

If $X\neq 0$ but $Z_{\perp}=0$ , then Lemma B.7(1) gives

$$ \psi_{\lambda}(1,0)<0, $$

again contradicting Eq. (27).

It remains to consider the nontrivial case $X\neq 0$ and $Z_{\perp}\neq 0$ . Since the main text fixes $\mu=\alpha_{k}/2$ , the lifted curvature ratio satisfies

$$ \vartheta_{\mu}=\frac{\kappa_{\mu}-1}{\kappa_{\mu}+1}=\frac{\beta_{k}-\alpha_{k}}{\beta_{k}}. $$

The rank condition in Theorem 4.2 is equivalent to

$$ \vartheta_{\mu}<\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{r_{\star}/r}}, $$

so Lemma B.6 gives some $\tau\in[0,a]$ such that

$$ \phi_{\vartheta_{\mu}}(\tau;a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})>0. $$

Applying Lemma B.8 at this $\tau$ yields

$$ \psi_{\lambda}\bigl(t_{1}(\tau),t_{2}(\tau)\bigr)\leq-s_{\mu}\,\phi_{\vartheta_{\mu}}(\tau;a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})\,\|E\|_{F}^{2}<0, $$

contradicting Eq. (27). Therefore $E=0$ .

Hence

$$ XX^{\top}=ZZ^{\top}. $$

Taking the $(1,2)$ -block gives

$$ UV^{\top}=U_{\star}V_{\star}^{\top}=M_{\star}^{\lambda}. $$

Moreover, $XX^{\top}=ZZ^{\top}$ implies that $X=ZR$ for some matrix $R\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{\star}\times r}$ with $RR^{\top}=I_{r_{\star}}$ . Hence $U=U_{\star}R$ and $V=V_{\star}R$ , so $U^{\top}U=V^{\top}V$ and

$$ \frac{1}{2}\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)=\|M_{\star}^{\lambda}\|_{*}. $$

Thus the factor pair attains

$$ h_{\mu,\lambda}(U,V)=\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})+\lambda\|M_{\star}^{\lambda}\|_{*}=F_{\lambda}(M_{\star}^{\lambda}), $$

which is the global infimum for $F_{\lambda}(M)$ in Assumption 3.1. Therefore $(U,V)$ is globally optimal. ∎

#### B.3.2 General balancing weights

The preceding certificate argument also yields an explicit rank condition for any balancing weight in $0<\mu<\alpha_{k}$ . We record this extension using the lifted curvature constants introduced above.

#### Corollary B.9 (SOSP recovery for general balancing weights).

Suppose Assumption 3.1 holds with $1\leq r_{\star}\leq r$ and $\lambda>0$ . Let $0<\alpha_{k}<\beta_{k}<\infty$ , fix $0<\mu<\alpha_{k}$ , and set

$$ m_{\mu}:=2\min\{\mu,\alpha_{k}-\mu\},\qquad L_{\mu}:=2\max\{\mu,\beta_{k}-\mu\},\qquad\kappa_{\mu}:=\frac{L_{\mu}}{m_{\mu}}. $$

Every SOSP $(U,V)$ of $h_{\mu,\lambda}$ whose product $M=UV^{\top}$ satisfies Assumption 4.1 with these constants and $k\geq r+r_{\star}$ is globally optimal and satisfies $UV^{\top}=M_{\star}^{\lambda}$ whenever

$$ \frac{r}{r_{\star}}>\left(\frac{\kappa_{\mu}-1}{2}\right)^{2}. $$

Moreover, the corresponding stacked factors satisfy $XX^{\top}=ZZ^{\top}$ .

#### Proof.

For $0<\mu<\alpha_{k}$ , the lifted curvature bounds Eq. (16)–Eq. (17) hold with $m_{\mu}>0$ , and the KKT slack in Lemma B.2 remains positive semidefinite. Put $t:=\sqrt{r_{\star}/r}>0$ . Since $\kappa_{\mu}\geq 1$ , Eq. (34) is equivalent to

$$ (\kappa_{\mu}-1)t<2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\vartheta_{\mu}:=\frac{\kappa_{\mu}-1}{\kappa_{\mu}+1}<\frac{1}{1+t}. $$

If an SOSP had $E=XX^{\top}-ZZ^{\top}\neq 0$ , Lemma B.7 would give a strictly negative certificate when $X=0$ or $Z_{\perp}=0$ . In the remaining case, Lemma B.6 gives a $\tau\in[0,a]$ with $\phi_{\vartheta_{\mu}}(\tau;a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})>0$ , and Lemma B.8 yields

$$ \psi_{\lambda}\bigl(t_{1}(\tau),t_{2}(\tau)\bigr)\leq-s_{\mu}\phi_{\vartheta_{\mu}}(\tau;a,b_{\mathrm{geo}})\|E\|_{F}^{2}<0,\qquad s_{\mu}:=\frac{L_{\mu}+m_{\mu}}{2}>0. $$

Both cases contradict Eq. (27). Hence $E=0$ , and balanced recovery and global optimality follow exactly as in the concluding step of the preceding theorem proof. ∎

For the main-text choice $\mu=\alpha_{k}/2$ , these constants reduce to

$$ m_{\mu}=\alpha_{k},\qquad L_{\mu}=2\beta_{k}-\alpha_{k},\qquad\frac{\kappa_{\mu}-1}{2}=\frac{\beta_{k}-\alpha_{k}}{\alpha_{k}}=\frac{2\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}}{1-\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}}. $$

Thus Eq. (34) recovers the main-text rank condition Eq. (6). Proposition 4.3 and the transfer argument below also apply to this general- $\mu$ guarantee.

### B.4 Proofs for the Transfer to Standard LoRA

#### Proof of Proposition 4.3.

Let $M:=UV^{\top}$ and $G:=\nabla\widehat{L}(M)$ . First-order stationarity of $\widetilde{h}_{\lambda}$ gives

$$ GV+\lambda U=0,\qquad G^{\top}U+\lambda V=0. $$

Left-multiplying these equations by $U^{\top}$ and $V^{\top}$ , respectively, and subtracting yields

$$ U^{\top}GV-V^{\top}G^{\top}U+\lambda(U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V)=0. $$

If $A:=U^{\top}GV$ , then the first term is $A-A^{\top}$ , which is skew-symmetric, whereas $U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V$ is symmetric. Their sum is zero, so both terms must vanish. Hence

$$ U^{\top}U=V^{\top}V. $$

Now define

$$ R(U,V):=\frac{1}{4}\|U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V\|_{F}^{2},\qquad h_{\mu,\lambda}=\widetilde{h}_{\lambda}+\mu R. $$

At every balanced point, $R(U,V)=0$ , so $(U,V)$ is a global minimizer of the nonnegative $C^{2}$ function $R$ . Therefore

$$ \nabla R(U,V)=0,\qquad\nabla^{2}R(U,V)\succeq 0. $$

If $(U,V)$ is an SOSP of $\widetilde{h}_{\lambda}$ , then adding $\mu R$ preserves both first-order stationarity and second-order nonnegativity. Thus $(U,V)$ is also an SOSP of $h_{\mu,\lambda}$ for every $\mu\geq 0$ . ∎

#### Proof of Corollary 4.4.

Fix the same parameter $\mu\in(0,\alpha_{k})$ as in Theorem 4.2. By Proposition 4.3, every SOSP of the standard LoRA objective Eq. (1) is also an SOSP of the balanced objective Eq. (2). Theorem 4.2 therefore gives

$$ UV^{\top}=M_{\star}^{\lambda}. $$

At this point, the balancing penalty vanishes, so

$$ \widetilde{h}_{\lambda}(U,V)=\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})+\frac{\lambda}{2}\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)=\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})+\lambda\|M_{\star}^{\lambda}\|_{*}, $$

where the last equality follows from the balanced square-root characterization of $M_{\star}^{\lambda}$ . Hence the standard LoRA factor pair attains the same value as the optimal rank-constrained matrix-space problem, so it is globally optimal for the standard LoRA objective as well. ∎

## Appendix C Additional Proofs for Section 5

This appendix section follows the notation of Section 5. The empirical distribution $\nu$ over supervised prediction instances defines $\widehat{L}_{\nu}$ . We first specify the certificate region and admissible family underlying the data-side bounds, then derive the cross-entropy identities and curvature certificate. Recall that $x$ denotes a supervised prediction instance induced by the original examples, $z_{x}(M)$ is the model’s pre-softmax logit vector for this instance, $p_{x}(M)=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{x}(M))$ is the predicted probability vector, and $q_{x}$ is the target probability vector. We also write

$$ Q_{\nu}(M,H):=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\|P_{\perp}A_{x,M}[H]\|_{2}^{2} $$

for the projected, unweighted coverage form.

### C.1 Certificate Region and Admissible Family

Fix the empirical distribution $\nu$ , search rank $r$ , and a regularized target $M_{\nu,\star}^{\lambda}$ from Assumption 3.1, with $r_{\nu,\star}=\operatorname{rank}(M_{\nu,\star}^{\lambda})\leq r$ . Let

$$ \mathcal{M}_{r}:=\{M\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}:\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r\}. $$

The certificate region collects the target–candidate segments in Assumption 4.1:

$$ \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{cert}}(\nu,r):=\bigl\{(1-t)M_{\nu,\star}^{\lambda}+tM:M\in\mathcal{M}_{r},\ t\in[0,1]\bigr\}. $$

For $k\geq r+r_{\nu,\star}$ , define the admissible family

$$ \mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r):=\left\{\begin{aligned} (\widetilde{M},H):\ &\widetilde{M}\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{cert}}(\nu,r),\\
&H\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}},\quad\operatorname{rank}(H)\leq k,\quad\|H\|_{F}=1\end{aligned}\right\}. $$

Thus the matrix points include both endpoints and the full intervening segments, while $H$ ranges over all unit rank-at-most- $k$ directions. The segment points can have rank up to $r+r_{\nu,\star}$ , even though each candidate update has rank at most $r$ . For a candidate-specific application, the same definitions may be restricted to the single segment joining that candidate to the target; the resulting bounds then apply to that candidate. Unless stated otherwise, the quantities below use the full family $\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)$ defined above.

The coverage bounds and nonlinear residual bound are

$$ \displaystyle c_{\nu,k} \displaystyle:=\inf_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}Q_{\nu}(M,H),\qquad C_{\nu,k}:=\sup_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}Q_{\nu}(M,H), \displaystyle\rho_{\nu,k} \displaystyle:=\sup_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}|R_{\nu}(M,H)|. $$

To define the softmax-weighting bounds, set

$$ \mathcal{T}_{k}^{+}(\nu,r):=\{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r):Q_{\nu}(M,H)>0\}. $$

Whenever this set is nonempty, let

$$ \omega_{\nu,k}^{-}:=\inf_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}_{k}^{+}(\nu,r)}\frac{G_{\nu}(M,H)}{Q_{\nu}(M,H)},\qquad\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}:=\sup_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}_{k}^{+}(\nu,r)}\frac{G_{\nu}(M,H)}{Q_{\nu}(M,H)}. $$

All extrema are understood as infima or suprema; attainment is not required. Their dependence on $r$ through the admissible family is suppressed in the subscripts, as in the main text. The data-side certificate is invoked when

$$ 0<c_{\nu,k}\leq C_{\nu,k}<\infty,\qquad 0<\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}\leq\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}<\infty,\qquad\rho_{\nu,k}<\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}. $$

In particular, $c_{\nu,k}>0$ implies $\mathcal{T}_{k}^{+}(\nu,r)=\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)$ , so all directional ratios used in the certificate are well-defined. The proof in Appendix C.3 then supplies uniform restricted curvature bounds on these same target–candidate segments.

### C.2 Cross-Entropy Hessian Decomposition

#### Proposition C.1 (Cross-entropy Hessian).

Let $z_{x}(M)\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$ be the pre-softmax logits for supervised instance $x$ , let $p_{x}(M):=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{x}(M))$ be the predicted probabilities, and let $q_{x}\in\Delta^{K-1}$ be the target probabilities. Define

$$ \ell_{x}(M):=-\langle q_{x},\log p_{x}(M)\rangle. $$

For any matrix direction $H$ , define the first- and second-order logit responses

$$ A_{x,M}[H]:=Dz_{x}(M)[H],\qquad\mathcal{B}_{x,M}[H,H]:=D^{2}z_{x}(M)[H,H], $$

and define the softmax covariance matrix $\Omega_{x}(M):=\operatorname{Diag}(p_{x}(M))-p_{x}(M)p_{x}(M)^{\top}$ . Then

$$ D^{2}\ell_{x}(M)[H,H]=\langle A_{x,M}[H],\Omega_{x}(M)A_{x,M}[H]\rangle+\langle p_{x}(M)-q_{x},\mathcal{B}_{x,M}[H,H]\rangle. $$

Consequently,

$$ \langle\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}_{\nu}(M)[H],H\rangle=G_{\nu}(M,H)+R_{\nu}(M,H), $$

with $G_{\nu}$ and $R_{\nu}$ as defined in Section 5.

#### Proof.

For $\phi(z,q):=-\langle q,\log\operatorname{softmax}(z)\rangle$ , one has

$$ \nabla_{z}\phi(z,q)=p-q,\qquad\nabla_{z}^{2}\phi(z,q)=\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^{\top}. $$

Applying the second-order chain rule to $\ell_{x}(M)=\phi(z_{x}(M),q_{x})$ gives the displayed identity. Since $\Omega_{x}(M)\mathbf{1}=0$ , common shifts of all logits are ignored by the Gauss–Newton term. Averaging over $x\sim\nu$ gives the identity for $\widehat{L}_{\nu}$ . ∎

### C.3 Proof of the Data-Side Curvature Certificate

We derive the conservative LoRA-RIP certificate used in Eq. (9). Fix an admissible pair $(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)$ . Since $\|H\|_{F}=1$ , the definitions in Appendix C.1 give

$$ c_{\nu,k}\leq Q_{\nu}(M,H)\leq C_{\nu,k}. $$

Moreover, the data-side restricted curvature condition in Section 5.1 gives $c_{\nu,k}>0$ , so every admissible pair has $Q_{\nu}(M,H)\geq c_{\nu,k}>0$ . The ratios defining $\omega_{\nu,k}^{\pm}$ are therefore well-defined on this family, and

$$ \omega_{\nu,k}^{-}Q_{\nu}(M,H)\leq G_{\nu}(M,H)\leq\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}Q_{\nu}(M,H). $$

Hence

$$ \omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}\leq G_{\nu}(M,H)\leq\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}. $$

Together with $|R_{\nu}(M,H)|\leq\rho_{\nu,k}$ , the Hessian decomposition in Proposition C.1 implies

$$ \omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}-\rho_{\nu,k}\leq\langle\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}_{\nu}(M)[H],H\rangle\leq\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}+\rho_{\nu,k}. $$

By homogeneity, the same bounds hold for non-unit directions after multiplying by $\|H\|_{F}^{2}$ . Therefore the data induce valid restricted curvature constants

$$ \alpha_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{CE}}=\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}-\rho_{\nu,k},\qquad\beta_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{CE}}=\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}+\rho_{\nu,k}. $$

Substituting these constants into the symmetric LoRA-RIP normalization $(\beta-\alpha)/(\beta+\alpha)$ gives

$$ \delta_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}\leq\overline{\delta}_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}=\frac{\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}-\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}+2\rho_{\nu,k}}{\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}+\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}}, $$

which is Eq. (9). Plugging this conservative value into Theorem 4.2 yields the rank budget stated in the main text.

### C.4 Mode Imbalance and Duplicate Sampling

#### Proposition C.2 (Group mass controls coverage conditioning).

A group mixture means the following two-stage sampling distribution: first choose a group $g\in\{1,\ldots,G\}$ with probability $\pi_{g}$ , and then draw $x\sim\nu_{g}$ . Equivalently, $\nu_{\pi}=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\pi_{g}\nu_{g}$ . Let $\mathcal{T}$ be the admissible comparison family for the mixture, for example $\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu_{\pi},r)$ . For every fixed $(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}$ ,

$$ Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\pi_{g}Q_{\nu_{g}}(M,H),\qquad G_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\pi_{g}G_{\nu_{g}}(M,H). $$

Let $(M_{+},H_{+})\in\mathcal{T}$ be a direction strongly excited by group $g_{+}$ , and define

$$ U_{+}:=Q_{\nu_{g_{+}}}(M_{+},H_{+}). $$

Let $(M_{-},H_{-})\in\mathcal{T}$ be a direction that is weakly covered under the mixture. For a possibly different group $g_{-}$ , define its weak-direction contribution and the leakage from the other groups by

$$ L_{-}:=Q_{\nu_{g_{-}}}(M_{-},H_{-}),\qquad\varepsilon_{-}(\pi):=\sum_{j\neq g_{-}}\pi_{j}Q_{\nu_{j}}(M_{-},H_{-}). $$

The leakage term $\varepsilon_{-}(\pi)$ is small when the groups are well separated in their projected logit-response directions. Then

$$ \sup_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}}Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)\geq\pi_{g_{+}}U_{+},\qquad\inf_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}}Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)\leq Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M_{-},H_{-})=\pi_{g_{-}}L_{-}+\varepsilon_{-}(\pi). $$

Consequently, if the denominator below is positive,

$$ \frac{\sup_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}}Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)}{\inf_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}}Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)}\geq\frac{\pi_{g_{+}}U_{+}}{\pi_{g_{-}}L_{-}+\varepsilon_{-}(\pi)}. $$

In words, a dataset can have poor coverage conditioning when too much mass is concentrated on a mode that already gives large coverage response, while another mode receives too little mass and is not covered by the remaining groups. Duplicate samples are the limiting case in which one mode is a single atom: they reinforce the projected logit-response directions excited by that atom rather than increasing coverage uniformly.

#### Proof.

Linearity of expectation gives

$$ Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)=\sum_{j=1}^{G}\pi_{j}Q_{\nu_{j}}(M,H),\qquad G_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)=\sum_{j=1}^{G}\pi_{j}G_{\nu_{j}}(M,H). $$

Evaluating the $Q$ -identity at $(M_{+},H_{+})$ and using nonnegativity gives the upper-side bound. Evaluating it at $(M_{-},H_{-})$ gives $\inf_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}}Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)\leq Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M_{-},H_{-})=\pi_{g_{-}}L_{-}+\varepsilon_{-}(\pi)$ . The ratio bound follows by combining the two inequalities. ∎

### C.5 Gradient-Sketch Proxy for Experiments

At a fixed operating point $M_{0}$ , the Gauss–Newton term can be viewed as a covariance on vectorized LoRA-update directions after they pass through the logit Jacobian. If $h=\operatorname{vec}(H)$ and $J_{x,M_{0}}$ is the matrix of the linear map $H\mapsto\Omega_{x}(M_{0})^{1/2}A_{x,M_{0}}[H]$ , then

$$ G_{\nu}(M_{0},H)=h^{\top}\left(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\nu}J_{x,M_{0}}^{\top}J_{x,M_{0}}\right)h. $$

Thus any low-dimensional sketch that preserves the main modes of the logit Jacobian gives an empirical proxy for the weighted coverage spectrum. The gradient groups used in Section 6 should be read in this sense: they cluster examples by a margin-Jacobian sketch at a shared reference point. These sketches are not estimates of the exact constants $c_{\nu,k}$ , $C_{\nu,k}$ , or $\omega_{\nu,k}^{\pm}$ , but they are aligned with the directions that enter the data-side certificate.

### C.6 Directional Softmax Saturation and Curvature Leverage

#### Proposition C.3 (Softmax covariance as variance).

For $p\in\Delta^{K-1}$ , $\Omega(p):=\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^{\top}$ , and any $u\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$ ,

$$ u^{\top}\Omega(p)u=\sum_{c=1}^{K}p_{c}u_{c}^{2}-\left(\sum_{c=1}^{K}p_{c}u_{c}\right)^{2}=\min_{a\in\mathbb{R}}\sum_{c=1}^{K}p_{c}(u_{c}-a)^{2}. $$

In particular, $\Omega(p)\mathbf{1}=0$ , so only centered logit perturbations contribute to Gauss–Newton curvature.

#### Proof.

The first equality is the usual variance identity under a categorical distribution with probabilities $p$ . The minimizing constant is $a=\sum_{c}p_{c}u_{c}$ . The identity $\Omega(p)\mathbf{1}=0$ follows immediately from the definition of $\Omega(p)$ . ∎

#### Proposition C.4 (Easy examples have limited Gauss–Newton leverage).

For $p\in\Delta^{K-1}$ , let $p_{\max}=1-\delta$ with $\delta\in[0,1]$ . Then

$$ \lambda_{\max}(\Omega(p))\leq\operatorname{tr}(\Omega(p))=1-\|p\|_{2}^{2}\leq 2\delta-\delta^{2}. $$

Consequently, for the single-example Gauss–Newton contribution

$$ G_{x}(M,H):=\langle A_{x,M}[H],\Omega_{x}(M)A_{x,M}[H]\rangle, $$

we have

$$ G_{x}(M,H)\leq(2\delta_{x}-\delta_{x}^{2})\|A_{x,M}[H]\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\delta_{x}:=1-\max_{c}p_{x,c}(M). $$

Thus a highly confident example cannot contribute much softmax-side Gauss–Newton curvature unless its logit-Jacobian response along the direction is large.

#### Proof.

Since $\Omega(p)$ is positive semidefinite, $\lambda_{\max}(\Omega(p))\leq\operatorname{tr}(\Omega(p))$ . The trace identity follows from $\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^{\top})=\sum_{c}p_{c}-\sum_{c}p_{c}^{2}=1-\|p\|_{2}^{2}$ . If $p_{\max}=1-\delta$ , then $\|p\|_{2}^{2}\geq(1-\delta)^{2}$ , which gives the final inequality. Applying the operator-norm bound to $u=A_{x,M}[H]$ proves the single-example claim. ∎

#### Proposition C.5 (Directional saturation decomposition).

For any admissible $(M,H)$ with $Q_{\nu}(M,H)>0$ , define

$$ \sigma_{\nu}(M,H):=G_{\nu}(M,H)/Q_{\nu}(M,H). $$

Then $G_{\nu}(M,H)=\sigma_{\nu}(M,H)Q_{\nu}(M,H)$ , and hence

$$ \displaystyle\inf_{\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}G_{\nu}(M,H) \displaystyle=\inf_{\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}\sigma_{\nu}(M,H)Q_{\nu}(M,H), \displaystyle\sup_{\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}G_{\nu}(M,H) \displaystyle=\sup_{\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}\sigma_{\nu}(M,H)Q_{\nu}(M,H). $$

In a binary-margin parameterization, let $m_{x}(M):=z_{x,1}(M)-z_{x,2}(M)$ , let $\phi_{x,M}$ be the Frobenius-Riesz representative of the linear map $H\mapsto Dm_{x}(M)[H]$ , and set $s_{x}(M):=p_{x,1}(M)p_{x,2}(M)$ . Then this becomes the scalar-weighted covariance form

$$ G_{\nu}(M,H)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\bigl[s_{x}(M)\langle\phi_{x,M},H\rangle^{2}\bigr],\qquad Q_{\nu}(M,H)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\langle\phi_{x,M},H\rangle^{2}, $$

for a softmax saturation weight $s_{x}(M)\geq 0$ . If $\sigma_{\nu}(M,H)$ is approximately constant over theorem-relevant directions, it mostly rescales both Gauss–Newton curvature extremes and does not improve the pure Gauss–Newton ratio. Directional saturation improves this curvature ratio only when the weighted mass increases the weak-direction floor more than it increases the ceiling.

#### Proof.

The first two identities are definitions. The binary-margin identities follow from Proposition C.3. For $K=2$ ,

$$ P_{\perp}A_{x,M}[H]=\frac{1}{2}Dm_{x}(M)[H]\begin{bmatrix}1\\
-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad\|P_{\perp}A_{x,M}[H]\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(Dm_{x}(M)[H]\bigr)^{2}, $$

which explains the factor $1/2$ in $Q_{\nu}$ under the centered-logit normalization used throughout the paper. The Gauss–Newton form retains the weight $s_{x}=p_{x,1}p_{x,2}$ . The final statement follows by comparing the pure Gauss–Newton ratio: a nearly constant $\sigma_{\nu}$ cancels in this ratio, whereas direction-dependent $\sigma_{\nu}$ changes the ratio according to where it places weighted curvature mass. ∎

## Appendix D Additional Experimental Details

This appendix records the protocols and full result tables for the rank sweeps and MNLI data interventions in Section 6. These tables report controlled single-seed runs. Appendix E presents multi-seed evaluations, landscape diagnostics, and robustness checks, with the settings specified for each study.

### D.1 Shared Protocol

The MNLI/MPNet and CIFAR-100/ViT rank sweeps and MNLI data interventions use a controlled probe-then-LoRA protocol. We first train a linear classification head on the frozen backbone, and then keep this head fixed while fine-tuning only the pre-specified LoRA module. This is related to linear-probing-then-fine-tuning protocols, but differs from variants that continue updating the classification head during the fine-tuning stage [Tomihari and Sato, 2024]. We keep the head fixed to isolate the effect of the LoRA update itself and keep the experiment close to the single-trainable-block setting analyzed in the main text. For the experiments in this appendix, unless stated otherwise, we use weight decay $\lambda_{A}=\lambda_{B}=10^{-4}$ , balancing coefficient $\mu=10^{-4}$ , learning rate $10^{-4}$ , and the initialization scheme in which the $A$ -factor is Kaiming initialized with scale $0.01$ and the $B$ -factor is initialized to zero. The train/validation split uses seed $17$ , and the tables in this appendix use optimization seed $0$ . We use Adam with explicit weight decay for these runs. The diagnostic and robustness studies specify their seeds and protocol differences in Appendix E.

### D.4 Gradient-Coverage Construction

The MNLI coverage experiment changes the data distribution without changing the subset size or label budget. The candidate pool is sampled once from MNLI train, and the final coverage proxy is defined by a gradient sketch with respect to the adapted matrix:

- 1. Use the frozen MPNet backbone and the trained linear-probe head as a shared reference point.

- 2. For each candidate example, choose the gold label and the strongest alternative label, and backpropagate the corresponding margin logit to the target query matrix.

- 3. Randomly project the activation and gradient-output factors to $16\times 16$ , producing a $256$ -dimensional bilinear sketch of the margin-Jacobian feature.

- 4. Normalize the sketches and cluster them within each label into eight groups, giving 24 label-conditioned gradient groups.

- 5. Draw no-replacement subsets of $17{,}526$ examples with the same label budget $(5847,5788,5891)$ but different mass over these gradient groups.

The conditions are a balanced distribution with uniform mass over the eight groups within each label, and two geometric long-tail conditions with decay factors $0.75$ and $0.45$ . Figure D.1 shows the resulting group masses.

### D.5 Saturation-Band Construction and Results

The saturation-band experiment uses the same MNLI candidate pool and the same 24 label-conditioned gradient groups as the coverage experiment, but keeps the quota for every label–gradient group fixed. It therefore changes which examples are selected inside each group, rather than changing the mass assigned to the groups themselves. For each example, let $p_{\rm gold}$ be the model probability of the gold label and let $p_{\rm alt}$ be the largest non-gold class probability. We compute the pairwise softmax-curvature score

$$ p_{\rm pair}=\frac{p_{\rm gold}}{p_{\rm gold}+p_{\rm alt}},\qquad s=p_{\rm pair}(1-p_{\rm pair}). $$

This reduces the multiclass prediction to the gold label versus its strongest competitor. In this pairwise view, if $m_{x}(M)$ is the corresponding logit margin, the Gauss–Newton contribution has the form

$$ G_{\nu}(M,H)\approx\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[s\,\bigl(Dm_{x}(M)[H]\bigr)^{2}\right]. $$

Thus $s$ is the softmax-side curvature weight, while $Dm_{x}(M)[H]$ determines the LoRA direction receiving that curvature. Within each fixed label–gradient group, we draw no-replacement examples from one of three quantile bands: easy, middle, and boundary. ## Appendix E Landscape Diagnostics and Robustness Evaluations

This section examines the optimization geometry and stability of LoRA fine-tuning through rank/checkpoint curvature, ambient matrix-space references, and multi-seed training. We also study the effects of data composition at a common reference point and along training trajectories, evaluate coverage across datasets, backbones, and adapter locations, and examine confidence-band selection on MNLI. The rank-sweep and MNLI data-intervention protocols are described in Appendix D.

Together, these evaluations connect rank-dependent optimization gains to data-induced geometry and the practical effectiveness of landscape-guided selection.

### E.1 Shared diagnostic protocol

Unless stated otherwise, the diagnostics use MPNet-base on MNLI, a frozen linear-probe head, a frozen backbone, and a LoRA update on the layer-10 query projection. Every coverage condition contains $17{,}526$ unique training examples with label counts $5{,}847/5{,}788/5{,}891$ . The shared data-aligned diagnostic basis has dimension $24$ and is obtained from the eight gradient-sketch groups within each of the three labels. Each ambient direction represented by this basis has rank at most $16$ . The data-condition diagnostics use $512$ examples per label and three diagnostic-sample seeds.

The rank/checkpoint diagnostic uses ranks $4,64,128,256$ , optimization seeds $0,1,2$ , and start, middle, and final checkpoints (epochs $0,5,10$ ). It evaluates projected logit-Jacobian and CE-Hessian actions in the same $24$ -dimensional basis. These actions are estimated by symmetric finite differences; a step-size check changes the projected matrices by at most $1.9\%$ and does not change the reported full-Hessian sign counts. Factor regularization and balancing Hessians are excluded when the ambient update $M$ is studied.

The data-condition diagnostic instead computes exact logit-JVP Gauss–Newton matrices and exact directional CE-HVPs in the common basis. The zero-update table uses the shared frozen probe point; the trajectory analysis evaluates matched rank- $16$ checkpoints from the three training seeds. The reported means and standard deviations are over the three independent diagnostic or training seeds, as appropriate.

#### Theoretical constants and empirical diagnostics.

We do not directly compute exact values of $\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}$ , $r_{\star}$ , $c_{\nu,k}$ , $C_{\nu,k}$ , $\omega_{\nu,k}^{\pm}$ , or $\rho_{\nu,k}$ . These quantities parameterize structural guarantees, rather than serving as per-run statistics. In classical matrix sensing and low-rank optimization, RIP relates measurement geometry to recovery and landscape guarantees [Recht et al., 2010, Ge et al., 2017, Zhang et al., 2021, Zhang, 2025b]. Its primary value in our framework is likewise the relationship it establishes between data geometry and rank requirements, not an isolated numerical constant for a particular run.

Exact certification is already computationally difficult for a fixed linear compressed-sensing matrix: the condition controls singular values across all supports of a prescribed size, and computing optimal RIP constants is NP-hard in general [Tillmann and Pfetsch, 2014]. Hardness also extends to approximate RIP certification [Weed, 2018]. For LoRA, the defining curvature bounds require uniform control over the continuous family of target-to-update segments and all admissible low-rank directions. Evaluating selected checkpoints in a diagnostic subspace does not compute these extrema. Likewise, determining $r_{\star}$ requires identifying a global minimizer of the nonlinear regularized matrix-space objective $F_{\lambda}$ and certifying its rank. Local optimization does not establish global optimality or uniqueness; $r_{\star}$ refers to the low-rank target specified in our assumption. The matrix-space references and threshold or energy ranks reported below describe numerical solutions, not certified global targets.

The informative consequence of the analysis is how these quantities interact: The sufficient condition permits larger LoRA-RIP values at larger ranks, while coverage, softmax weighting, and nonlinear residual curvature enter the data-side certificate in explicit ways. Our experiments examine these mechanisms through controlled rank and data interventions, attained objectives, projected GN and CE-Hessian spectra, and multi-seed performance comparisons. The projected spectra characterize local geometry, rather than the theorem’s uniform LoRA-RIP constant. Lower attained objectives at larger ranks and the changes in geometry and performance under coverage and confidence-band selection provide complementary, qualitative evidence for the rank–data relationship developed by the theory.

## Appendix F Limitations

Our theoretical analysis focuses on single-matrix LoRA fine-tuning with cross-entropy loss under low-rank target and LoRA-RIP assumptions. The resulting rank bounds are sufficient rather than necessary, leaving room for tighter characterizations of the relationship between adapter rank and data-induced geometry. Our empirical evaluation examines this relationship through controlled classification experiments across datasets and backbones. Extending the theory to joint multi-layer adaptation and evaluating the data-selection principles in larger-scale generative fine-tuning are natural directions for future work.
